THE NATIONAL SUPPLY .OF NITROMEN,—Y9II will be pleased to hear that there is a good prospect of the abate- ment of the difficulty of procuring supplies of ammonia for agriculture in this country. In the report of Mr. R. Angus Smith, the inspector under the Alkali Acts which his Just been published, I find the following agreeable intelligence: I mentioned the enormous value of the ammonia alone obtainable from the 15,000,000 tons of coal now made into coke if the process said tc; be so successful at Besseges should be found successful here. If we were to treat all the coal used in this country in the same way we should have above six times as much ammonia, which would be capable of in- creasing our crops by £50,000,000 sterling of value." Since I received this report I have heard that the process is worked by the Great Western Railway Company. The inspector is no enthusiast, but a practical man of science, so that I hope the doleful anticipations of those who think that Nature has worked herself out, in an agriculture sense, in our pleasant islands may not be realised but reversed.—Gold Clay in Agricultural Gazette. WHY THE EGGS DON'T HATCEL—Yea, why they fre- quently fail to hatch has puzzled ,even our oldest breeders frequently, and the troublearises from a multitude of causes, some of which we will call attention to, so breeders can in- veatigate the matter themselves, One great muse of infer- tile eggs _rests with the male bird, owing to a want of stamina or to exposure, or overfeeding. It may, also, be constitutional, for we have seen birds which gave every evi- dence of power, strength, and health, which proved useless in the breeding pens, the trouble being inherited in an in- tensified degree. This is a point which is seldom thought of. Too many hens to a cock often produces the same un- desirable results, while overfeeding both the cock and the hens produces consequent sluggishness and inability to pro- duce fertile eggs. Really good and fertile eggs may be in- jured by a sudden jar, by being chilled or overheated, or by being handled too much and too roughly. If a good hatch is desired, none but the freshest eggs should be selected, and these from stock known to possess the requisite amount of stamina, while Oily ehould be handled just as little as possi- ble and as carefully as can be done. Even after the eggs have been set, they are still liable to injury in many ways, and the adage "don't count your chickens before they are hatched," is a very trite one. The hen may be a restless one, and may take a fancy to leave her nest at the most critical time, leaving the hens to chill, and thus destroy the young birds; or she may be clumsy, as many of the Asia- tics are, and in tumbling in and out of her nest destroy a few of the eggs, the contents of which coat over and render worthless the remainder. Two hens May seek to share the honours of one nest, to the neglect, perhaps for only a single day, of the other nest, and a nest of choice eggs may be lost in this way. Owing to being set in a very dry place, with a dry nest of straw or other material raised up so as to crin- stantly become still drier, aided by the heat from the hen, many of the young chicks are unable to leave the shell, the surrounding skin (of the egg) becomes harsh and dry, ad- hering to the young chick and effectually imprisoning it until it is smothered to death. By making the nests on the ground, or using a , fresh sod in the bottom of the nesting box, as well as by sprinkling the eggs with tepid water two or three times during the process of incubation, generally remedies this evil.—Poultry Monthly. SELF HELY IN Aamcnrarrau.=-It may fairly be asked- What 'is Agricalture doing, through its leaders, to hell it, self? A belief has repeatedly been expressed in these columns that Parliamentary assistance is not likely to save us—if for no other reason' because it will be so long in reaching us that the " sick man" will have "gone over to the majority" before the wounds can be bound up by the Legislature, or oil and wine be poured in. As to the help_ the season may bring, it is of no use here to dwell on that. Yet it may be gratefully acknowledged that the weather of 1581 has been, so far, singularly well adapted to help the removal of some of the worst of our drawbacks—such as sodden soils, a plague of grubs and slugs, the offspring of wet, and conch-grass and other fleshy-rooted weeds. But, besides clearing out rubbish from the land, men's brains need clearing too. How many exploded prejudices have to be got rid of—how much receptiveness needs to be cultivated before any new suggestion can take root and thrive! Our principal sources of new ideas are the press and the public exhibitions. Of the action of the former it is best to say nothing here. "Who tells most lies ?" asks a Chinese proverb, "The man who talksthe most about himself." Though the drinker makes wry faces, there may, after all, be wholesome goodness in the cup. But debt, however -courteously it be offered, is the cup of a siren, and the wine, spiced and delicious though it be, an eating poison. The man out of debt, though with a flew in his jacket, a crack in his shoe, and a hole in his hat, is still deb son of liberty, free as the singing lark above him; but the debtor' though clothed in the utmost bravery, what is he but a serf upon a holiday:-a slave, to be reclaimed at an instant by his owner,

SIX LITTLE FEET TO COVER. Six little feet to cover, Six little hands to till. Tumbling out in the clover, Stumbling out of the sill. Six little stockings ripping, Six little shoes half worn, Spite of that promised whipping, Skirts, shirts, and aprons torn! Bugs and bumble-bees catching, Heedless of bites and stings; Walls and furniture scratching, Twisting off buttons and strings. Into the sugar and flour, Into the salt and meal, Their royal baby power Throughout the-house we feel. Their little heads all sunny, -

A JUNE DAY. And what is so rare as a day in June? Then, if ever, come perfect days; Then Heaven tries the earth if it be in tune, And over it softly her warm ear lays : Whether we look or whether we listen, We hear life murmur, or see it glisten; Every clod feels a stir of might, An instinct within in that reaches and towers. And, groping blindly above It for light, Climbs to a soul in grass and flowers; The flush of life may well be seen Thrilling back o'er hills and valleys; The cowslip startles in meadows green, The buttercup catches the sun in its chalice, And there's never a leaf nor a blade too mean To be some happy creature's palace; The little bird sits at his door in the sun. Atilt like a blossom among the leaves, And lets his illumined being o'errun With the deluge of summer it receives; His mate feels the eggs beneath her wings, And the heart in her dumb breast flutters and sings; He sings to the wide world, and she to her nest,— In the nice ear of Nature which song is the best? Now is the high tide of the year, And whatever of life hath ebbed away Comes flooding back with a ripply cheer, Into every bare inlet and creek and bay; Now the heart is so full that a drop o'erfills it, We are happy now because God wills it; No matter how barren the past may have been, 'Tis enough for us now that the leaves are green; We sit in the warm shade and feel right well How the sap creeps up and the blossoms swell; We may shut our eyes, but we cannot help knowing That skies are clear and grass is growing; The breeze comes whispering in our ear, That dandelions are blossoming near, That maize has sprouted, that streams are flowing, That the river is bluer than the sky, That the robin is plastering his house hard by; And if the breeze kept the good news back, For other couriers we should not lack; We could get it all by you heifer's lowing— And hark I how bold chanticleer, -Warmed with the wine of the year. Tell all in his lusty crowing! Ja3ms RUSSELL LOWELL. °77e Vision of Sir Launfal."

PREPARING GIRLS FOB MARRIAGE IN TllNlS.—Plump- nese, such as would be considered exuberant in the cold and critical North of Europe, constitutes the popular ideal of female beauty in the Regency of Tanis. Among marriage- able young ladies of that province slenderness of form and delicacy of proportion are regarded with justifiable aversion, as disqualifications for the wedded state. The fatter a maiden the better is her chance of making a good and early Imatch. To be abnormally obese is to be certain of drawing la prize in the matrimonial market, and the loveliest lithe- ness remains unwooed, while homely corpulence can pick and choose from among a throng of eligible suitors. How deep a root this predilection for capacious charms has struck in the Tunisian manly bosom may be gathered from the fact that widowers desirous to marry again, ehould they haply, moved by family or pecuniary considerations, select a bride whose dir-ensioos are reported to fall something short of those to which their previous experiences had ac- customed them, are wont to send the "dear departed" girdle and bracelet to the parents of their too exiguous be- trothed. On receipt of these articles, conveying a delicate hint that it might be expedient to make up for nature's shortcomings by some judicious treatment, the bride's papa and mamma proceed to fatten her with assiduity and despatch. For some weeks she leads the life of a Strasburg goose, and when she has attained the necessary goodly pro- portions her naptials are celebrated to the entire satisfac- tion of everybody concerned in them. (Moak° should be in great demand among "parents and guardians" at Tunis.— .Dailv Telegraph. _

the creditor. HIOH-HEELED Boors.—Ladies who wear high-heeled boots may sometinies wonder why they suffer so much from backache. A doctor lately hada fair patient who complained very much of pains in her back. She could no longer dance, and walking was a daily growing torture. He was puzzled, gave her a tonic, and asked her to call again. She came, said she was no better, and fell into hysterics. He was more puzzled, and hearing that several of her lady friends suffered in the same way, he asked her to bring them. They came—a melancholy band. They had left their nods and becks and wreathed smiles on the door step, and gazed at the doctor with undisguised agony. Be made them walk about the room. It was the promenade of purgatory. Then be smiled at his own simplicity, and told them they must wear slippers and woollen stockings for a week, and then shoes with scarcely any heels. It was now their souls, and not their bodies, that were torn with anguish. But they yielded, and their backs were racked no more. The moral is too obvious to be pointed, or, rather, so pointed as to be

A RAILROAD BLOCKED BY A YOTTNG LADY'S FOOT.—A tititroad at San Francisco was the other day blocked by a young latly's foot. From the account of the matter given by the San Francisco Chronicle at seems that as the young `lady stepped oat of a car at the end of California-etreet, and was crossing the track, her foot slipped and was caught fast in the crack 'Where the wire cable passes. Some imperfec- tion in the road.bed had saused the narrow aperture to ex- pand, and the young girl's foot was entrapped. The engineer of an approaching car saw the obstacle on the road, and, alighting with the conductor and several passengers, endea. voured to release the foot; but their efforts were in vain. Car after car arrived, but they were unable to proceed, until at last all traffic on the road had practically ceased, the cars being drawn up "in funeral row," and the passengers having .to pursue their journey as best they could. An immense crowd assembled, and the air was rent with cries of—" Push your foot forward," "Full it back," "Tip it sideways," "Lift your heel higher." The unhappy young lady in the meantime -was almost fainting, but *served in her efforts to extricate her foot. An attempt was made to prize the Iron rails forming the cable channel further apart, but they firmly resisted the pressure brought to bear upon them. Reporters from all the "down town dailies" having heath of the occurrenCe were congregated on the spot, and the ex- citement became absolutely thrilling. Messengers were at last despatched for appliances to take up a section of the , road, when at this juncture a tall brawny Englishman forced his way through the throng, and in a cheery voice marked by the Dorretshire dialect, shouted out, "la' ye tried on- fastenhe the young Teddy's shoe?" Ten buttons flew at once from as many buttonholes., and in the twinklinglof an eye the foot was free.

- NICE WQREMANSECIP.--A watchmaker in N'ewcastle, Pa., has ooMpleted a set of three gold shirt studs, in one of which is a2watch that keeps excellent time, the dial being about three-eights of an inch in diameter. The three studs are connected by a strip of silver inside the shirt bosom, and the watch contained in the middle one is wine up by turning the stud above, and the hands are set by turning the one below. But perhaps the most remarkable thing about the litiputian machine is that it works with a Pendulum, like a clock, and the pendulum will act with ease and accuracy in whatever position the timepiece is placed, even if it be placed upside down. In a recent letter from Banza Montiko, near the Yellala Falls of the Congo, Mr. Richards of the Livingstone (Congo) Inland Mission, mentions that he had visited two towns a short distance off, where no European has hitherto been. He also learned that there were two other farther on, and he therefore thinks there must be a larger population in the district than was supposed. One of the towns Mr. Richards describes as the "nicest African town" he has yet seen in the Congo region. It has a broad road, and the huts on each side are ranged almost in line, though detached from each 'other. A nearly straight row of trees is planted on each side of the road, and another line crossing it forms an arch- way. The people appeared more intelligenethan their neigh- lpours, but were very shy for some time. 7 Dr. Ziemer's paper on maximum daily' rainfall in the Mitt heilungen must have cost its author a vast deal of trouble. Towns where four inches of rain have been recorded within twenty-four hours are apparently numinous, and amongst them are Breslau, Brussels, Geneva, Trieste, Milan, and Genoa. The author has neglected to mach English authori- ties, or he might have found that London, Liverpool, and other English town sbelong to the same category. Verifiers, with fourteen inches of rain within twenty-four hours, heads the list of European towns ; Parneah, with thirty-five inches, exhibits the maximum throughout the world. We may observe that 12.5 inches of rain fell in a single day at Portree in the Isle of Skye. This, according to Mr. Buchan, is the maximum quantity until lately registered in the British Isles. A NEW TOEYEDo.—Another invention has just been added to the already long list of marine infernal machines. A Roumanian engineer has invented a new description of torpedo or submarine boat, whose peculiarity is that it is capable of mantenvring under water for twelve hours at a stretch. It is able to act at depths of from 100 ft. in riv3rs to 700 ft. or 800 ft. in the sea. It is able, through the agency of screws, to rise or sink noiselessly, and either suddenly or gradully by successive stages, and can move or manceuvre in any direction. The illumination of the vessel is internal, and enables the officers upon her to see for a distance of 130 ft. under the water. Upon the surface of the water the vessel is managed and manceuvred as any ordinary ironclad boat. If everything that is affirmed concerning this new torpedo boat is true, it will be a decided improvement upon the most eccentric vessel ever constructed in this country, the Poly- phemus, launched list Week.—lron. A MUSHROOM arLine me TUB- MAMMOTH CAVE OF KEN- Tim—The novel proposal (we learn from the Scientific American) has been made by an enterprising Frenchman to thetrustees of the Mammoth Cave to rent a portion of the cave for raising edible fungi. He has been cultivating mushrooms in the neighbourhood of New York, but com- plains of want of cellar space, and of the conditions of tem- perature and moisture as not uniform enough for the best results. The portion of the cave which he has in view is that known as " Audubon's Avenue," the first passage to the right after entering the cave. It is about half a mile long and contains little of special interest, unless it be the swarms of bats in "The Great Bat-room." The rich deposits of bat guano that have accumulated there for centuries would, no doubt, prove serviceable, when mixed with other fertilisers, in growing the fungi. The soil is at present very dry, but might easily be moistened to any desired degree. The idea of thus utilising caverns has long been a familiar one, and practically realised in France. One cave at Montrouge is said to have six or seven miles run of mushroom beds- an- other, near Frepillon, 16 miles; a third at Mery, ever 2L miles. The special advantage of subterranean culture lies in the uniformity of temperature, which in the Mammoth Cave hardly varies from 56 deg. Fah. all the year round. Mushroom culture is found highly remunerative. It is thought choice mushrooms would find a ready market in Louisville, Cincinnati, and .other western and southern

A moulder, named George Carey, of Bolton, left work on Whit-Thursday, for a holiday. He commenced to drink heavily, and on Friday last he drank a pint and a half of rum. Two young clergymen were disputing so loudly on a knotty point of theology that they awoke a big dog that had been sleeping on the hearth before the floe, whereupon he began to bark furiously. An old preacher, who had been quietly sipping his tea while the disputants were talkihg, gave the dog a kick, exclaiming—" Hold your tongue, y.tou silly brute I You know no more about it than they do V' Minnritn Lune:—lt is not so difficult Jas you think to behave to a husband so that he shall remain for ever in some measure a husband. A word from you at the right time will not fail of its effect; what need have you to play the suffering virtue? The tear of a loving girl, says an old book, is like a dewdrop on a rose; but that on the cheek of a wife is a drop of poison to her husband. Try to appear cheerful and contented, and your husband will be so; and when you have made him happy, you will become so, not in appearance, but in reality. The skill required is not great. Nothing flatters a man so much as the happiness of his wife. WO:tax IN THB Ear.—The 14 of a woman in the East Is but cheerless. The Hindu respects and cares more for his cow, horse, and ass than he does for his helpmate.- Never being permitted out of the four walls of her domicile, she is little better than a simpleton. Childish, and fond of childish intrigues, she has no hand in the training of her children. Her husband places no confidence in her, and his love is shared by many. She is accustomed to hear fearful tales as to the doings of the strange white man—of his horrible ; appetite, of his tremendous strength, and of his imperious ways. Like all women, she has much curiosity, and if by 1 any chance she pays a visit to a European house, or a European lady pays her a visit, her eager questions about her fair sister's social standing elicits from her expressions i of wonder. Government closes on certain days to Ow European and male native the gardens and places of public resort, and we are glad to say that some, though very few, i native gentlemen have so far overcome their superstitions ' as to take their wives and daughters on that pleasure trip. But a woman may live from youth to old age and never see the paving-stones of the street on which stands her house. I —The Californian. ADIATEIIR TICKET Coraxertuu.—A good story is told apropos of a noble lord who was recently returning from the races. In the adjoining compartment were eight book- makers, who, 4* cleaned out" by successive failures, were travelling without tickets, hoping by a turn of good luck to escape payment. At last one of them, during a stoppage, hit upon a brilliant idea. Pulling his cap down over his eyes and buttoning his coat, he went to the carriage of the noble lord and his friends, and, assuming an official air; col- lected all their tickets. These he distributed among his own friends, and on the train reaching London the noble lord had a n rrow escape of seeing himself and his friends taken into custody for attempting to defraud the railway company, for despite their assurances, the officials declined to believe that anyone had been audaciouS enough to collect these pas- sengers' tickets. The thing was too absurd. It was only by paying their fare a second time that the noble lord and his friends escaped from the clutches of the railway ser- vants.

FREE EnoceTrox.—When it was once laid down that every child must go to school, as was for the first time defi- nitely determiled in 187 es there was (remarks the Times) no escape from tSe necessity of facilitating the payment of the fees of the large and perhaps increasing class whose parents I cannot or will not pay. She always made little biscuits the size of an egg, and she would leave 'ern an hour to swell by themselves, and they would grow into 121 b. loaves. I thought to myself you are a leaf-er. He continued his growing tale, and said: Once there was a man. He went into the woods and chopped doWn four trees. He used the four stumps for corner posts, and be built him a nice log-houee on those stumps. There he and his family went to bed in thuehoi,astev. The next morning he found himself and family psx feet in the air, with a lot of Indians down below waiting to cut their hair off, and the Indians did scalp the whole of 'ens.' Says he, Respected sir, those Indians each one sawed off a tree; then each Indian Sat on a stump, and those slumps grew the Indians up to the house, and then they scalped the fa It certainly was the greatest case of up a tree I ever heard of."

TRE STREET Cnossxn.—We have no words of blame for Mr. Bottlewasher. He meant well. He got sick wading through the mud on crossings, and,so he invented his street- crosser. It was a tremendous spring located in the toe of each of a pair of overshoes. When the wearer stepped his foot down fiat it didn't work, but when he arose on tip-toe . .

the spring jumped nn clear across the street. Mr. Bottle- washer started out to try the invention. The first attempt he made was at Park-square, and the spring wasn't strong enough to clear it, but set him down with great violence square in the puddle, and he got badly spattered. But he wasn't discouraged. Be tried it on Bromfield-street, which is narrow. That time the spring seemed to have more . .

_ force, for it shot him clear across the street and through the open door of an eating-house, and be came in such violent contact with a man who sat with his back to the door that both he and the table went over, and both gentlemen were mixed up with the dinner on the floor. The upset man had to be held while things were explained, and even then said that if it was tried again somebody would get hurt. Then Bottlewasher went out and tried the thing on Tremont- street, and that time he just cleared the street and upset a fat man where he alighted. The fat man proposed to stab him and could with difficulty he pacified. This broke I Bottlewasher's heart, and he took off the overshoes and gave them to Count Fondowhiski, an Italian nobleman who col- lects bottles, rags, &c., about the street. Mr. Bottlewasher didn't explain the invention to the Count, who put on the 1 overshoes. He started of, and, coming to a crossing, pro- posed to tip-toe across. As he was .stooping over, with his pack on his back, the result was that he was not jumped across the street, but sent across by seven sopsersaults and ten handsprings, while the air was just filled with bottles, rags, ttc., from his pack. He threw ell people and a dog when he reached the sidewalk. A policeman grabbed him and lifted him up on tip-toe. The spring worked, and both were hurled into the mud and got their months full of it. The officer got him to the station at last, but he had a hard time of it; and two gaolers, trying to get him downstairs, got him there, and themselves too, in sudden order. Then they discovered what the matter was. The Count was re- leased, and has sworn a vendetta against Mr. Bottlewasher, and when ke gets well will see that gentleman..—.Bestoca Post.

The same success attended the ; the hour." Irish Church Bill through its remaining stages. Its pro- The widespread dissatisfaction which prevailed in Ireland ; grass through Committee, it is true, was exceedingly slow; ' did not rest purely and simply op religious grounds, but but at length, exactly three mouths after its introduction in ; sprang undoubtedly from the old' enmity of race—from the the Commons, the third reading came on. The motion was natural antipathy of the conquered to the conqueror. But' strentesnalyopposed. It and its author were unsparingly ;as religions inequality or the Church Establishment was denounced. But Mr. Gladstone made a final and eloquent the only remaining vestige of conquest—the last remnant' defince'of his scheme. He maintained that the measure 'of the ascendancy of the conqueror—it was justly regarded was neither unjust, illiberal, nor harsh; neither would it ; ,as the fontal spring of Ireland's woes. No sooner had Mr. permanently cripple Protestantism in Ireland. "The Gladstone acquired the Premiership, than. he directed his Church," said Mr. Gladstone," may have much to regret in energies to the removal of that which the Irish people re- respect to temporal splendour, yet the day is to.come when garded as a symbol of conqaest and gross injustice. it will be said of her, as of the temple of Jerusalem, that '-the glory of the latter House is greater than that of the former,' and when the most loyal and faithful of her chil- dren will learn not to forget that at length the Parliament of England took courage, and the Irish Church was dis- established and disendowed." The Government majority again was a very large one, being no less than 114. We need not follow ite progress through the House of Lords. The debate thereon was one of singular ability. Lord' Derby addressed the House for the last time with all the wonted fire and earnestness of the "Rupert of Debate." The division took place at three o'clock in the morning of June 19th, in the very fullest House that ever assembled, there being no fewer than 325 Peers who recorded their votes personally, besides 18 who paired; 13 English and three Irish prelates voted against the Bill. The Bishop 'of Manchester, "under gentle pressure, retreated from the House without voting, as he had intended, with Bishop Thirlwall," who alone of all the Bishops voted for the Bill, whilst the Archbishops of Canterbury and York retired within the rails of the Throne and so became virtual ab- sentee spectators of the Division. When, however:the numbers were reckoned, they were found to be Contents l79' Non-contents 146-33 So far the Bill was safe. It might still, however, be muti- lated in Committee. But after more angry discussion the Lords ultimately passed it, and on the 26th of July the Irish Churchßill received the Royal Assent. The first gun in this Parliamentary warfare was fired on May Bth, 1868 s. and in less than a year the citadel in Ireland was stormed and the victory won. The Queen's Spe!sch which inaugurated the Session of 1870 while spaying in its words was abundant in its pro- mises. It condensed a great deal of matter into a small' compass. As we read the spiritless and barren speeches of the dreary Palmerston era, when so little was promised and even that little was not done, and contrast them with the brief but pointed speech read on the 10th of February,. 1870, we feel that we have passed into an entirely new state of things—that political dilettantism has happily got* out of fashion and that the Government of the country, is in the hands of men who understand the wants of the country and are determined to meet them. There is nothing here of a desire to get through the Session easily by the post- ponement of all questions which are likely to create diffi- culty—nothing of the spirit which prompts Governments which desire to have peace in their time never to do to-day what can be put off till to-morrow. Mr. Gladstone and his colleagues had evidently learnt the lesson that a daring policy was best fitted to awaken the enthusiasm of their friends and to command success, and shaped their course accordingly. • First in the list of measures for the session and that with which we are now principally concerned, was the endeavour to settle a question which had battled the ingenuity of seve- ral Governtnents,.by amending "the laws respecting the- occupation and acquisition of lend in Ireland in a manner adapted to the peculiar circumstances Of that country, and calculated, as.herMisjesty believes, to bring about improved' relations between the several classes engaged in Irish agri- culture." Five-days after this intimation, Mr. Gladstone laid before a crowded House his Irish Land Bill—a measure- which grappled with the Irish difficulty in a bold and 'statesmanlike spirit Sir Bounden Palmer described the bill as "large and important, but not revolutionary," yet, at. the same time, a "humiliating necessity." Leave was given. to bring in the bill, and the date for its sepond reading was fixed for the 7th of March. The debate on the second read- ing commenced on the 7th of March and continued till the 11th. On that day Mr. Disraeli, who had been absent from the House on account of sickness, appeared in his place and' spoke against the measure, declaring that. "a more compli- oated, a more clumsy, or a more heterogenons measure was never yet brought before the attention of Parliament." At the conclusion of the debate the numbers were :—For the eecond reading, 442; against, 11. In Committee 300 notices of amendments were given, but the bill went through Committee with only such alterations as the Government consented to accept. It was then carried up to the Mane of Lords, where it excited;considerable dis- cussion, but after three nights de '' bate the second reading was carried without division. A fierce struggle took place in Committee. but eventually this important measure passed through the Upper House with no serious alteration, and on the Ist of August it received the Royal assent. We have ventured to call Mr. Gladstone "Ireland's Friend," and surely these two measures will support us in this assertion. Even if he had not framed the Irish Church Bill—the most remarkable legislative achievement of modern times—this Irish Land Bill upon the very face of- it proclaims ;Mr. Gladstone to be Ireland's friend. The measure itself was based upon a principle which very wise heads had repudiated, and which was essentially ov2l in I the English Administration of Ireland. Sir Robert' Peel had been Irish Secretary and had studied Ireland for a quarter of a century; Lord Palmerston was an Irish landlord, had a perceptible dash of Irish humour, and, character, and sym- pathy in him, and brought to all questions one of the coolest and clearest heads of the century; but both Peel and Palmerston never swerved from the position that the rela- tion between landlord-and tenant ought in Ireland to be sub- stantially what it is in England and Scotland, a_ matter of contract. But the Principle of Mr. Gladstone's measure was that respect should be had in Ireland neither to abstract see-. tics nor to English and Scottish precedent, but to Irish cus- tom. Mr. Gladstone accepted Ireland in 1870 as she was. He saw that she was a Roman Catholic country, and,though thinking Protestantism better than Roman Catholicism, he disestablished and disendowed the Protestant Church of Ireland. He found in Ireland peculiar customs regulating the occupancy of land, and, though believing that the sys- tera of contract which prevails in England is the better system, he brought in a bill to ratify and legalise the Irish laud custom. And whatever may be our opinion as. to the practical results of that bill, one thing at least every, man who has one spark of generosity or justice in his disposition must admit, namely, that the Irish policy which, as Leader of the Liberal party, Mr. Gladstone inaugurated in 1869- and 1871), was one of told, complete, and unprecedented friendliness. Mr. Gladstone was all things to Ireland, in order that he might gain the hearts of Irishmen. To do justice to Ireland, he sacrificed his sympathies as a Pro-: testant ; to show mercy to Ireland he put in; abeyance his principles as a political economist. After years of peddling statesmanship, and skin-deep remedies for radical disordera, her Majesty's eighth Prime Minister redressed the wrongs of centuries, and paid lsac.k to Ireland the debt which Eng- land so long owed her. So far as nature is concerned Ireland might be one of the finest countries in the world. Her climate, bathed in the warm waters of the Gulf Stream, is singularly mild; so much so that the myrtle will live the winter through in the open air. Benda her unrivalled pastures and pre-eminent aptitude for green crops, and hence also the appropriateness of the name the "Emerald Isle." Her scenery is exquisite sag her soil peculiarly fertile. Moreover, the Irish people halve much that is naive and noble, enthusiastic and , generous, ingenuous and true in their constitution. Their hospitality is mcessive, and their wit is proverbial. Their poets have ascended the heights of Parnaesns and climbed the hills of Zion—drawn rich draughts from the Castation fount es well as from the watere of Siloam. Their orators in thrilling, imaginative, yet forcible eloquence, have often sounded the spirit-stirring tocsin of nationality. Their toldiers,have driven their bayonets through phalanxes that never reeled in the shock of war before, and when death fell in showers upon them they never hesitated to precipitate themselves upon the foe. Nevertheless, poor Ireland, in- stead of being a sainted isle, seems rather a vessel of wrath "built in eclipse and rigged with curses dark," and as every heart has its own bitterness so has every state, and Ireland is ours. For very many years we, the most masterful nation on the face of the earth, have been trying to solve the problem of Irish government, •and 4pparently in vain. ;The solution of the problem seems to be as far off as ever. Priding ourselves on the art of government, boasting that we bold under strong control alien races in'elistant quarters of the globe, we are yet tantalised by the fact that here is a people at our own door—the shores of whose fair island can be seen from our western coasts, whom we have had for at

THE COMET. The following has been received from the Astronomer- Royal :

• Royal Observatory, Greenwich, Saturday. The comet was well observed here last night (June 24th), and its position was accurately determined with the altazimuth as well as with the transit circle. At the time of Meredian Passage, it was in R. A. 5 hours, 38 mins. 39 secs., N. P. D. 40 deg. 36 mins. 35 secs.,forming a nearly equilateral triangle with Capella and Beta Aurigie, the tail extending 7 or 8 degrees nearly in the direction of the role Star. The head was far brighter than Capella or any other star in the heavens. In the telescope it showed a structure somewhat resembling Coggia's comet of 1874, with two interlacing arcs of light, that on the preceding side being much brighter and more extensive. There was also a very striking straight wisp of light extending from the nucleus nearly in the direction of the axis of the tail. The comet was examined by Mr. Christy with the large spectroscope, using a dispersion equivalent to that of four prisms of sixty degrees. The continuous spectrum was so bright that only the brightest of the three cometary bands could be measured. It was found that this band coincided in position with that in the flame spectrum of carbon—wave length s,l6s—and not with that in the second spectrum of carbon. , as given by a vacuum tabe containing vapour of alcohol. No polarisation could be detected. The comet was seen from Warrington and the neighbour- hood on Sunday and Monday night in the north-cast, and attracted a great deal of attention. it appeared soon after dusk set in, and as the night advanced became more luminous. Its tail is remarkably noticeable, being fan- shaped, and shedding its brilliance in an upward direction.

div.p: "Your dress," said a husband to his fashionable wife, "will never please the men." "I don't dress to please men.," was the reply, "but to worry other women." The last, best fruit which comes late to perfection, even in the kindliest soul, is tenderness towards the bard, forbear- ance towards the unfortunate, warmth of heart towards the misanthropic—Richter. After the officials of a Kansas town had vainly endeavoured to drperse a mob, a minister mounted a box and made the simple announcement :—" A collection will now be taken up." The result can be easily guessed. Happiness is like manna. It is to be gathered in the graine and enjoyed everyday; it will not keep; it cannot be accumulated; nor need we go out of ourselves nor into re- mote places to gather it, same it has rained down from heaven at our doors, or rather within them. The best part of one's life is the trerformance of one's daily duties. All higher motives, ideals, conceptions, sentiments, in a man are of no account if they do not come down and strengthen him for the better discharge of the duties which devolve upon him in the ordinary affairs of life. At Manchester, on Tuesday, Susan Smith, the wife of a Liverpool sailor, was cemmitted for trial on a charge of attempting to murder her infant child. The woman was being removed with other persons in a van to Crumpsall when one of her companions saw her tie a string round the , ohild's neck and pull it till the child was black in the face. She was with difficulty prevented, andafterwards said it was ' all through drink. A curious case of of "employer's liability " was heard at the Oldham County Court, on Tuesday. The plaintiff and defendant were both working colliers, and the former had been engaged by the latter to assist him. While they were following their occupation the defendant's pick. struck the plaintiff's knee, doing him some injury. The judge con- sidered that there had been carelessness in wielding the pick, and he gave judgment for the plaintiff fors.-. Hamm FOR TWENTY YEARS.—An inquest was held at Liverpool on Tuesday on the body of Elizabeth Hatchinson, 56 years of age, the wife of a cotton porter, living in a cellar in Milk-street. The husband of the deceased paid that for the last 20' years she had been constantly drinking, and took little or no food. She had been sober for a fortnight only since Christmas!. She went to bed on Saturday night, and on Sunday when he awoke be found her lying beside him dead. The medical evidence showed that death was the result of drinking, and a verdict accordingly was given. Mr. Broadhurst, M.P., Addressing a meeting of operative engineers at Birmingham, denied that trade unions had driven trade from the country, or that they reduced the competent workman to the level of the insompetent by fixing a minimum rate of wages. To show how to-day Eng- land could compete in making machinery, even with those countries that placed a high tariff upon English manufac- tured articles, Mr. Broadhurst stated that he recently met in a railway carriage an American manufacturer who was travelling to Leeds to order machinery for his factory in , one of the Western towns of America. He explained that he was not a Free-trader, but he found that he could come to England, order his machinery in Leeds, import it to his factory in the Western States, pay a fair price to the makers at Leeds, and also a4O per cent. duty when it landed in America, and still save £4OO as compared with the price he veoubl have to pay in the States. ORCHARDS ought to be multiplied a thousand-fold, and Spare corners and sides and slopes of 'rally:aye, byways, and hedges, should be planted with all manner of fruit trees, and particularly with the Blenheim orange, and those of the mulberry Kind, to ensure the health of the masses of the people, and especially for growing youth. Flesh meat does not afford to the system that vigour and vitality which good ripe fruit does, or would, if the young of the community could have a sufficiency. Fruit, more than almost any other kind of food, supplies the greatest and grandest fend of life- giving properties, and consequently the greatest amount of vital or electrical power. It is man's holiest and best food.. Trees and shrubs that yield no life-giving virtues to thel human system should be rooted up, to give place to the best and noblest fruit trees. If our nobility would devote a por- tion of their vast estates to the production of fruit it would be a boon of inestimable value. It would work wonders in weaning people from tobacco and alcoholic drinks; health would spring up as it never has before, and virtue and morality would supersede depravity. Except mankind eat that kind of food intended as their highest and best, and ' drink its juice—unfermented—they have no le in them. What a noble sight, in the course of a few years, would all , our public parks, such as Bushey, Richmond Greenwich, and others, present, if, instead of huge chesput and other trees, the best kind of apple, pear, and mulberry trees, also innumerable black Hamburgh grape vines, were to spring up in all directions. Why should not the masses have their' blood enriched by good fruit when it could be done so easily? God would give the increas.e if man only put his hands to the plough; and the glorious sun now pouring down its blessed influence on a few orchards would shine beneficently over the whole surface of the habitable -lobe were it all one orchard. What an effect on the minds and bodies of future generations! Nor should we have long to wait before its benign effects would be made manifest. At present ft 18 next to impossible for the mass of the. people 0 obtain that amount of life-giving lruit which would be so beneficial to them. Land in abundance could be used for vineyards and apple orchards. OUT commons, heaths, woods, and forests could be cultivated for fruits. What better curative agent can be found? Many diseases now common Would Yards like snow before the sun if fruits were more freely used. Fruits contain thee true water of life, being made by fun- erring wisdom, as the best and holiest food and drink or man—The Nature of Tobacco. By Jas. Driver, R.N. HOUSE OTT LORDS.—MormAv.,

The Royal assent was given by Commission to 41 public aid private Acts, including the Lancashire County Justices and th 3 Consolidated Fund. Their Lordships having de- bated an Irish railway bill, the Marquis of HERTFORD called attention to the state of the British cemeteries in the Crimea' and an explanation WAS given by the Earl of Molt- LET which was deemed satisfactory.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Mcvnalr. RUSSIAN ANNEXATION OF TURCOMAN TERRITORY.—Sir Charles Dilke, replying to Lord Sandon, said the Turcoman territory annexed by Russia extended as far as Astrabad, and this was 190 miles from the frontiers of Afghanistan. SUBSMIES TO TEE A.FGHAN AIILEEn.--In answer to Lord Sandon, the Marquis of HARYINGTON stated that the total amount given to the Ameer of Afghanistan was £390,000. OPIUM TRAFFIC 1/24 Marisa BUR/LAlL—Replying to Sir, Wilfrid Lawson Lord HARTINGTON stated that the number' of retail opium flhops in British Burmah had been reducedl from 68 to 27.—Sir WILFRID inquired, amidst laughter, 1 Whether the owners of the suppressed shops had been corn- pensated.—Lord Haaturorowsaid he was not aware of it. MAGISTRATES GUILTY OF 'eaRRIJET ELECTORAL FRAC- YICES.—The ATTORNEY GENERAL, in reply to Mr. Caine, -said be wasinfonned by the Lord Chancellor that out of 27 magistrates reported by the commissioners as guilty of cor- rupt practices at elections had placed theirresignations in his hands. The remaining 12 had placed statements with the Lord Chancellor Which demanded further inquiry, and any apparent delay there might seem tribe arose from the desire of the Lord Chanoellor that no injustice should be done.—ln reply to Sir R. Cross, the ATTORNEY GENERAL added that the numberhe had given did notinclude mayors and members of corporations. These enjoyed their power by statute, with which the Lord Chancelloreould not inter- fere acept by special Act of Parliament. , Tim PROCLAMATION OF WATERFORD.—Mr. R. POWER asked what number of.agrarian offences had been committed in the city of Waterford since the let ofinnuary 1881.—Mr. Fonsran, in reply,-said he was informed that there had been lone serious case of assault committed at the fair, and two I cases of intimidation recently: but bewent on to say that the number of agrarian offences 'WES not the sole ground upon which the 'Government exercised their discretion in proscribing &district. It bad been deemed necessary to pro- 'claim the county, and, to make this effective, the city was iincluded.—lnthe•course of the discussion which followed IMr. HEALY asserted that the real mason was that there was an estate of several thousand acme in the county owned by the Duke of Deorrashire, whose son was a member of the Cabinet, and it was convenient that the agent of the estate should have power to put in gaol any of the troublesome Land Leaguers Who had prevented him from getting his rents. The only remark the CHIEF SECRETARY condescended to make on this extraordinary -statement was that neither side of the House would expect Mm to take any notice of it. After movinglhe adjournment of the House, the Leaguers' proceeded to heap upon the members of the Government • such epithets as vile, foal, gross, tyrannical, unjust, cowardly, infamous, Brummagem Castlereagh, spy, informer, traitor, unfair, outrage. The motion for the adjournment was rejected by 305 to 28.—Mr. HEALY then expressed his indignation at the temporarrclosing of the telegraph office at Craughwal, and was informed by Mr. Forster that the step had been rendered necessary by the arrest of the tele- graphist 'under the Coercion Iti.ct. THE TELEGRAPH DEPARTMENT.—RepIVing to Mr. O'Donnell,'Lord F. CAVENDISH stated that it was thedesire of the Government that the new scheme respecting the pay and hours of the telegraph clerks should come into opera- tion with as little delay aspossible, but that if an agitation involving the threat of a strike were continued, it nnghtbe necessary to suspend the operation of the new scheme. THE SMALLPDX EPIDIDSIC IN LONDON.—Dr. CAMERON attempted to draw attention to the smallpox epidemic in London, remarking that there had been 9,000 cases and 1,500 deaths.—The SEMLER, however, pointed out that the hon. member was not entitled to debate a question which was down for discussion on a future day. The 'House afterwards went into committee on the Land Bill.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—TIIESDAY. TIDE ',VETERINARY SURGEON BILL. - In committee on this bill Lord ABERDARE sought to insert a clause to exempt veterinary surgeons from liability to serve on juries, but be was defeated upon a division, and the bill passed through committee.

IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

General for Ireland. since last night. The Conservatives had only to make a show of a certain amount of opposition, and to get the assistance of the. Whig members of the Liberal party, in order to obtain any concession from the Prime Minister. Instead of dealing with the case himself, the Attorney-General for Ireland was put op to play the part of Cassio by giving the bill a stab in the back.—Mr. OLADSTONZ indignantly protested against this charge, and mid that if the Government made a concession, however draall, to members opposite, it was denounced as a change of front; while if they made an amendment in the directionl desired-by Mr. ParnelPs group, it was not estimated at all, Whatever its magnitude.—Mr. Straw astpressed his convic- tion that do' particular concession had been made to the landlord which would materially; damage the bill. The antendmert was negatived.— After considerable discussion the ATTOIINNT•GENEHAL moved a series af amendments by which, where the rent is £lOO or upwards and not exceeding £3OO, the compensation given by the clause is limited to three years' rent; where it is above £3OO and not exceeding noo, to one year's Tent. The amendments mowed by Mr. W. IL Smith were nega- tived, and the Attornori-Creneralts proposals were carried by large majorities. The House ,divideA on the question that clause 5 stands part of the bill, and the Government majority was 96. Clause 6 was readily disposed of; and on .d:ause the Attorney-General brought forward his promised amend- ment, giving the landlord the right to seek the intervention of the court after demanding an increase of rent which the tenant declined to accept.—Mr. CHAPLIN moved an amend- ment omitting 'the qualifying words, and alas giving the landlord power to appeal to the court whenever he choose ; but Mr. Gladstone declined to accept this proposal, on the ground that it would place in the hands of the landlord an instrument 'which might be used against the poor tenant. The Government's amendment was ultimately agreed to, and clause "7 was under discussion when the Rouse rose.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—TIECHSBAY. MISCELIHNEOUS.—EarI GRANVILLE stated that he had Very good reason' for knowing that there was no foundation for the tumour that the President of the United States ' has sent over a secret mission to report ,on the condition of Ireland. The opposition of Lord Denman to the Govern- ment measure for dealing with Charitable Trusts proved unavailing, and the bill passed. THE GnszX 'FRONTIER.—The long promised debate on the Greek frontier question was initiated by Lard Stmtheden and Campbell, who moved for papers.—Earl GRANNILLE remarked that the noble Lord was more Turk- ish than the Turks, and objected to an arrangement which they had agreed to and were determined to loyally carry out. The noble Lord objected to the concert of Europe mctly at the moment that concerted action had settled the question which had been one of considerable difficulty. A •conventionlad been signed which made arrangements for evacuation tobe completed within tive.months, and although Her Majesty's Government hhol not gained for Greece as much as at one time they desired, Greece would have little cause to complain of the result, -seeing that she had ob- tained a cession of 5,000 square ,miles, while she kaalsecured an excellent line of military frontier, and had acquired ilmost the limits of her ancient kingdom. He believed that the 'settlement would lead to improved relations be- tween Turkey and Greece, and a difficulty had been removed from Europe generallv.—The Marquis of SALISLIIRY was not dissatisfied with the results arrived at, but criticised the 4, circuitous route" by which they had been attained.— After remarks from the Earl of Rosebery and ,the Earl of Kimberley, the motion was withdrawn. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Tnnusucy. EVICTIONS IN IRELAND.—IIET:PARNELL brought forward the case of an evicted tenant rnrn ed M'Cabe, who had since been living with his family i miserable hovel during a sever frost; but Mr. Foßsri-lt nut a very different com- plexion upon the case when he ited that the man at the time of his eviction owed three ye. I's rent, which was very little over the poor law valuation, grit he had not lived in a 'boyel during the winter, and that he Lad been and was still employed as a labourer. Some further information was volunteered by Colonel TOPTENHAM, which the Chief SEC- TETARY said had come from a source which he should con- Sider trustworthy. This was to the effect that the man had • paid no rent since 1872, that he had been in the receipt of a weekly sum from the Land League, and that he could have obtained a good house, tut was paid by the Land League to remain in a hovel. RAILWAY Ountsows.—The President 'of the Board of Trade was interrogated as to the expediency of requiring fresh means of signalling in cases of assault in railway car- riages, and the right hen, gentleman remarked that on the London and Brighton line, where a murder had recently been committed, the mode of communication adopted ap- peared to be the best that had hitherto been tested, and it was difficult to say how it was to be further perfected. The Board of Trade had no power to make a requisition upon the railway companies to adopt other precautions. THE ORDER OF BITSINESS.—SIT S. NORTHCOTE Was anxious to know what were the intentions of the Govern- ment as to morning-sittings, and the PRIME BirmarEn in- formed him that for the present be thought two morning sittings per week would be sufficient to expedite public business. The Government certainly intended to press the Land Bill as the first order on Wednesdays. THE Liton LAND BILL.—The House again went into Committee on the Land Bill, and dealt with the question of leaseholders. Subsequently there was a discussion on tho position of the labourer.—Mr. 'FORSTER said the Govern- ment thought the question would be best treated in a new clause which he undertook to introdnce.

W 4143 BIRDS' PROTECTION, &c., ACT A2TANDHENT BILL. —Lord DALHOUSIE obtained the second reading of a bill to provide that wherever it is lawful to kill birds it shall also be lawful to sell them, and so to retnove an existing ationialy. TiaA THIRD BUFFS. The proposed alteration of the facings of the 3rd Regiment of Infantry (the Buffs) gav,. rise to a debate on the new Army Organisation scheme,-- which did not lead to any result. COMMERCIAL TREATIES.—Sir C. DILKE, after stating that the Commercial Treaty wirh Italy would probably be pro- longed, informed the House that negotiations were, COM- menced last year with a view to the conclusion of treaties with Italy, Spain, and Portugal, and they had been tem- porarily suspended. Under certain eventualities the-con- elusion of commercial treaties with these countries might be of considerable importance to British trade. THE NEW FRENCH TAlaFF.—Replying to Lord Bandon regarding the translation of the French tariff into English, Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, in effect, repeated his answer to Mr. Stuart Wortley a few days ago, that he did not think that a translation would be worth the expense and delay which it would entail. He added, however, that he would consult the-chambers of commerce in the country as to whether a translation was desired. THE. FUTURE OF THE IRISH LAND BILL—MOTION .Blr MR. GVADSTONE.—Mr. GLADSTONE rose to move that on and after Wednesday next the several stages of the 'Land Law (Ireland)% Bill have precedence of all orders of the day and notices of motion on all days when it is set down among the orders, until the house shall otherwise determine. He said theliouse would be in a considerable degree prepared for this motion by the known desire of the Government to allow no business of their own to interfere with the duty of press- inrcorward the Land Bill. The sentiment of the im- portance of the Land Bill was not confined to the ,Gevern- meet and their supportere, but was shared by many who in a party sense did not belong to the majority. For thirteen sittings the house had been in committee on the bill, and had onlycompleted four clauses. No doubt the bill contained many complex details, but other measures which he enu- merated had equally. complex details, and without being too sangtiine he expected that progress would have been more rapid. At any rate, this was the 28th June, and equivalent to the.EBth July of an ordinary session; and seeing that the session commenced a month earlier than usual, and that the house had' been occupied throughout with matters that re- quired the closest attention, it was fair to ask with what other measures the Government intended to proceed. (Hear, hear.) On this point he was not prepared to make any statement. not being able to form any definite expectation as to the conclusion of the committee on the Land Bill; hut as he did not look forward to the probability, or even the possibility, of any endeavour to carry through the House after the Land Bill, any measure likely to be the subject of prolonged and general controversy, the House might dismiss any idea of that kind. But in respect of the limited catalogue of measures with which the Government wished to proceed, he wished to reserve any positive state- ment until next week. There would be a general desire to know the Government anticipation as to the probable dura- tion of the session. (Hear, hear.) The only difficulty was the Land Bill, and in the disposal of that the Government would spare no exertions; but subject to that consideration the Government would do their best to secure the proroga- tion the first weak in August. (Hear, hear.) So far as tbe Government were concerned, they would not interpose any obstacle, apart from the Land Bill, to interfere with the pros- pect thus held out. In the course of a very short time he hoped to state in detail what the intentions of the Govern- ment were. DEATH OF let. EDMOND BEALES. Mr. Edmond Beales, judge of County Courts Circuit 35, died at his residence, :Osborne House, Bolton Gardens, on Sunday. He was the son of Mr. Samuel Pickering Beales, of Newnham, Cambridge. He was born on July 3rd, 1803, and was consequently seventy-eight years of age. He was called to the bar at the Middle Temple in 1830, and practised as a conveyancer, and was revising barrister for Middlesex from 1882 to 1886. He unsuccessfully contested the Tower Hamlets in 1868, and was president of the Reform League from 1865 to 1869. The following year he was appointed a county court judge. Mr. Beales was the author of several :pamphlets on Parliamentary reform, but his name will be mere particularly recollected in connection with the Hyde Park riots, when the railings were pulled down some years ago. Mr. Beales was also President of the Workmen's Peace Association, having only just been re- elected by an almost unanimous vote at the recent annual meeting of the Association.
CHESHIRE QUARTER SESSIONS.

The Midsummer Quarter Sessions for the county of Chester were commenced on Monday, at Chester Castle, Mr. Horatio Lloyd presiding. The Deputy-Chairman, in his charge, congratulated the grand jury on the decrease in the number for trial, nine, as compared with the number in the corresponding quarter of last year. There were nineteen prisoners for trial at Knutsford on the following W•rdnesday—a decrease of two from the same period last year. The County Treasurer (Mr. C. Townshend) presented his quarterly statement, which showed that the payments for that period had amounted to £27,881 155., which included £14,227 155., the fifteenth instalment of the cattle plague loan. A rate of 2d. in the pound producing £22,422 105. 2d. was passed. The general police rate was fixed at id. in the pound, and the local police rates ranged from id. to Id. in the pound. The Deputy Chief-Constable (Lientenant-Colonel Cope) submitted the return of crime for the quarter ending the 31st ult., which showed a total of 2,355 apprehended and summoned, of whom 67 were committed for trial, 1,948 summarily convicted, and 340 discharged. This was a de- crease of 26 apprehended and summoned as compared with last year. There was a decrease of 63 males and 6 females for drunkenness as compared with the corresponding quarter of the previous year. During the quarter 8 persons had been proceeded against under the Sale of Food and Drugs Act, of whom 7 were convicted and 1 discharged. Lieutenant-Colonel Cope, deputy chief-constable, reported that since the adjourned sessions on the 24th of February, foot-and-mouth disease had appeared in six places in the county, 34 cattle and 13 swine had been affected, 65 re- covered, including 26 remaining under treatment at the date of the last report. There were 8 cattle on one farm in the townsbip of Marple affected with the disease. No case of pleuro-pneumonia bad been reported since last sessions. Swine fever had appeared in five places, and 10 animals had been affected. The Deputy-Chairman, in moving that the necessary steps be taken to fill the office of chief constable of the county, said he was sure they all greatly regretted the loss of the late Captain Arrowsmith, who had been chief constable for four years, and who for some years previously held the ap- pointment of deputy. On the whole he might say Captain Arrowsmith was an active, intelligent, and efficient officer, and he was sure that above all he desired to do his duty. (Hear, bear.) He presumed no alteration would be made in the salary which was fixed at £5OO a year and £l5O for travelling and other expenses.—Mr. W. F. Tollemache said he had heard it said that some one from Scotland Yaid should be appointed. He thought the office should be filled by gentlemen officers of the Army or Navy, and the subor- dinate offices of superintendents and sergeants should be filled from the ranks.—Mr. J. H. Teebe said he thought it unfair towards applicants to suggest that one from Scotland Yard or elsewhere would be appointed.—The motion to ad- vertise was carried. A grant of £1,200 was made for executing alterations in the magistrates' rooms at Chester Castle. A grant of £l,BOO was also made for the purchase of land (rein Sir Philip Egerton for the use of the asylum in irrigating their sewage. The salaries of the county coroners for the five years en- suing were fixed as follows :—Mr. Churton, £5lO (no altera- tion); Mr. Yates, £386 (decrease of £21): Mr. Johnson, £407 (increase of £61); Mr. Ridgway, £B5 (increase of £10). The adjourned quarter sessions for the county of Cheshire were held on Wednesday at Knutsford. Mr. Horatio Lloyd, deputy charman, presided. Mr. Marshall, referring to the appointment of an examiner i of the accounts of the Altrincham Gas Company at the last sessions, applied for an extension of time for presenting of the examiner's report, stating that he held in his hand a letter from Mr. Rycroft, one of the petitioners, in which he assented to that course on condition that the Company paid the costs of the adjournment. This they were quite willing to do.—The Clerk of the Peace (Mr. Charles Potts) said that the report had been handed in, and was in his possession.— , Mr. Marshall said there were powers under the statute to call witnesses and examine them, but the parties were not prepared to go on, and though the report was in the hands of the Clerk of the Peace he still requested that the matter might stand over. It was arranged that it should stand over until the October sessions.

Mr. Marshall said he held in his hand a petition in char- acter to that referred to in the previous matter applying for the appointment of an examiner of the accounts of the the North-Cheshire Water Company. The petitioners were Mr. Ellis Lever, Culcheth Hall, Bowdon, and Dr. C. A. Burghart, Brooklands. The practice was hardly settled by the Court as to whether notice should be given to the Com- pany affected. In this case notice had not been given, and if the Court were of opinion that notice ought to be given in order to enable the Company to oppose the petition if they thought fit, then he would ask for liberty to apply at the adjourned sessions. The Chairman said that so far as he remembered the statute was silent as to notice, and to that extent it might be considered an ex-parte application. He thought it would be better to give the company notice, because he could not lose sight of the fact that in other cases where orders had been made serious cost had been thrown upon the Company. —lt was agreed that the N.rth-Chishire Water Company should have a month's notice, and that the matter should be again brought before the Court at the adjourned sessions on the 4th August. The Chairman, addressing the Grand Jury, said their labours would not be at all heavy: The number of priso- ners for trial (22) was exactly the same as at that time last year, and therefore he had no remarks to make one way or another with reference to crime in the country, excepting that he observed in the calendar the names of several very young offenders of a class that he hail hoped they were, by the aid of reformatory and industrial schools, gradually losing sight of.—The cases tried were of no public interest.

BAND Of Horzt T. Wits%Fora:l.—The Band of Hope con- nected with the United Free Methodist Chapel, Winston!, had their annual tea on Wednesday, at Woodford Hall, by the kind permission of Mr. Joseph Slater, who takes a great interest in all temnerence organizations. The day being fine a great many friends went and enjoyed their open air tea immensely, and no doubt the yonng people appreciated the games after tea into which they entered most heartily, whilst their elders either looked on or strolled about the pretty scenery surrounding the hall.

MANCHESTER COTTON, THURSDAT.--There is no improvement here. The demand for Eastern fabrics continues light, and , prices are alone sustained by engagements which are reduced slightly day by day. There is a great firmness exhibited generally, and buyers find orders difficult to execute; both time and price interfere with the execution of many fabrics. Yams are scarcely so fl-m as on Tuesday. Sales continue very ; moderate both for home consumption and for export. LIVERPOOL PROvISIONS. THURSDLY.—Beer firm in value. Pork in strong consumptive demand. div.head: STATE OF IRELM,
div.p: STATE OF IRELM,

In the Queen's Bench in Dublin, on Monday, Walter Phalan was charged with the murder of Mr. Boyd, near New Ross, on the Bth of August last. The prisoner's brother is also charged with the crime, but the Crown decided to try him separately. The deceased and his father, who is a land- lord, were driving along the road when a body of men fired at him. The trial in Dublin of Walter Phelan, charged with the murder of Mr. Boyd at New Ross, was concluded on Thurs- day. The jury—consisting of nine Protestants and three Roman Catholics—returned a verdict of not guilty. The prisoner remains ia custody on the charge of shooting at Mr. Boyd, sen. Thurles was the scene, on Monday, of the sale of the in- terest of eight tenants in their farms. The Land League adopted the new tactics of keeping away the people, and causing the elaborate preparations made by the Government to go for nothing. V 45,41., was sent out to people to keep away from the **spiel Archbishop Croke gave an order early in the morning ;directing the public houses to be closed, thereby anticipating an order of the magistrates to the like effect. Other places of business were likewise losed, In sympathy, it was said, with the farmers whose Irma were about to be sold. In any caee, however, no one mold think of disobeying the order of, the Land League or is Grace the Archbishop. A large force was drafted into ie town, consisting of over 100 extra police, 100 men of the 34th Regiment, and 50 men of the 20th Hussars, all under the command of Mr. Hamilton, R.M., and the Hon. Mr. French, R.M. Mr. Goddard and Mr. Newton, of the Pro- perty Defence Association, were escorted to and from the railway station by a large force of military and police, the procession consisting of a body of the Hussars in front, and followed by police, after whom came about eighty men of the 64th Regiment, and these were brought up by a body of the Hussars. A black flag was hoisted on the top of an old castle which overlooks the Court House in which the sales were held, and was kept there until the conclusion of the sales. The tenants of the farms attended, but in every case they allowed the farms to be knocked down to Mr.l IGoddard. 1 At a meeting of the Liverpool Ladies' Land League held lon Sunday, the following resolution was passed:—" That as sectarian displays have long proved a source of discord, sub- versive of the best interests of Ireland, and a powerful weapon of subjugation in the hands of hostile Governments, we earnestly appeal to our countrymen, Protestant and Catholic, to abstain from all party demonstrations on the approaching anniversaries, and in a spirit of mutual forbear- ance unite for the Common good of the country." At a convention of Land League delegates, held in Letter- kenny, it was stated that many of the shopkeepers failed to render assistance to the people in their struggle, and it was resolved to urge upon the central executive to duly con- sider whether any steps could be taken to establish a co- operative agency, whereby the friends of the people could be further encouraged and enabled to supply all their wants at reasonable and just prices. At Kilmallock Petty Sessions, two men named Byrne and Ryan were sent for trial at the assizes, bail being taken, on the charge of having formed part of a riotous mob which on the 15th inst. attacked and stoned two farm servants in the employment of a farmer who has 'incurred the hostility of the Land League. The men had been at mass, and on leav- ing were chased all the way home, the defenclants,as alleged, taking an active part in the stone-throwing. During the past week 25 writs were executed in the county Cavan, in the presence of an overwhelming force of 200 infantry, 50 cavalry, and 200 police. In all cases of evictiou the tenants were 'replaced as caretakers. In one case of peculiar distress the officers of the troops and con- stabulary subscribed the amount of rent due—namely £6— leaving the League, if they chose, to pay the costs, which amounted to about SS. Several Irish delegates proceeded to Versailles on Monday to place a wreath at the feet of the statue of Hoche. A banquet was given in the evening, at which Mr. Egan, treasurer of the Land League. James Stephens, and the correspondents of some Dublin and New York papers were present. Speeches were delivered by the two first-named. A Mullingar correspondent says that an atrocious murder was perpetrated on Monday evening at Ballagh, two miles from there, by a labourer named Daly, who had been pro- secuted by a man named Curran for cutting wood and grass. Curran was passing Daly's house when the latter rushed out at him with a pitchfork, which was wrested from him. He then stabbed Curran several times with a knife. Curran died on Tuesday morning. The murderer was immediately arrested. Mr. Bence Jones, on Tuesday, at Clonakilty Quarter Sessions' recovered ejectment decrees against two of his tenants but at the request of the latter, who promised to pay a half year's rent, a stay of execution was granted. A large force of police proceeded on Tuesday to Mount Neill, county Waterford, to attempt the seizure of the stock on six farms, the occupiers of which had refused to pay more than Griffith's valuation. The endeavour, how- ever, was abortive, as no stock was to be seen on the farms in question. A Labourers' Land League is being established at KB- lonney, near Macroom, and the movement is extending and receiving the support of the county gentlemen. The labourers allege that the farmers are dismissing them and giving them insufficient wages, and that as the farmers, whom they have supported all along in their agitation, are ungratefully turn- ing their backs upon the labourers in the hour of need, the latter must only try to protect themselves. If this move- ment should make any had, and it is receiving the support and encouragement of the landlords, it may considerably weaken the power of the Land League. 1 On Tuesday night the house of a process server named WAnliffe was attacked by a party of men who were armed and disguised. They beat MAuliffe, and fired several shots, one wounding M'Auliffe's brother on the right arm. The gang then robbed the house of £3O, and decamped. Three persons have been arrested. An appeal to the Irish electors of Great Britain, signed by Messrs. Parnell, Justin M‘Carthy, and T. P. O'Connor, members of Parliament, has been issued. In it attention is drawn to the great influence which can be exercised in a large number of English constituences by Irish voters. It is urged that the action taken by the present ministry, and the present Liberal representatives, makes the organisation of the Irish voters more necessary than ever. Several of the Liberal members who were meet ardent in the cause of coercion were men who would not be in Parliament were it not for Irish electors, who, it is pointed out, may have any day an opportunity of repaying the treacherous ingratitude of several Liberal representatives as it deserves. Thorough organisation is therefore imperative.
