div.head: TTIE LATE 3IR. THOMAS LEA, OF WHISTON. PULPIT REFERENCE AT HUYTON QUARRY.
div.p: TTIE LATE 3IR. THOMAS LEA, OF WHISTON. PULPIT REFERENCE AT HUYTON QUARRY.

At the Huyton Quarry Mission Church, on Sunday even- ing, a sermon was preached by the Rev. F. W. Briggs, M.A., of Grove-street, Liverpool, in which special reference was made to the late Mr. Thomas Lea, of Whiston. The weather was fine, and there was consequently a very large congrega- tion. The service was opened by the singing of the favourite hymn of Mr. Lea (190 Wesleyan hymn book), and prayer having been engaged in, the hymn commencing "Rock of ages cleft for me" was sung, after which the rev. gentleman made a few remarks as to the manner in which the services would henceforth be conducted in the church, the building, which was formerly regarded as an nridenomi- national place of worship, haying been taken over by the Wesleyan body. He said that, respecting the history of the church, perhaps they knew about it more than lie did. They knew how it had become what it was from very small beginnings in connection with the earnest work of Christians, and how God had blessed their labours and made them suc- cessful. They knew also what changes had taken place; some had removed from the church, perhaps it might be, that their love had waxed cold. But, anyhow, such were the circumstances that it was found desirable that it should no longer be regarded as hitherto, as an undeaeminational place of worship, and knowing that there were very many Wesleyans in the neighbourhood, but chiefly, be might say, through the earnest request of the late Mr. Lee, who was one of the trustees, it was decided to offer the place, if it could be so arranged, to the Wesleyans. After a great deal of correspondence and intercourse with the trustees or their representatives, it was arranged that the Wesleyans should now carry on the work very much as it had teen carried on. There would probably be service twice on the Lord's Day, together with the Sunday school, and there would be an ad- dition of a week evening service. Most of them knew what to expect. After mentioning the doctrines that would be preached in the church, Mr. Briggs said class meetings would be instituted, and those who liked to unite them- themselves,.he should be very glad to meet st the close of the service. On every alternate Wednesday evening there would be public worship in the church, and on the other Wednesday evening there would be a prayer meeting as usual. Mr. Lea was anxious they should take charge of that church, and his request had gone very far with him (Mr. Briggs). He might say that Mr. Lea had very much loved the people of Whiston, his mind and thoughts being continually in that direction, and, they might be sure, they were in his heart to the last. The 948th hymn was then sung, after which the rev. gentleman preached from St. Paul's First Epistle to the Thessalonians, chap. iv., verses 13 and 14, "But I would not have you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning them which are asleep, that ye sorrow not, even as others which have n 6 hope. For it we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so them also which sleep in Jesus will God bring with him." In concluding a very earnest and impressive discourse, Mr. Briggs said their late friend, Mr. Lea, was undoubtedly in ' Christ. Now, he (the preacher) was told that Mr. Lea could never point to the time and place when he first obtained a consciousness of his acceptance by God, and so one could 'speak of the time when he passed from death unto life. The process was not to be detected, not to be seen, but they knew that the change had been brought about by its results. He could not see the tendency of their minds, nor they of his, but they could judge what it was by his deportment, by his character, and by his life. He could say most confi- dently as the bereaved family could say, to all who knew Mr. Lea, that he had walked and conducted himself as a' Christian. Mr. Lea gave evidence that he was in Christ byi walking after Christ, by putting on His character, and be- lieving the gospel. Were there not many present who could testify to it? Was not his life a life of consistency, and, was he not most emphatically of oneness in Christ? Mr.i Lea came over there from Cheshire souse 28 years ago, an during the whole of his residence at Whiston they knew be had walked and conducted himself as an obedient and eon 4 Blatant disciple of Jesus. His life had been, in all respectsl as it becometh the gospel of Chriet.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY DROWNING CASE AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE EXTRAORDINARY DROWNING CASE AT WARRINGTON.

The adjourned inquiry relative to the death of Joseph Taylor, 8 years of age, son of James Taylor, tanner, Mer- sey-view, Latchford, was resumed at the Golden Lion, Latchford, on Tuesday.—P.C. Powell said that abotst 20 minutes to 8 o'clock, on the evening of the 21st June, he was at Black Bear Bridge, and saw a crowd of people on the canal bank. He enquired what was the matter, and a man told him that a boy had been drowned. On going to the spot, he found the statement correct, and enquired if any one was present at the time, when the witness, James Taylor, was poiated out to him as having been with the deceased. He asked the boy how it was his companion was drowned, ' and he said he saw the deceased playing with a dog on the bank and then saw him in the water, but did not see him fall in. He did not know whether the deceased was pushed in or whether he fell in.—The Coroner: So that he never said anything to you about having noticed the boys? Wit- ness: He did not, sir.—The Coroner : Can you give us any idea how long it would be after the occurrence took place that you were there? Witness: I was told it was about half- past seven when deceased went in, and I was there quarter of an hour afterwards.—The Coroner: And you did not see any boys running away? Witness: I did not.—The Coroner: Did you see this boatman that they talk of or the other man Dooley? Witness: I saw a man in the water, but I cannot tell who it was.—By a Juryman: There was a black dog there, and it appeared as if it had just come out of the water.—William Henry Bate, clerk, 301, linutsford- road, said at a quarter to seven o'clock on the evening of the 21st June he was passing the turnbridge over the canal at Black-lane, Latchford, and saw James Taylor and another by on the bridge, and a third boy lying on the bank and trying to pull a dog out of the water. He pulled the last mentioned boy away from the water, lifted the dog out of the canal, and then went home. On the way he turned round and saw James Taylor running across the bridge with the dog under his arm. About quarter of an hour after he got home he saw a boatman running along the bank with a pole, and he went back to the bridge and saw the deceased taken out of the canal.—By the Coroner: He did not see any boys running away. There were only three present.—By Inspector Proffitt: He had seen the body, but could not identify the deceased.—James Taylor was then re-called, but he adhered to his former statement that the bridge was pushed by some boys and that deceased tell into the water in consequence.—The Coroner, in summing up, said a more extraordinary case be certainly had not had before him since he had had his ap- pointment. He pointed out that the witness Taylor adhered to some of his statements, but in others was rather contra- dictory. But he did not suppose however much more they waited they would arrive at how the lads were there. He thought there was not the slightest doubt that the poor lad had met his death by being drowned in the canal, but whether by these lade carelessness or not would, he was afraid, be a mystery as they would never find it out. But he did not think there was any necessity to prosecute the case further. They were satisfied the lad was drowned, and he thought the jury would be justified in returning a verdict that the deceased was drowned in the canal at rfatchforcl and that certain boys at present unknown were guilty of in- human conduct in running away. That would leave it open for further proceedings to be taken if the lads were found out.—The jury agreed to this course, and an open verdict was returned.

EXTRAORDINAAY SCENE AT A FUNEBAL.—A scene of a disgraceful character took place on Wednesday, at the funeral of Mr. Bywater, auctioneer, Coseley. A short time ago Bywater publicly presented a living man with an oak coffin, and this caused great public indignation. At the ' funeral yesterday, 5,000 persons asaembled decorated with blue ribbons, and did damage to the deceased's property. Whilst the service was being performed they yelled and, shouted, and sang "Over the Garden Wall" and other popular airs. A serious disturbance followed, and several persons were badly crushed. '

WARRINGTON V. LATCHFORD.—WetTingtOO won the toss, and decided to put in their opponents on a carefully prepared wicket. Messrs. Davies and Dinwiddie were first to sippose the bowling of J. 0. Lawton and Clarke. Dinwiddie was run out quickly in attempting to run a close bye. Merry, the cap tam of the Birch Club, Manchester, next followed, but was dismissed by a good " yorker " from J. C. Lawton, with the total at eleven. Clarke was now changed for C. G. Lawton, who went on at the pavilion end. Of the remainder the only player who could make anything like a stand against the ex- cellent bowling of the brothers Lawton was J. T. Moore, who was finally dismissed by a good catch at long-on by Wallington after a well-earned thirteen. The innings closed for 0 runs. After an interval of ten minutes the batting of Warrington was commenced by the captain, H. Fairclough, and Tucker, to the bowling of Merry and Worth- ington. The were steadily rose to 23, when Tucker was bowled by a good ball from Merry. Clarke came in, and soon com- menced to make the game lively. By careful play the next wicket did not fall until 50 was registered, when Faircicugh was easily caught at wicket. Edwards followed, having the assistance of a runner, but was soon dismissed by one of Coxon's "peculiars "—three wickets for 52. England joined Clarke, and both betimes commenced to punish the bowling. Numerous changes were tried, but all were ineffectual to sepa- rate the batters, and when the stumps were drawn they were still "not out," ths total being 208. Clarke's 103 was composed of one six, four fours, eleven threes, twelve twos, and singles. This score is the highest single score that has been made for several years on the ground. He was at the wickets for two hours and ten minutes. England played steady and careful cricket for his sixty. Both players were loudly applauded on their return to the pavilion. Sr. PETER'S BELFRY.—At the Consistory Court of the diocese of Liverpool, on Tuesday, the Bev. Canon Espin presiding, an application was made by Dr. Watkins, church- warden of St. Peter's, Newton-le-Willows, for a faculty to pull dokn the present stone belfry and replace it by a wooden one, and also to repair the west window, the cost of the alterations to be defrayed by voluntary contributions. The faculty was decreed in terms of the citation. Eautats-rowts• Cuont Tarp.—The members of the Earles- town Parish Church choir, with a number of friends, took their annual trip on Saturday last. Blackpool was the spot chosen. The day was passed in visiting the numerous places of interest, with which Blackpool abounds. The members dined together during the day. Excellent arrangements were made • and their programme, which ad- mitted of some excellent harmony, was carried out to the satisfaction of all The afternoon, being fine, added con- siderably to the pleasure of the trippers. PROSECUTIONS BY.THE FACTORY INSPECTOR.-011 Satur- day, at the County Police Court, Newton-le-Willows, before Colonel McCorquodale and Messrs. J. H Birley. and R. Houghton, Messrs. Walton and Co., of the West Lancashire Flint Glass Works, were summoned at the instance of Captain Brewer, Her Majesty's inspecter for this district, for contraventions of the Factory Act by employing three chil- dren under the age of 14 years, between eleven and twelve o'clock on the night of the 26th May last. One of the chil- dren so employed was under the age of eleven years, and although it admitted having been at work for half an hour, the magistrates gave the defendant the benefit of some doubt which they considered existed in the case, and dis- missed it. In the other two cases, however, the defendants wet e convicted, and fined £3 in each case, with 17s. each costs in addition.—They were also summoned for illegally employing a child under 14 years of age in the glass-melting house on the same day, and for that offence were fined £2, and ordered to pay also .£1 2s. costs.—John Walton, em- ployed in the same works, was charged with obstructing the inspector in the discharge of his duty, and this case being also proved, the Bench inflicted a penalty of £3, he being also required to pay 17s. 6d. costs.—John Houghton, father of one of the children illegally employed at Messrs. Vi'alton's establishment, was mulcted in a penalty of ss. and 16s. costs, for allovcing his son to be employed in their glass-melting house on same dty as already mentioned._ There was a further summons against John Houghton for not sending his son to school; but this case was adjourned for a fortnight for the attendance of the school teacher, who had been summoned as a witness, but a mistake had occurred in the service of the summons. •

mit üßrimum.—The common laburnum like the corn- mon thorn, is well able to brave the smoke ()fa city and sub- sfst on the worn-out, sooty soil of the most dejected London garden. In the squares and open places we see fine trees that flower gloriousiT but occasionally we meet with pretty good examples in dirty holes and corners that seem to be utterly unfit for any kind of tree-life. But when we have I seen ihese, and been thankful that such bits of sunshine, as they seem, should drop down into nooks so needing them, and have then gone into the country and seen laburnums again, what a difference! In a really well-furnished country guden the laburnums are equal in splendour to any trees that are grown. Instead of calling them fountains we might csil them mountains of gold.—From" Familiar Garden Rowers" for July.

LORD BEACONSFIELD'S Wtta,.—The executors of Lord Beaconsfield, according to Truth, have sent in the necessary papers for the grant of probate, and have sworn the gross assets, including insurances, at £75,000, which is reduced by corresponding charges and debts to a little over £6,000, uPon which probate duty is paid, but this amount includes the valuable library, the heirlooms, and other unconvertible property. It is understood that if the whole estate were capable of immediate realisation there would be barely suf- ficient to discharge the debt upon Hughenden. Lord Beaconsfield's plate, fine works of art, and a few pictures and prints are to be sold at Messrs. Christie's rooms, billing.. street, on July 14.

- AN INDIGNANT LETTER TO THE PITEMIEL-011 Wednes- day, a conference of delegates from the industries affeated by the sugar bounties was held in London, to consider Mr. Gladstone's recent letter on the subject. Representatives from Bristol, Birmingham, Hull, Leeds, Liverpoo', Ply- mouth, Glasgow, Greenock, Dundee, Leith, and other places, attended. Mr. Kelly (London), the secretary, and the Premier's letter had aroused great indignation. He had been betrayed by the permanent officials of the Board of Trad into an erroneous statement. .A letter was drawn up in re ply, expressing disappoititment and indignation, accusing the Cabinet of sanctioning the ruin of British industry, ag threatening to transfer the question from neutral ground to a political arena. A special court composed of five judges has given an im- portant decision in an appeal relating to the payment a school fees. The appellant represented the School Board of the parish of Belgrave, Leicestershire. The respondent, being the father of a child seven years of age, was summoned for not causing his child to attend school. On the hearing the magistrates dismissed the summons. The respondent had sent his child to the school, but she was refused admis- sion in consequence of her not bringing the school fees. Lord Coleridge said what they had to consider was whether it was or was not providing elementary instruction by send- ing a child to the door of a school under circumstances which it was known would prevent the child's admission to the school. He thought not. It seemed to him clear that the object of the Act was to see that a parent did his duty and caused his child to receive efficient elementary education, and he came to the conclusion that the fees prescribed by the Board according to the code to be paid was a condition precedent to the child's entering the school. The decision of the magistrates must be reversed, and the case would be sent back to the magistrates to rehear and decide upon. The other learned Judges concurred. A ',atm COMPANY IN DIFFICULTIES.—On Monday the directors of the Midland Land and Investment Company, Limited, issued circulars to the shareholders recommending that the affairs of the undertaking should be voluntarily wound up in liquidation. Nominally the assets show a balance to the good of £71,436 over the liabilities, but thin estimate is based on the assumption that the undertaking is a going concern, and the directors have lent £60,000, for which they hold no security. They express the fear that an adverse winding up would result in serious losses. The cause assigned for the failure is the depreciation in value of land and buildings. The Birmingham Post says that the properties belonging to the company consist of land, house property, and other buildings in Birmingham; in various parts of London; as Knutsford, in Cheshire; and in other places. Amongst these in Birmingham are valuable pro- perties at Aston, in Walmer-lane, at Highgate, and the offices of the company in Colmore-row. It is only proper to add that the hankers of the Land Corporation, the Birming- ham and Midland Bank, are fully secured.

Herr Most, of the Emilteit, was brought up at the Central ' Criminal Court, on Wedne.day, for sentence. Lord Cole- ridge said the prisoner had been convicted of a foul libel, and his offence was aggravated because while in safety hina- self he had incited,others to commit murder. He was liable to a sentence of penal servitude, but considering the jury's recommendation,tchmercy the sentence would be 16 months' imprisonment with bard labour. A conference 0 licensed victuallers in connection with the National Defence League was held at Westminster, on Wednesday. A resolution was passed deprecating the bills , for closing public-houses on Sundays, referring more par- ticularly to the Welsh bill, the third reading of which is fixed for July 3. Delegates from 250 towns attended. The Coroner's inquest relative to the explosion at the Bucknall Colliery, near Hanley, by which eight lives were lost, was concluded on Wednesday. The explosion was caused by the ignition of an accumulation of gas forced on to naked lights by a rush of water from some old workings, which were pierced in the process of driving a " thirling.' It was stated by the mines inspector that there had been a breach of the Mines Regulation Act in the neglect to make bore-holes, .1' hi c h would have indicated the PrirnitY of water, and in the use of naked lights in a seam which W 35 of known to be gassy; and the jury returned a manslaughter against Mr. Perrins, owner and manager o the colliery. verdict i THE CHURCH IN WALES. THE YEW CHAPEL AT PRFSCOT WORKHOUSE. LAYING .A/UNDATION STONE. On Thursday afternoon the "cereelatty of laying the foundation-stone of the new Workhouse Chapel took place in the presence of a large number of Guardians, tho inmates ' and officials of the Workhouse, and a number of ratepe.vers and others. The weather was very inclement, rain descend- ing nearly the whole of the time. The chapel will be of the Gothic style of architecture, and will be built of brick with stone facings. Accommodation will be provided for 250 persons; and the estimated cost of the building is £l,OOO. There ,will be two vestries and two entrances to the chapel, one of each for the Protestants and the other fer the Roman Catholics. The pulpit, altar rails, and seats will be for the common use of all. The architect is Mr. Gandy, of St. Helens, and the builder Mr. Wm. Gore, of Gateacre. The company having assembled near the site of the building a portion of a specially-prepared order of service was gone through, the officiating clergyman being the Rev. J. H. Scott, vicar of Whiston, after which Mr. Wm. Tyrer, on behalf of the Guardians and officials of the Workhouse, presented the Rev. T. Chambers with a silver trovilel and an ivory mallet inlaid with silver, and formally requested him to lay the foundation atone. The trowel bore the following inscription :—"Presented by the Guardians arid officers of the Prescot Union, to the Rev. Thomas Chambers, M. A., upon his laying the foundation stone of the Workhouse Chapel, Whiston, June 30th 1881." Mr. Chambers sin- cerely thanked the Guardians and the 'officers of the Union, for the very handsome trowel and mallet they had presented to him. In the course of his life he had received manypresents and had many souvenirs of interest, but be promised them that amongst all the treasures he possessed the trowel and ' mallet would occupy a prominent place, if not the most prominent. (Hear, hear.) He should keep them as long as he lived, and regard them not only as a souvenir of that interesting and memorable occasion, but also because they had taken the opportunity of showing him their goodwill and kind regards by presenting him with that very hand- some testimonial. (Applause.) The rev, gentleman then laid the stone in a workmanlike manner. Under the stone was placed a bottle containing a copy of The St. Helens Examiner and Prescot Wecklg News, and other papers, with some come; also a doeoriplion of the building, the architects and builders' names, a list of the names sr the Board of Guardians, chief officers, &c. The following was engraved on the face of the stone :—"This stone was laid by the Rev. Thomas Chambers, M.A.. June 30th, 1881." After laying the stone, the rev, gentleman said to him that day was a very happy one, inasmuch as he had been permitted te lay the foundation stone of the church for the Joint use of t'he Protestants and Roman Catholics who were, and might be, inmates of that Union Workhouse. He could not refrain from stating that during his absence from home he had observed from a report of the last Board meeting that an objection was raised to the site selected. He read with considerable surprise and regret the discussion on the subject. He was glad, however, that the expiring efforts of one or two of hie brother guardians were frustra- ted, and that the business of that day had not been needlessly and vexatiously delayed. He was at a loss to conceive why the objection was not raised before the plans were sent to London and sanctioned by the Local Government Board. The subject had been duly considered and discussed, and it was at the Chairman's suggestion, if he remembered rightly, that—to use his own words—" the bit of ground at the east end " was selected ; and he hesitated not to state that in his Opinion it wee the best place they could have chosen. If tbe workhouse had to be enlarged, and no doubt it would be at some future time, let the new buildings be erected in the field on the other side, thereby making an egress for the poor infirm persons from either part of the house, so that they may Meet in the church, which will be centrally placed, and so save a long walk, which in their condition of health is much to be desired. Besides, what could be more in good taste or uniformity than that this ecclesiastical building, such as that chapel would be, should be the scene and recognised centre of that spiritual life of which, as Guar- dians of the Prescot Union, they were bound to provide for, as well as the temporal wants of, the poor creatures committed to their charge? The new offices of the new board room would find in good time their own place, and should be held snb- ordinate to making provision for the worship of Almightly God, which demanded their first care, and in the act which they had performed had found its due, though tardy, recognition. Comment had been made and speculation had been rife as to how the scheme for the worship of the two denominations would answer. He might tell them that he had no doubt whatever about its success in his own mind. It had been found to answer in gaols, garrison towns, and continental cities, notably in Baden Baden, when the Lutherans, members of the church, and Roman Catholics had worshipped at different times in one building, and that a Roman Catholic cathedral. The only matter to settle between the officiating ministers was the hour of service, and he felt that on this point there would be no difficulty. The arrangement might be safely left in the hands of the chaplain and the Rev. Father Henry. His experience of the Rev. F. Henry in arranging the details for the con- struction of the building with a view to the services of the Roman Catholics and Protestants, had led him to that con- clusion. He might state that the pulpit, altar rails, and seats would be for the common use of all. The longer be lived the more was he convinced that "the unity, peace, and concord," which they all desired and prayed for, would best be realised by a harmonious working together of the clergy and ministers of all denominations. (Hear, hear.) He might illustrate that by giving them his own recent experience. Al the workhouse be had been engaged most Pleasantly and cordially with the Rev. Father Henry in carrying out the details of that building, whilst, at the same time, at the far end of his parish he had been working on equally pleasant terms, on a school committee, with two excellent Wesleyan ministers. The maxim which e had. made, his Own, throughout hie somewhat prolonged ordained life, was:— "Unity in essentials. Liberty in non-essentials, Charity in an things." (Loud applause.) This was the spirit in which the idea for the building of that church was concerned; that was the spirit in which it had been carried out, and he should wish it to be engraven on the foundation-stone if possible. (Renewed applause.) The company then separated, and the guardians partook of refreshment in the board-room. CIIZSTER ELECTION.—Private information has reached Chester that the writ for a fresh election is not likely to be long delayed. Mr. Cornwallis West will be One of the Liberal candidates, but the second has net yet been selected. The Right Hon C. Raikes will, it is said, contest the city in the Conservative interest. A communication has been re- ceived from the Lords Commissioners of Her Majesty's Treasury calling upon the City authorities of Chester to pro- vide the sum of £3,352, the expenses of the inquiry into the corrupt practices at the election. To raise this sum it will be necessary to levy a rate of between 54. and ed. in the pound, a much smaller amount than was generally antici- pated in the city from the length and minuteness of the inquiry.

of the police in permitting Lefroy to al) out of their reach has for the present deprived them of the evidence of one witness who is able to unravel the mystery. The state in which Lefroy reached Brighton, and the condition of the carriage, proved that he had had a desperate struggle with some one ; but whether that struggle was with the " countryman " •or with Mr. Gould does not yet appear. The countryman seems as yet only to have a mythical existence, and if such a person did travel with Mr. Gould and Lefroy it appears strange that he should have so unaccount- ably disappeared, for even murderers do not seek safety by jumping from trains when running at ex- press speed as this train was. Whoever the murderer was, he seems to have gone about his work in an unprecedented manner, for although he evidently used a pistol, he killed his victim by cutting and wounding. Whether Lefroy's injuries were other than such as he might have suf- fered in a struggle in which he was the assailant does not appear from the evidence of the doctor who attended his wounds, and it is obvious that much may turn upon this point. Meanwhile, the case has its warnings and its lessons as well as its mysteries, and it is not even now too soon to infer from it one or more lessons as to the conditions under which railway travelling is conducted here, more especially as a murderous assault is alleged to have been committed on Thursday night upon a clergyman between War- rington and Liverpool. Both these cases prove that the present means of communication with the driver or guard of a train is by no means an infallible source for passengers in peril. This second outrage occurring so soon after the more serious one at Balcombe is not calculated to reassure timid people, who are now likely to fancy that an assassin may lurk in every railway carriage. With these incidents fresh in the public mind, it is not only timid people who will ask whether it is altogether compatible with public safety that trains passing through long tunnels should be un- provided with lights, and whether the present system of building a carriage in compartments is the best that can be devised—better than the American ssytem, which allows free passage from one end of a train to another, and which is there- fore free from the sometimes fatal danger of isola- tion. The most ordinary observer will admit that neither of these outrages could have been commit- ted with such impunity in a carriage built on the American system.

div.head: LOCAL NOTES.
div.p: LOCAL NOTES.

The gentleness of womaa has often been dwelt upon by our poets. She has been spoken of as "a ministering angel" when pain and anguish wring the brow, and so she may be; but there is another side of the picture, judging by proceedings which have lately taken place in Widnes Police Court. One woman named Ann Quinn has been committed to the Liverpool Quarter Sessions on a charge of biting a piece off a woman's ear, and another is awaiting her trial for kicking another female in a most frightful manner. Such proceedings as these remind one of Otway's flees

"What mighty ills have not been done by woman? Who was't betrayed the Capital? A woman! Who lost Mark Antony the world? A woman! Who was the cause of a long ten years' war, And laid at lest old Troy in ashes? Woman! " Well, I would not subscribe to these lines, but say that it is even pleasant at times to be deceived, when the deceiver is some fair daughter of Eve. Mr. R. B. Starr, of London, still goes on hammering away at his delightfully charming theme "Why Pay Rent? " and in the Runcorn and Widnes district he has got many to determine upon giving the Starr-Bowkett Society a fair trial. Of course, the path of a member of such a society will not be strewn with roses. Benefits in this life must be paid a certain price for, and there is no proposal that can be sub- mitted which has not its shady side. The law of 3ompen- sation prevails in all things. During one evening last week the West Bank Board Schools, Widnes, had a very narrow escape of being burned down owing to the alleged carelessness on the part of some one. Pending investigation, it may be prudent to say little on the matter; but when it is remembered that the schools cost the ratepayers several thousand pounds—l believe abeut ' .£6,ooo—it will be admitted that the enquiry ought to be conducted to "the bitter end," wherever that may lead. One I will begin to think that the manner in which the various political parties have praised the British workmen of late years, has tended to make him careless, and, iu some cases, remarkably thick in the skull. Who can forget the man- ner in which the landing stage at Liverpool was destroyed 'by the child-like proceedings of a workman who was evi- dently a thorough simpleton ? ' Th.° Census Office officials in London are evidently deter- mined to throw the cegis of their protection over all docu- ments which have came into their possession during the numbering of the people. They have refused to supply the Widnes School Board authorities with certain particulars required for making educational statistics.

Notwithstanding the curious character of the weather, the Northern Counties Championship meeting at Widnes proved a capital success. However, as it is considered by the com- mittee that the gathering was not one in which local men had a sufficient chance of proving successful competitors, I hear there is to be another meeting within a very short time. The Widnes School Board have not accepted the sugges- tion of Mr. Owens, who was understood to speak on behalf of the Nonconformists, that the vacancy caused by the dis- qualification of Mr. Martin Taylor, should be filled by the election of Mr. Stringer, but their choice has fallen upon Mr. Hartland, a gentleman who was for many years a mem- ber of the Board. Perhaps this the wisest course they could have adopted considering the fact that Mr. Hartland was generally liked by the members, and that he understands the work, which a new member would be a considerable time in learning.

However various may be the opinions held as to the manner in which the members of the Salvation Army carry on their spiritual warfare against " the world, the flesh, and the devil," there are very few amongst your readers who will be inclined to say that they are not entitled to protec- tion, so long as they do not become a public nuisance. If it affords them any gratification to carry a flag inscribed with the terrible letters "Blood and Fire," and to fall in line for the purpose of aping the doings of the brave defenders of our country, why should their original plan of campaigning be interfered with. Their boldest opponent must admit that they show an ability to draw into their halls and "salvation factories" many who are "without God and without hope in the world," who would never dream 7f entering the chapels and churches, in many of which it would be a very easy matter indeed to find abundance of room for them. The members Of the Wesleyan and other denominations carry on home mission work in a certain fashion; but from a conver- sation which I had the other day with a labourer in this particular field, I am given to understand that it is not un- frequently found that the superintendent of a circuit takes a very lukewarm interest in this special kind of evangelistic work, and is very seldom seen at the mission room. Another difficulty attends the home mission work of these denomina- tions. It appears that the missionary is instructed to do his best to get those who have joined or other to attend the cause at the mission to become connected with what is spoken of as "the big chapel." div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 2, 1881.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 2, 1881.

The Rev. Chancellor Espin, when, presiding the other day at the Liverpool Consistory Court, and fixing the fees to be charged for marriages at Newburgh Church, near Orme- kirk, remarked that if the fees for marriages in church were higher than those charged by the registrar, it had a tendency to send people to be married elsewhere. It appears that this v‘xed question of fees for marriages has occupied serious attention its other parts of the world besides Lancashire, for I learn that in the Far West squabbles frequently arise respecting the officiating ministers' fees. The .Albany Sunday Press states that a peaceably minded parson has recently published a carefully graduated scale of his charges to avoid mistakes. It is as follows :—" One marriage plain, eight shillings; ditto, kissing the bride, twelve shillings; ditto, trimmed with one groomsman and one bridesmaid, sixteen shillings; two shillings extra for each additional groomsman or bridesmaid. Bachelors past forty charged extra, maidens of age ten per cent. off. Mileage will be charged in long distance matches; liberal reduction to clubs. Payment in cash; no money refunded for poor goods. Come early and come often." - -

The articles bearing the title "Travels in the East" have attracted considerable notice in Runcorn and Widnes. I have read many similar productions in newspapers, but none written in a more graphic and interesting manner; and in slying this I believe lam giving the general opinion of of those of your readers who are entitled to judge.

The very commodious building lately occupied by Mr Thos. Beasley, in Waterloo-road, Runcorn, who has removed to Overton, belongs to the Board of Commissioners, and there is some talk of utilising it for the public offices. There will, undoubtedly, be a difficulty in finding any Runcorn gentleman who will pay the large rent demanded for a house, the situation of which has been so much injured of late years. I One would very much like to know how much longer the work of making a slope to the railway footbridge at Run- corn, is to be delayed.

- , Waterloo Bridge is still in the same state as ever, and from what I hear, is likely to continue a disgrace to the town in wet weather. Most of the commissioners use the Hector's Bridge, and surely the ordinary ratepayers can afford to wait a little longer for "the good time coming." The meeting of Runcorn ratepayers, on Thursday night, proved a very tame affair indeed. The day when these gatherings were of so lively character as to form capital newspaper reading to those who were of an humourous turn, seems to have gone. It must afford the ratepayers gratifica- tion to know that it is pretty certain such meetings will in future be held in Bethesda Congregational school-room. The room in Alcock-street was a veritable black-hole of Calcutta on ratepayers' gatherings,, as those who were so much interested in town's matters as to go through the discomfort of attending, were packed like herrings in a barrel, and com- pelled to breathe a most vitiated atmosphere. No wonder that under such circumstances the war of words, at times, became.something terrible to hear, and pereonalities were most freely indulged In. At the meeting On Thursday even, ins., Mr. George Moss was elected a member of the Burial Board, and Messrs. Thomas Norman and James Handley, who have most ably discharged their duties whilst acting as the ratepayers' representatives in the past. were re-elected unanimously. Mr. George Marshall must have given offence to a strong section of the rate- payers, for there was not a single person present who was bold enough to submit his name to the meeting. Possibly his somewhat extreme action on the Sabbatarian question as affecting the cemetery may have had something to do with the matter. Mr. Moss is likely to prove a shrewd and prac- tical member.

I hear that some of the Local Board members at Widnes are moving with the object of getting Mr. Allen, ac- countant, appointed as clerk to attend to the general busi- ness, and employing a legal gentleman specially whenever they require the aid of his services. FLACCUS.

WIDNES CONGREGATIONAL SUNDAY SGUOOL.—On Sunday the anniversary sermons of this school were preached, in the morning by the Rev. C. Bingant, Wesleyan Methodist superintendent, and in the evening by the Rev. J. Yonge, of Wycliffe Chapel, Warrington. In the after- noon the Rev. T. Carver (Baptist) delivered an address to the scholars and friends. Collections were made after each service.

PROSPEOTFVE RUNCORN SCLIOOL EXIMTNTIONS.—It 18 I stated that H. M. Inspector of schools is to hold his animal visit at the various places and on the dates mentioned below, viz.:—Mill Brow Board School, July 4th; the Roman Catholic schools, July sth; Holy Trinity girls, July 11th; Holy Trinity boys and infants, July 12th; the Parish Church school, 13th and 14th; Shaw-street Mission, 14th; the Wesleyan schools, 20th and 21st. MESSRS. GOSSAGE AND Sorts' Excunsrox.-On Saturday, the workpeeple belonging to Messrs. Gossage and Sons' firm, Widnes, had their annual out, which is provided by the employers. Though the weather was of a most unfavourable character at the time rod In.- .t.rti^s iron, WM.°o to th° place of destination—Southport—two trains were despatched from the London and North Western Station, with excur- sionists numbering about 200. The morning proved a rather cheerless one for the pleasure seekers, but the weather during the rest of the day was of a very fair description. The return journey commenced at half past six, and Wid- nes was reached a little after eight o'clock. Much credit is due to Mr. Sansom, the station master, for the admirable manner in which the arrangements for the despatch of the passengers were carried out. NELSON-STREET WESLEYAN MISSION 13 alit OF HOPE.- On Monday evening, the monthly meeting (being the last of this session) was held in the above Mission-room. Eighty children and fifty adults belonging to the Band of Hope sat down to an excellent tea provided at the expense of Mr. Thomas Norman. The schoolroom was very tastefully decorated for the occasion with choice ferns and flowers and suitable mottoes, and reflected great credit upon the ladies who took part in putting up the decorations. The follow- ing ladies presided at the tables: Miss Withington, Miss Cooper, and Miss Kirkham. After tea the public meeting was held, and owing to the unavoidable absence of Mr. Thomas Norman, Mr. Jno. Withington occupied the chair. The entertainment was a very enjoyable one, and highly appreciated by the large audience. During the evening several recitations were given by the children belonging to ithe Band of Hope, and temperance songs ind duetts by members of the Camden choir, '

SERIOI:79 WOI7NDING CABII AT IttiNooll24.--.A.t the Cheshire Quarter Sessions, on Thursday, before Mr. J. Wood and other magistrates, Dominick Coleman, 21, and Patrick Coleman, 24, labourers, brothers, were indicted for having unlawfully wounded Thomas Hughes, at Halton, on the Bth of June. Mr. Burke Wood prosecuted, and the prisoners were defended by Mr. Marshall. On Whit-Monday afternoon, prosecutor was going from Halton to Runcorn, when he met the prisoners. Dominick called him a foul name, tripped him up, and threw him on the loon The other prisoner, Patrick, kicked him on the head, which caused him to bleed very much. He was kicked several times about the body, but he put his hands over his eyes and could not see who kicked him when on the ground. The prosecutor was taken to Dr. McDougall's. who examined him and found a wound one and a half inches long on his head, penetrating to the bone, which seemed to have bled prorusely.—The jury found Patrick guilty of unlawfully wounding, and Dominick guilty of a common assault. The former was sentenced to nine months' and the latter to six months' hard labour.

A Yountrut BURGLAR, AT RUNCORN. —At the Knutsford Quarter Sessions, on Wednesday, Robert Wm. Barrow, 17, labourer, was indicted for having entered the office of Messrs. Walker, flint mer chants, Runcorn, and stolen therefrom two coats, the property of George Moss; a Coat, the property of Charles Povrnall ; three coats, belong- ing to Charles Potter Walker;_ and 58 postage stamps, the property of John Walker. He was further charged with stealing a shirt, a pair of drawers, a pound of ham, and other articles, the property of Joseph Sidley, at Runcorn, on the 25th of May. Prisoner pleaded guilty. Mr. Burke Wood, Iwho prosecuted, stated that some of the articles were stolen Ilfrom'a boat belonging to the Bridgewater Navigation Co., which was in the graving dock at Runcorn. undergoing re- pairs. The lockers in the cabin had been locked up by the captain on the night of the 25th of May: on going the fol- lowing morning he found the place had been broken into and Ithe lockers prized open with a marlin spike, and the things abstracted. The prisoner was subsequently apprehended and he made a statement to the police constable in which he admitted he took the things, and he also pleaded guilty to breaking into the offices of Messrs. Walker, who carried on business as flint merchants, at Runcorn, and stealing a number of coats. Panes of glass had been broken in the window, so as to enable the prisoner to enter. Six drawers had been forced with the marlin spike, wi.ich had been stolen fron the boat, and which was found in the office. Fifty-eight postage stamps had been taken from one of the drawers. Some time after the robbery a number of men who were walking along the canal bank discovered a parcel which contained the stolen coats. The prisoner, it appeared, rob- bed the boat, then went to office, and amongst other things he stole a pair of handcuffs.—The prisoner was sentenced to imprisonment for 12 months and one day. SAD ACCIDENT TO A BOY AT HUTTON QA.RILY.—On Monday evening, a sad accident happened to Henry Kil- shaw, five years of age, soa of James Kilshaw, of Edge-hill, whoLi e wasrpoo 10. n aO sti th et ehvi es ngi nr ag in d was playing in the school yard close by, and, while climbing nm ocit hu ee rst tn HthueyltiotntleQfueal lrorwy: over a wall, he fell and broke one of his legs just above the ankle. Dr. Gorst was called in, and he set the injured limb, and the boy is now progressing in a favourable manner. A young woman named M‘Kelvey was tried at th Central Criminal Court, on Thursday, for the murder of abailiff named John Martin, by throwing vitriol on his face and head. The jury stopped the case and acquitted the accused.

ACCIDENTS AT RUNCORN.—The 24th ult, was an un- lucky day at Messrs. Wigg Bros. and Steele's works, Old Quay, Runcorn, as three accidents happened upon it. The first was to a young man named George Orme, Mason-street, whose right eye was injured by some sulphuric acid falling upon it. The second, to a young man named Wm. Henry Hayes, stone-street, who had one of his hands drawn into some machinery which was in motion, and badly crushed. The third was to Thomas Wainwright, of Shaw-street, who received severe scalds through falling into hot copper liquor. The men were attended by Dr. Mouritz, and are now doing well. A WIDNES COLLECTOR OF SUBSCRIPTIONS DECAMPS.— A few weeks ago the timekeeper at Messrs. James Muspratt and Sons' works, Widnes, left under somewhat peculiar circumstances, and a number of his fellow workmen decided to raise him a subscription. A certain man, who not long ago came from the district of St. Helens, made himsetf very prominent in the matter, and collected about £l5 outside the works; but he is now missing, and is stated to have gone to the United States. The result is that the proposed subscription has fallen through, and as the collector is said to have taken his subscription book and the money which it represents with him, no doubt with the object of pushing his fortunes in the dominions of Uncle Sam. Fortunately, the rogue did not get hold of another £5 or £B, which had been . collected by the foremen, and this, we understand, has been given back to the subscribers, the proposal to make a pre- sentation to the timekeeper having come to an untimely end.

PRESENTATION AT RUNCORN. —On Wednesday even- ing, the choir of the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Runcorn, gave a complimentary tea in Regent-street schoolroom to Miss C. E. Morton, eldest daughter of the Rev. Jos. Morton, superintendent minister of this station, who is leaving the town for the Widnes and Warrington circuit. After tea had been partaken of, and the tables cleared, Mr. E. Billingsley, the organist, stepped forward and said: —"Ladies and gentlemen,—You all know we are about to loose Miss Mor- ton, a contralto voice in our choir. She has now been with us a long time, during which she has put in a greater Hum- ber of attendances than any other member of the choir. She was very rarely absent either morning or evening, and this proves she did not consider it 'a task ' but just the reverse, viz., 'a pleasant duty.' If all members of choirs would emulate this spirit we should rarely see empty choir pews. (Applause.) Miss Metton has by her frank open- hearted manner made herself very dear to us, and we all regret having to part with her. The place occupied by her in the choir will not easily be filled up. Her delight ap- peared to be in doing her best. I trust she will shine still brighter in her fresh fields of labour. We could not part with her without making her some slight present as a memento of the esteem and respect we feel towards her. With this in view, at a meeting held by the choir, I sug- gested a lady's silver watch with suitable inscription in the interior and a Whitby jet chain. This was agreed to, and I think I never received a more spontaneous and willing subscription, the result being that I have to present you, Miss Morton, on behalf of the choir, with this watch and chain. I ask your kind acceptance of it, and trust God will bless you with good health and long life to wear it, and that wherever you may be and what- ever circumstance you may be placed in, you will never forget your Runcorn friends. (Loud applause.) Miss Morton (who appeared quite taken by surprise at the gift), attempted to reply, but was so overcome that she had to sit down. Her father (the Rev. Joseph Morton), who was present,: said: Ladies and gentlemen—l have had many surprises in my life. The first was, when my first child, a daughter, was born 21 years ago. I was very fond of her, naturally so. I have had many similar surprises since, but I dearly love my first, who is the recipient of your handsome present this evening. I may say that she is ardently attached to our cause, and is always anxious and willing to be doing, whether it be in the choir, in the Sunday school, or any other office, her greatest desire is to be active. As you are aware, myself and wife have not had the best of health—far from it—during our sojourn in Runcorn. This will account for many of my shortcomings. Ido not know how it is you don't give me a present. (Laughter.) You know lam both good looking and eligible. However, it has come into the family; so the daughter has made up for the father. I have to thank you, Mr. Billingsley, and all the choir for giving this handsome present to my daughter, and also for the kind feelings you have manifested towards her. I know she will prize it, and will never forget whereever her lot may be cast, her Runcorn friends—the Primitive Methodist Choir. (Loud applause.) The remainder of the evening was passed in playing the usual games on these occasions, and spending a very pleasant time together. a - •

- - - SOCIETY OF CITEISICAL INDIISTMES.—The first general meeting of the Society of Chemical Industries was held on Tuesday, at the Institute of Civil Engineers, Great George- street, Westminster, under the presidency of Professor Roscoe, of Victoria University, Manchester. Although the society was only formed three months ago, it now numbers upwards of 300 members, who are connected with the chemical trade in different countries. The trade of Widnes, St. Helens, and Liverpool was largely represented. After the secretary (Mr. George E. Davies) had read the report, showing the progress the society had made since its forma- tion, Mr. E. K. Muspratt (of Liverpool and Widnes) read a paper on the recent legislation on noxious gases, and re- ferred to the various laws and enactments which had been ' made from time to time for the purpose of diminishing,the nuisance createdby noxious gases. He said that those who had studied the effect of large quantities of coal smoke admitted the blighting effect it had upon vegetation and the discolouring effect on building stone. He also spoke of the injury done by the emission of hydroohlorio acid from alkali works, and stated that for the purpose of mitigating the nuisance in Liverpool and Lancashire tall chimneys were constructed. Mr. Muspratt also said that be consi- dered that the aim of legislation ought to be to enforce the adoption of the beet praCtiaid means for the condensation or the rendering harmless of noxious fumes whereever and however produced, He next referred to the Alkali Bill now before Parliament, and said that it would be seen front a MOO of it that very little progress had been made in legislation affecting noxious gases. He criticised several of the clauses of the bill, and gave as his opinion that the bill of the present session would have very little effect in silencing the Noxious Gas Association of Lancashire, and the complaints of the South-Eastern Sanitary Association of London. A discussion on Mr. Muspratt's paper followed, and a vote of thanks was accorded him. Professor Roscoe, in an address, alluded to alkali manufacture, remarked that Englishmen would be proud of the work they had accom- plished in that great field. It was not too much to say that since the discovery of the process of manufacturing alkali from common salt by M. Is Blanc important improvements in this branch of industry had been effected by Englishmen. In proof of this he need only mention the names of Look, Muspratt, Gossage, Gamble, Shanks, Glover, Hargreaves, Deacon, and Weldon. Each of the names of the persons mentioned not only represented a revolution in some part of the process, but taken together they recalled the only revelutionary Change which the country had produced. The proceedings were continued on Wednesday morning, Pro- fessor Roscoe, of Victoria University, again presiding. Dr. Siemens read a paper on the use of coal gas as a heating agent, in the course of which he argued that by the use of gaseous fuel the nuisance caused by the emissions of smoke would be obviated. He advocated different supplies of gas for domestic use, one of a high quality for illuminating pur- poses, and the other of a cheaper and poorer description for heating purposes. If gas heating comes into general use three or four times the present supply would be required, and in meeting the demand he suggested that gas companies should lay down two sets of mains. Professor Roscoe said the suggestion was a bold one, and he hoped it would receive the attention which its importance and originality deserved.

WARRINGTON UNION SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMTSITTEE. —A. meeting of the committee was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday, the Rev. G. F. Roberts in the chair, and present the Rev. John Yonge, Messrs. Garnett, Day hysh ire, Cooper, S. Sutton (assistant clerk) and 13 Hobson ( ttend thee officer.) Mr. Hobson reported that during the p,st month, three schools had increased their average attendance. time had decreased, and two remained tl,o s 'me as last moot). Win- wick school showed the I ~rgeq inrrez.se, Or hr] et me next, and Penketb followed with a small increase. The school holidays during the past month had been one cause of the decrease in attendance another cause doubtless being that in those schools which bad passed the Government examination some scholars had been withdrawn for work, and their places had not been filled up by new scholars. He noticed that the school attendance committee of the borough thought of ap- plying to the Education Department for permission to reduce the standard from the 3rd to the Sud for half time employ- ment. If that was done he was afraid he would experience some difficulty respecting their byelaws, when they con- sidered that the committee's standard for half time employ- ment ard full time employment was the 4th standard, and it was desirable the standards for both half time employment and full time employment should be as nearly uniform as could be got for the better working of the Education Act, especially by those school attendance committees or districts joining eaeh other, as scholars living in one district go to school, and also wished to go to work in another district, or vice versa. The Chairman remarked that 11Ir. Hobson was an- ticipating a difficulty which might not arise, and on the suggestion of Mr. Derbyshire. the matter was postponed for a month.—A letter was read from the Chairman of the Man- chester School Board, enclosing copy of a memorial which had been drawn up at a conference of school committees, and expressing a hope that the committee would co-operate with them by forwarding to the Educational Department as soon as possible a separate memorial in the same or similar terms. The substance of the memorial was that the memorialists wished the granting of school fees in non-pauper cases to be removed from the Guardians to School Attendance Com- mittee. In a short discussion which ensued, the members did not see their way to adopt the memorial, which was left over until the next meeting.—The Assistant Clerk read a letter from Messrs. Buckton, Greenall and Co., enclosing an account of .£3 4s. for prosecutions under the Education Act. A conversation took place, from which it appeared that the amount was for the costs of summonses which fell upon the committee, and the clerk said it was a great shame that a summons and order should cost 83. 6d., but it was accord- ing to the scale fixed by the county. He, however, expressed his willingness to see the magistrates' clerks on the matter, and the committee agreed to this course. Ask for MARGERISON'S Registered White Windsor SOAP Preston, 40. pound.
