Pnoxonow FOR TILE Ram. Wx. RoaxxsoN, OF RUN- corm—The Rev. W. Robinson, curate of Holy Trinity Church, Runcorn, has been appointed senior curate of St. David's, Neath, near Swansea, of which the Yen. Archdeacon Griffith, 8.D., is rector, and be will commence his duties about the end of this month.

THREATENING LETTER TO THE BISHOP or LIVERPOOL. —lt is stated that the Right Rev. Dr. Ryle, Bishop of Liver- pool, has received a threatening letter, which was of such a nature that the police authorities have thought it advisable to place two extra constables on duty in the immediate vicinity of his lordship's residence in Abercrombv-square.

THE REORGANIZATION OF THE ARMY.-Mr. Childers, after full consideration, has decided to increase the number of Militia Engineer Regiments y hen the forthcoming Re- organization of the Army is carried out as it was it first proposed to do, it having been pointed out that the duties of Military Engineers are such as to necessitate a great deal of extra time being demanded from both officers and men to enable them to obtain an insight into the scientific subjects which form an important part of their training. MYSTERIOUS AFFAIR IN CitxsitruE.—On Tuesday evening the son of Mr. Darlington, Snab Farm, Cheshire, aged 19, was found in the road near Mr. Dodd's, of Chol- mondeley. He was conveyed to Mr. Dodd's, but only lived one hour. All he was able to state was that he had been thrown out of a trap. The cause of death is, however, most mysterious, as the only mark on him was a slight bruise on the leg. An inquest will be held. Much sympathy is ex- pressed for deceased's parents and relations, he being a very promising young man. - -

- - THE CAsit or THE Ray. S. F. Grugus.—The Church Association declined •to give their consent for the appointment of an early day for the hearing of the appeal in the case of the Rev. S. F. Green. Therefore, as there are ab nit 20 cases with priority of claim awaiting hearing in the House of Lords, it is possible that some months may elapse before the case can be reached. This decision on the part of the Church Association is looked upon by the rev, gentleman's friends as a vindictive one, and has caused great surprise, as it was confidently ex- pected that being a case affecting Ihe liberty of the subject it would be heard before the long vacation. The reverend gentleman's legal advisers will, it is expected, move ex parte for an early day, notwithstanding the refusal of the prose- tion to give their consent.

UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH, NORTHIVICH.—The quarterly meeting of the. Northwich circuit of the United Methodist Free Churches was held in the school-room of Witton-street Chapel, on Monday last, Mr. George Dutton presiding. The Rev. J. Batten expressed his intention to retire from this circuit at the expiration of the year ending August, 1882, and a committee was appointed to invite a suc- cessor. Mr. George Slater was elected representative to the Annual Assembly in London. The financial statement showed that the income did not quite meet the expenditure. The Rev. J. Batten gave a very interesting account of the Liverpool and Northwich district recently held at Aberyst- with. An increase of 20 in the district was reported, and of 800 in the connexion. A tote of thanks to the Rev. J. Batten for his interesting and encouraging report was unani- mously adopted.

- - At the Preston Quarter Sessions, on Wednesday, a man named Thomas Strickland, who had beaten his wife with a poker to the peril of her life, was sentenced to five years' penal servitude, the Chairman (Mr. Higgin, Q.C.) remarking that it was his Intention, if he could do so, to teach people like the prisoner that they could not kick one another or pick up a poker and at the brains out of their wives or neighbours simply to gratify a momentary passion. The learned Chairman seems to regard these attempts at wife murder with less complacency than "Her Majesty's Judges," and nobody but the Bill Sikeses themselves will regret if the magistrates of the County will remit all such cases to his jurisdiction instead of sending them to courts of assize, which used to be a tribunal much dreaded by domestic savages of Mr. Strickland's class.

THE AMALGAMATED ASSOCIATION OF OPERATIVE COTTON SPINNERS, &c.—A representative meeting of this association was held on Sunday in Manchester, 45 districts being re- presented. Amongst other business there was a discussioa on the wages question, as affected by the present system of payment, there having for a long time back been a feeling amongst spinners that payment by weight was liable to great abase on account of the tendency to spin the yarn finer than the spinner was paid for. In many districts the difficulty has been obviated by inducing payment by length, with indicators to register the work done, which has had the best results, and is giving satisfaction to all concerned. These points were fully brought forward by the representa- tives from Mossley, who made an application for support in their attempts to get the master spinners to adopt the sys- tem. The following resolution was unanimously passed "Believing that the system of payment by length of yarn spun as measured by indicators is sound in principle and equitable in practice, this meeting hereby expresses its satisfaction at the efforts being made by the Mossley spin- ners to obtain its adoption, and agrees to render them every support required." NORTHERN CIRCIIIT.—TITE SIIMZER ASSIZES, ISSI. The following circular has been issued by the Clerk of Assize and Associate :—The commission for holding these assizes will be opened at Carlisle on IVeduesday, the 6th July.; at Appleby on Friday, the Bth July; at Lancaster on Saturday, the 9th July; at Manchester on Wednesday, the 13th July; and at Liverpool on Tuesday, the 26th July. In pursuance of "The Rules of the Supreme Court, December, 1179," causes may, at any time after notice of trial has been given, be entered for trial in the district registry of the city or town where the trial is to be had, or with the associate at the assize town as heretofore. The general entry of causes assize town will commence immediately after the opening of the reepeCtlYe commissions, and will close at nine o'clock the same evening. On entering a cause, two copies of the pleadings must be lo:!:ed, one for the use 4:4 the judge and the other for the associate. Soiiel fere are requested to endorse very shortly on the pleadings the nature of the action—e.g., "slander," "breach of contract," "goods sold" —and to omit the usual endorsement of notice of trial. The court will sit for the despatch of business on the day after the commission day, at each place (omitting Sunday), at eleven o'clock a.m. The trial of special jury causes will commence at Manchester on Friday, the 15th July, at the sitting of the court, and at Liverpool on Friday, the 22nd July, at the same hour, unless the court shall otherwise order. A list of causes for trial each day (except the first) at Manchester and Liverpool, will be exhibited in the corridor of the court and in the library.

LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE BRANCH OF THE BRITISH MEDICAL ASSOCIATION.—The fifty-fifth annual meeting of the above branch was held in the Town-ball, Preston, on Wednesday, Dr. Lund, of Manchester, the retiring president, in tlie chair.—The president for the ensuing year (Dr. Brown, of Preston), delivered an address, in which he referred to the comparatively great mortality in Preston, the annual average rate during the decade ending with 1880 being 29 28 as against 28.39 for the decade which ended with 1850. He concluded by stating that by making the rules of health a part of the education of the working classes much good might be effected, but what was wanted most of all was a realising faith in their importance.—The secretary then read the annual report. An invitation had Wen received from Chester to hold the next annual meeting of the association there, and the council were in favour of this, and also of Dr. M'Ewer, of Chester, being the president for next year.—Dr. Hoyle, of Manchester, proposed that the report and statement of accounts be adopted.—Dr. Barr, of Liverpool, seconded the motion, which was adopted.—Dr. Barron, of Southport, and Dr. Walker, of Manchester, were appointed vice-presi- dents for the ensuing year.—Dr. Steele, of Liverpool, was appointed the financial local secretary.—Medical and surgical communications were then taken into consideration, the contributors thereof being Dr. Grossman, of Liverpool; Dr. Dixon Mann, Manchester ; Dr. Haddon, Eccles; Mr. W. Whitehead, Manchester ; Dr. A. T. H. Waters. Liverpool ; Dr. Lloyd Roberts, Manchester; Mr. Rushton Parker, Liver- pool; Mr. Farrar, Morecambe; Dr. Thorburn, Manchester; Dr. Walter, Manchester; and Dr. Wallace, Liverpool.

ST. HELENS EXCURSIONISTS AT LLANDUDNO.—An ex- cursion to Llandudno in connection with the St. Helens Congregational Sunday Schools teok place on Friday last. The excursionists numbering several hundreds left St. Helens railway station about 6-30 a.m., and reinforced on the way by contingents from Peasley Cross, Sutton, Widnes, and Ditton had a rapid run to their destination which was reached about 9 o'clock, having ea route dropped a few pas- sengers at Rhyl, Colwyn Bay, and Llandudno Junelion. Arrived at Llandudno the excursionists were left to their own devices for the day; either to congne their attention to the many attractions of Llandudno itself by sea and land, or to make up parties with carefully arranged schemes of enjoyment and sight-seeing in a more inland and rural direc- tion. It would be well nigh impossible to enumerate all the possible ways and methods of spending a day which Llan- dudno as a centre affords to the active excursionists, and the experiences of not a few of the many parties made un last Friday quite sufficiently attest that Llandudno is no means too distantly situated as regards St. Helens eve.n for one day's trip. One party's arrangement included a visit to Conway and its castle with an exhaustive acquisition of its legends and traditions retailed for a small fee by the guide ; then to Bettws-y-Coed, whence all the famous scenes of beauty which lie within such easy reach such as the Fairy Glen, Miner's Bridge, the Swallow Falls, Cape! Curig a sight of Snowden) were eagerly prospected, and then after returning to Llandudno to windup the time yet remaining, a row round the bay, or a walk or ride up the Great Orme, either on donkeys with their accompanying ludierities, or with the more dignified celerity of the wagonnette or drag. A large number made their way by train to Bangor and passed the day among the beauties of Menai Straits, while others went 'by boat to Menai Bridge returning by rail, thoroughly delighted with everything they had seen. The weather was everything thatcould be desired, and singularly enough it happened as last year that Friday was the first really fine day of last week they had had in Llandudno. The returning train left Llandudno about 7-30 in the evening, and arrived in St. Helens about 11 o'clock, and judging from the chorus of pleasure heard on every hand the .arrangements of the day had given unalloyed satisfaction to
LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

THE POWDER MAGAZINES IN THE MERSEIL—Mr. TEE- vELYAN,replying to Mr.Summers,said the Board of Admiralty after due consideration had fixed the stations of floating magazines in the Mersey. The greatest precaution was being taken with regard to those stations there, the Revenue cruiser being engaged watching them. Lord Northbrook was now at Liverpool, and if any additional precautions were nerded, no doubt they would be ordered. THE PROCLAMATION OF WATERFORD.— Mr. FORSTER, replying to Mr. R. Power, said it was felt necessary to con- tinue the proclamation oiWaterford.—Mr. COWER asked if Waterford was not proclaimed in order to arrest the local secretary of the Land League Branch there ll—Mr. FORSTER could not give a definite answer to that question.—A dis- cussion arose as to the loss of time occabioned by putting trifling questions.—Mr. NEWDEGATE suggested some super- vision as regarded questions to be pnt.—Mr. GrAnsrola said the object was one that demanded comprehensive con- sideration.

THE IRISH LAND BILL.—The Rouse then went into com- mittee on the Irish Land Bill upon clause 7.—Mr. BIGGAR moved the insertion of words after the amendments already made to provide that if the rent payable by the tenant ex- ceeded what the court considered fair rent, the tenant should get credit in his coming rent for what the court believed to be the overcharge.—Mr. GLADSTONE opposed the addition. —Mr. Petunia. qupported it.—Mr. MITCHELL HENRY be- lieved the present a bogus and clap-trap amendment, and opposed it. On a division the amendment was negatived by 305 against 24. The other amendments were withdawn.— Captain AYLMER moved the omission of the first word of section 4 of the clause, with a view to making other amend- ments.—A discussion ensued, in which Mr. Grans-mien de- fended the sections and said they had been framed to main- tained good feeling between landlord and tenant which should continue without having recourse to litigation. If it was desired of those who represented the landlords that the sections should stand over for further con- sideration he should not object. Eventually Captain Aylmer' first amendment was accepted by Mr. Gladstone. —Mr. BIGGAR insisted on a division being taken when there appeared for Captain Aylmer's amendment 361, against 35. The other amendment having been agreed to, the section was after amendment read as follows :—" The rent fixed by the court in this act referred to as the judicial rents shall be deemed to be the rent payable by the tenant as from the 'period commencing at the rent day next succeeding the decision of the court," and was ordered to stand part of the bill. Sections five and six were omitted.— Lord C. FITZMAIIRICE moved the omission of the words in the seventh section which raised again the question of the right of landlords of resuming the hold- ing for the purpose of benefiting labourers by erecting cot- tages. The words it was proposed to omit set out that such should not be done during the first fifteen years of the tenancy.—A long discussion ensued.—Mr. GLADSTONE op- posed the omission of the words. He said that the bill set out that the first fifteen years should be treated exceptionally for the purpose of composing Ireland and settling disputes between class and class—For the amesdment 146, against 266.—The sitting was then suspended.—

div.head: LATEST TELEGRAMS. &c.
div.p: LATEST TELEGRAMS. &c.

A meeting in aid of the building fund of the city of Lou don college was held at the Mansion House yesterday, the Lord Mayor presiding. Mr. Mundella said he had never witnessed a more successful institution, and appealed foc help to carry on the work. He thought there should be no difficulty in raising £lO,OOO, in this, the richest city of the world, and was surprised that the city guilds had not come forward with kelp. Mr. Edward Clarke, ,M.P., a former student, urged the guilds to contribute while they had an undisputed right to dispose of their money. A telegram from Vienna, dated yesterday, says :—The authorities have expressed their intention of dealing severely with those who took part in the recent excess at Prague. These disturbances have, however, been greatly exaggera- ted. What has been magnified into a political riot was merely a fight between the German students and the Czeghian mob, although as these disturbances are fre. quently taking place, the authorities are now determined to prevent their future occurrence.

On Thursday Sir John Iles Mantell imposed a fine of £5 and costs upon William Hollingworth, the keeper of a "people's dispensary" in Ashton New Road, Bradford, for having issued A false certificate with regard to the death of a child. The prosecution was instituted by direction of the Registrar General. In connection with a similar case which was brought before the Court last week, Mr. T. A Giddings, a surgeon, was summonadto answer to a charge. of perjury; and the stipendiary magistrate, being of opinion that a prima facie case has been established, committed the defendant for trial, but accepted bail for his appearance at the assizes.

A very bad case of fraudulent trading came before the West Riding Quarter Sessions Court, on Thursday. The Prisoner, George Glover, a boot and shoe dealer at Dewsbury, filed a petition for liquidation last November. He had within the preceding two or three months obtained large .quantities of goods, giving in payment acceptances which were ultimately dishonoured. An auction of these goods was held, extending over 15 nights, and the prisoner retained the whole of the proceeds, the creditors not receiving a far- thing of payment. Glover was sentenced to nine months' imprisonment with hard labour.

At the West Kent Quarter Sessions, on Thursday, Mr Talbot, M.P., presiding—a sentence of one month's imprison- ment passed by the Dartford magistrates on the Rev. J. H. Candy, rector of Swanscombe, for assaulting a boy named Howard, and wounding his head, was reversed on the ground that the injury was accidental, and not malicious. A fine of £5 was substituted, with £5O costs, and the defendant bound over for twelve months.

The commission for negotiating the new French treaty hold their last meeting to-day, the proceedings being of a strictly formal character. The French commissioners will return to Paris on Wednesday to submit their work, and the French ambassador will follow them on the Monday. It is not expected that the present propositions of the English commissioners will be accepted by Fr2”...e mins. rnissioners of the latter count's- state that if the present treaty falls through tht r Government will endeavour to re- open the lisotiation on some fresh basis. Lad night's Gazette announces that General Sir Frederick Roberts has been appointed appointed a member of the Council ofiGovernors of Forts George, Madras.

I Captain Pearso.3, a Cheshire county magistrade, residing I at Macclesfield, received yesterday a notice calling on him to resign, or show cause why he should remain on the com- mission of the peace. Captain Pearson was scheduled by the Royal Election Commissioners as guilty of corrupt practices.

Mr. Gladstone has again written to the sugar operative!' committee regretting the disoppointment cause d by the for- mer letter, but stating he endeavoured to base that reply upon the fact of reasoning.

Mr. Parnell has issued an appeal to the Irish electors of Great Britain in view of the " approach of the period for registraron of voters." He says that in ordinary times, "when no great wave of ezcitement or passion rises to float one of the great English parties into power," the Irish vote can turn the whole political scale, and he claims that at Coventry, with an electorate of some 9,000 persons, a few hundred Irish voters recently won a seat, while at Knaresborough " some 32 Irish voters procured the defeat of the candidate of the Ministry." It is thus clear to him that the Irish vote can be made of importance even in con- stituencies where there are comparatively few Irishmen, and he urges the desirableness of organisation. The fierce struggle going on will, he says, decide the great question whether Ireland belongs to the Irish nation or the alien garrison. _

div.head: BRIGHTON MURDER.
div.p: THE BRIGHTON MURDER.

The officials at Scotland-yard have still every reason to believe that Lefroy is somewhere secreted in London, and if that be the case they are satisfied that their arrangements are so complete that he cannot possibly escape. Every port in the United Kingdom has been communicated with, and a sharp watch is being kept on all outgoing vessels. It is not likely that the inquest will be concluded to-day, but will probably be adjourned again till Wednearlay. The officials in Scotland-yard have every reason to believe that they have now obtained a substantial clue to the whereabouts of Lefrey, and that before long be will be in custody. They, however, naturally refuse to state the locality in which they expect to make the arrest. Superintendent Williamson, of the Criminal Investigation Department, has left London in connection with the matter. All the common lodging. houses, coffee-rooms, drc., have been watched.)

The statement that Lefroy cannot be at large many hours is very much strengthened by a remark made at the in- quest by Dr. Hall, the surgeon who examined his wounds at the Brighton Hospital. That gentleman is of opinion that in a very short space of time Lefroy will be obliged to seek the aid of a doctor or an hospital, as inflammation will supervene in one of the more serious wounds on his head.

Nothing has up to last evening been heard of the where- abouts of Lefroy, although the rumours of his arrest, which were so numerous on Thursday, prevailed throughout the whole of yesterday. The excitement which had reached, an intense pitch, was, if anything, intensified yesterday, everyone seeming anxious to know whether the man wanted had been captured, and, constituting hinaself for the time being an amateur detective, keenly suspicious of any person bearing the slightest resemblance to the published descrip- tions in newspaper sketches of the supposed murderer, and the offer of the reward for his capture, can scarcely be said ,to have increased the excitement as to his apprehension ' where the excitement was already so intense. It is not known for certain that Lefroy was last seen in Liverpool* street, in the north of London, on the morning of Tuesday last, and the police, who are confident that he has little or no money, think that he can't have got far away, and that it will not be long before he is in custody. Although he may have shaved himself, it is believed that he will be easily recognisable, from the fact of his head having been partly shaved in consequence of the wounds. The Brighton railway company yesterday morn- ing received a telegram from Seaforth, Sussex, to the effect that a young man answering to the published descriptions of the missing man made enquiry at Seaforth station last night as to the next train for Whitehaven. Upon receipt of this information the company at once issued issued urgent instructions to their staff to scrutinise all passengers by the company's steamer to Dieppe, and the police were also com- municated with. The railway authorities were also informed that a man answering the description, and seemingly much exhausted and very ill, was seen concealed under a hedge upon a farm at Shoreham Kent. This farm is surrounded by a wood where it was thought the man might have con- cealed himself. Another report was afloat that Lefroy had been seen in the Strand upon the !roof of an omnibus, but this turned out to be altogether incorrect. A proposition was made to the police yesterday that bloodhounds should be employed in endeavouring to track Lefroy, if, as sup- -p he still was:wandering in the country. Owing, how- eyoesre,d o the time the fugibive has been at large it is not thought likely that they will be of use and the suggestion will not be adopted. The searching the neighbourhood of Wallington, is still carried on with vigour as it is believed by many that he is hiding in one of the numerous woods in the district with which he is perfectly acquainted. It is again believed by many that he has committed suicide. Meanwhile a carefal watch is being kept on the house at Wallington, night and day, every care being taken that he shall not escape if in the neighbourhood.

• Richard Ludlow Bruges, a magistrate of Wiltshire, was Indicted in London, on Thursday, for publishing a false and malicious libel concerning the Countess of Lonsdale. It was proved that Bruges was insane, and he was discharged.

LLA.NFAMFECHAN, NOETH WALES. Sir,—The following, taken from the report of the year 1980 of the Carnarvonshire combined sanitary district, by Hugh Rees, M.R.C.S., L.S.A., medical officer of health, may be of interest to many of your readers, who, at this season a ye: r, are seeking a pleasant and healthy watering place on the charming coast of North Wales. The report speaks for itself, and needs not any comment.—Yours,&c., T.G.M. Manchester, June 28th, 1381.

.• Lianfalrfechan Local Government Sanitary District—The sanitary state of this district has been exceptionally good. The only death from disease of a zymotic character was one from whooping cough. It did not entirely escape from measles, but the cases were few and mild. The rates of mortality were ex- eePtionally low the general rate being 10•5 per 1,000, while the infant mortality was nil, no child under one year of age having died in the course of the year. The death rate lathe lowest that has been recorded in the combined district since its formation. and nothing under a per 1,000 has previously been noted under the head of infant mortality."

STARR BOWKETT BUILDING SOCIETIES- Sir,—There appears in your issue of Saturday last a report of the lecture npon "Starr Bowkett " 22nd Societies, given at Runcorn on Wednesday the,22n inst., and reference is made to a " disturbing element ' from War- rington. We should like permission to state the causes which led up to the parties from Warrington attending at this meet- ing. Mr. Starr promoted a society at 'Warrington and in his lecture distinctly stated none of his societies had been wound up. Some correspondence subsequently passed through the papers, and a gentleman who had taken a prominent part in the formation, working, and winding up of a London society, made certain charges against the societies generally, which Mr. Starr, as we think, rni.erably failed to refute, although he attempted to do so. The best proof of his failure lies in the fact that the proposed Warrington society, which had pre- viously made fair progress, could not add to its numbers after the appearance of these letters, and the general ex- pressed conviction was, that the arguments against the " Starr Bowkett " societies had not been disposed of by the founder: Our position was unfortunately becoming worse, and after giving the thing a lengthened trial, the Board (comprised of men of business capabilities) unanimously decided to dissolve the society, rather than involve the shareholders in more loss, which, under the circumstances, seemed inevitable. This Mlle had the full approval of the members, and yet Mr. Starr contemptously describes the Board as "Noodles." But this is not the only objectionable language we have been sub- jected to. Mr. Starr's letters to us since the collapse of the ,Warrington society, have been more or less characterised by a want of everything that is courteous and gentlemanly. And why? Simply because we did not lend ourselves to a con- cern which had no prospect of success. These letters are accompanied by a threat to sue us (the undersigned) for value of books supplied on behalf of the society, to which we cannot have the least objection. We and our friends attended the lecture at Runcorn with a view of putting questions bearing directly upon "Starr-Bowkett " societies, and showing the Runcorn people that Mr. Starr carefully avoids anything of a character to suggest doubts as to the real object for which these societies are floated. The ques- tions were evaded, as we feared they would be, and since it would be unfair to burden your space by asking an insertion _ of them, we shall, nevertheless, be prepared to supply copies to any person wishing for same, and we venture to think that en a perusal they will at least reflect before attaching themselves to such societies. 'We would ask whether Mr. Starr will refute the statement that he and his agent get £5 ss. direct from the society, £27 2s. from the solicitor, £5 ss. from the surveyor, and the secretary has also to pay £lO 108. for what is termed "royalty "—total, £4B 2s. Then again, the printing, ctn., is generously undertaken by Mr. Starr, and we are not wide of the mark when we say the account is at least 15 to 20 per cent. in excess of what it would be were the books and bills purchased from a local firm. Even in this local tradesmen do not participate. Mr. Starr boastfully stated he would meet us in public, but he has refrained from giving us such a challenge, and, what is more, he dare not, unless, of course, be intends to adopt his usual method of stifling legitimate questions. We are sure Mr. Beckett and his colleagues have the welfare of their fellow townsmen at heart, and they have a perfect right to their own opinions even to the extent of designating the parties from Warrington as "hole-and- corner men," a statement which we assume was made on the impulse of the moment. If Mr. Beckett and his brother offi- cials will communicate with us we will go a little deeper below the surface than Mr. Starr does. Prominence is given to the statement that £lOO is lent " free of interest "for 121 years, whereas nothing is so fallacious. That amount is certainly advanced the first year, but in the twelfth year only £8 is practically lent, and all the while the subscrip- tion of 6d. per week is going on and has to remain in the Society indefinitely. Mr. Starr's own tables prove that the whole of the appropriations cannot be advanced in 18 years, and we challenge him to show which of his societies have accomplished this. Apologising for having trespassed on your valuable space, we remain, yours obediently, TAYLOR AND LONGBOTTOM, Secretaries to the late Warrington Starr Bowkett Building I Society. I".S.—When forming the Warrington society we had no idea of the benefits Mr. Starr would derive from it, nor did we know anything of the practical working of the societies.

div.head: MURDER 0 THE BRIGHTON RAILWAY. MYSTERIOUS AFFLTR.
div.p: MURDER 0 THE BRIGHTON RAILWAY. MYSTERIOUS AFFLTR.

The Brighton correspondent of the Standard, telegraph- ing on Monday, esys:-1 mysterious murder was committed on the Brighton railway this afternoon. On the arrival at Preston Park Station of the 2-0 p.m. express train from London Bridge, a ticket-collector found a man alone in a trst-class carriage with wounds on his head, and covered with blood from head to foot. He gave his name as Arthur Leroy, of 4, Cathcart-road, Wallington, and stated that when the train started there were in the carriage with him an old gentleman and .a man of about -fifty years of age, having the appearance of a countryman. After pass- ing Croydon Station, and just as the train entered a tunnel, he says a shot was fired, and he felt a blow on the head, but remernbered nothing further until the arrival a the train at Preston Park. He bad no idea who fired the she,. After his wounds bad been attended to he returned to London, in company , with two police constables. About seven o'clock in the evening the dead body of a gentleman, about 00 years of age, was found lying in the six-foot way in Balcombe -tunnel, about 18 miles from Brighton. From an address found in a pocket-book, it is believed to be that of Mr. Gold, a retired corn merchant, of Claremont,terrace, Preston, near Brighton. The body had been stabbed in several places. Mr. Gold left his home on Monday morning for the purpose of collecting dividends in London, and was expected to return by the 2 p.m. express. it is believed that he had a large sum of money in his possession. The carriage in which Lefroy arrived at Preston was saturated with blood, and two bullets are embedded in the woodwork. The outside of the carriage door and the long wooden step were also covered with blood. A gentleman who travelled , by the train states that he heard the report of firearms near sCroydon.

Another correspondent states that Mr. Lefrov, who de- scribes himself as "an anther and a journalist," stated to the Brighton police that he left London on Monday by the 2 o'clock express for Brighton, and his fellow passengers were an elderly gentleman and a person dressed as a country- man. After leaving Croydon be was fired at, and being struck with some instrument he was rendered insensible until be arrived at Preston, a suburb of Brighton. He was found to be considerably injured, and was attended at the County Hospital. Later in the day the body of Mr. J. Gold, an elderly gentleman, a steckkroker in London, and a season ticket holder on the Brighton line, who resides at Preston, was foundon the line in Balcombe tunnel. No tidings have been heard of the countryman. At the inquest, on Wednesday, the wife of a labourer living at Honey said that from her cottage, as the train passed, she saw two gentlemen struggling together. A bullet wound has been fond in the head of the deceased. A pas- senger by the sante train as the deceased on Monday, and who rode in the next compartment, deposed that he heard four reports as the train entered the tunnel. The inquest was adjourned till Saturday. Lefroy, the supposed murderer, is still at large. The utmost efforts of the police in the search for Lefror, the suspected murderer of Mr. Gould on the Brighton Rail- way, have been without avail. A tramp was detained at Qraveseud on Thursday on suspicion, but was released in the Course of the afternoon. Rumours of all kinds were current, but Lefroy had not, at the time of writing, been beard of since he absconded from Wallington.. A reward is offered for his apprehension.

CODIEINED ADITESITIS PENNY POSTAGE AND INLAND REVENGE STAMP.—A combined adhesive postage and inland revenue stamp, which can be used for the purposes for which the adhesive penny postage stamp and the ordinary adhesive penny inland revenue stamp have hitherto been available, will shortly he issued. The present adhesive penny postage etamps.aud. adhesive penny inland revenue stamps will continue to be sold until the stocks on hand are exhausted, and they will for the present remain available for either postage or receipt purposes. It is to be under- stood that the new stamp, when used for postage, must have no printing or writing placed on its face by the public. Any stamp so marked will not he accepted for the payment of postage. A meeting of Scotch members of Parliament was held yesterday afternoon in one of the conference rooms at the House of Commons, for considering the state of Scotch business hi Parliament and ascertaining the views of mem- bers as to what measures should have the preference this ' session. There were about forty Scotch members present and among those who took part were Sir W. Harcourt, Mr Mundella, the Lord Advocate, and the Solicitor General for Scotland. An informal discussion took place lasting about two hours, the result showing that the bill most in favour was the Educational Endowments Bill for Scotland. The bill next in favour appeared to iee the Entail Bill, the object of which it was stated was to assimilate the Scotch Is much as possible to the English law in that respect. It ' was understood that the Poor Law Bill and the Sheriff Sales Bill mlght be allowed to stand over, with several other measures, until next session, whilst the passage of the bills gen.erally appsoved by the conference would be pressed this liespOD.

WARRINGTON POLICE CASES. MONDAS.—Before the Mayor, and Alderman Davies. RE-APPEARANCE OF THE JEFFREYS.—Mary, and Margaret Jeffreys, mother and daughter, were charged with being drunk and committing a breach of the peace by fighting in Sugar House-yard, on Saturday night —P.C. Powell de- posed to being called to the yard, after having been called 'three times previously, to separate the defendants who were fighting. Defendant Margaret was very drunk and violent; and when the mother attempted to go home to Silver-street, the daughter caught hold of her and pulled her back. The defendants caught hold of one another and "fought just like men." Replying to the Mayor, Mr. Hunt said the mother was in the act of removing at the time, and they were taking away the last thing—the bed.—Defendants denied they were fighting, but said the neighbours were illusing them. Mrs. Jeffreys, to confirm this statement, produced a handful of hair which had been pulled from her head, and said "Mrs. Dacey, her three sisters, mother and father, illused her as it was not fit for a dog to be used." The Chief Constable pressed the case against the daughter, who was sent for 14 days imprisonment, the mother being discharged. Yorrrustri, TIPPLERS.—Edward McLoughlin, and Michael Flanaghan, two youths, were charged on warrant with being drunk and disorderly in Upper Bank-street, on the 11th inst., and were each fined 10s. and costs,.cr 14 days. His 42ND APPEARANCE.—DanieI Connor, (GO) who made his 42nd appearance ha all, and fourth this year, was sum- moned for being drunk in Ashton-street, on the 19th June.— P.C. 28 proved the case. Mr. Hunt said If Daniel had half a pint of beer, some people would imagine he had had half a gallon—(laughter)—he got so excited. Daniel was fined ss.

and costa. - AN AMATEUR DRIVER. Patrick McDonnell and John McKee were charged with beingdrunk in Marsh House Lane, on the 14th June, and doing wilful damage to the amount of £3 by breaking a gas lamp in Orford Lane, the property of the Warrington Corporation.—The prisoners were recruits, and on the previous Friday afternoon about five o'clock, the son of Mr. Kerfoot, farmer, Orford Avenue, was about to pro- ceed to Warrington with a horse and cart, when McDonnell got hold of the reins and asked for a pass. The two wrestled about the possession of the reins, and ultimately young Ker- foot jumped out of the cart to fetch his father. On doing so he saw McDonnell jump on the shafts of the cart, take hold of the reins, and gallop away with the pony and cart. He told his father, and on going out again he observed that a gas lamp was broken, and that McDonnell was lying on the ground, while the horse was running away.—McDonnell was fined 20s. and costs or a month, and McKee was fined 10s. and costs or 14 days. REFUSING co Qurr.—John Kilcourse, who appeared with his head bandaged, was summoned for refusing to quit the Little Horse Shoe, kept by Mr. John Aspinall, when reques- ted to do so. Ile was fined 103. and costs or 14 days. WALKING DAY Cntgartarrrs.—Edward McElroy was fined ss. and costs for being drunk and disorderly in Arpley-street, on Walking day. The defendant said he had been teetotal nine months previously.—Michael Quinn for being drunk and disorderly in Dallam Lane, on Walking Day, was fined ss. including costs. TrEsnay.—Before Aldermen Chandley and Webster. THE 55TH APPEARANCE.—John Noon was charged with being drunk and fighting in Bank-street on the previous evening. It was stated that this was his 55th appearance, and he was fined 10s. and costs, or in default 14 days' im- prisonment. A WORTHY EXAMPLE.—Matthew Plum, a bricksetter. was charged with leaving his stepson chargeable to the nom-, mon fund of the Union.—Mr. Harbourne said that on the 2nd inst, prisoner's wife applied to the Guardians for relief for her stepson, aged 9, who was ill. The boy was visited by Dr. Joseph, who ordered him brandy and soda water, as he was very weak. He had that for seven days, and on the 17th inst. the boy was admitted into the Workhouse. The amount expended in relief was 15s. Bd.—Prisoner pleaded guilty; and Alderman Chandley said the beasts of the field did not abandon their young as the prisoner had done his child.—An erder was made for the amount with costs, or in default 14 days. WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Davies and Councillor

Fairclough. THE HIT elm THE FUNERAL—Thomas Phillips was charged with committing an aggravated assault on his wife Margaret. It appeared that up to a few weeks ago the pri- soner and his wife had been living apart under a judicial separation, but at his solicitation she gave him another trial. On Sunday night about 10-20 prisoner . entered the house and lighted a piece of paper at the fire. She asked him what be wanted, and he gave her a " clout " on the head and dazzled her. He then went upstairs and she followed. He opened the cupboard to get his "tall hat to go to the woman's funeral" with whom he had been lodging. Prose- cutor said something to him and he kicked her downstairs, took her to the front door, knocked her to the ground and "used her shamefully."—At the suggestion of the Bench the parties agreed to "make it up," and the case was adjourned for a month. ASSAULT ON TIM POLICE BY A CARTER.—Thomas Foy, a carter for Mr. Collins, was charged with being drunk and committing a breach of the peace in Scotland-road, on the previous night ; and also with assaulting ,P.C. Hennessy whilst in the execution of his duty, doing damage to his watch to the amount of 5s.—P.C. Hennessy said he saw prisoner and another man fighting and he went to separate them, but they kept boxing and kicking across him. The prisoner kicked him on the body with his foot, pulled his watch from his pocket and broke it. He took him into custody, and whilst on the way to the police station he assaulted him several times, and conducted himself most "fearfully,"—P.S. Spinks deposed to seeing the prisoner strike the constable on the breast, and said prisoner had his legs twisted round the constable, and a regular struggle took place. The watch was afterwards brought by a man to the police station, and was broken.— Prisoner said he was in a beerhouse getting a glass of ale, when a man took his horse and cart away. He followed, and told the man he ought not to have taken it away without telling him, and a quarrel ensued.—Alderman Davies said it was the prisoner's duty to see that the cart did not go away. —Mr. Hunt observed that the man who took the cart away had been sent by prisoner's employer.—For being drunk prisoner was fined ss. and costs, ss. damage, and 105. and costs for assaulting the police, total £1 75., or in default 21 days' imprisonment. A BEGGING IMPOSTER.—SamueI Smith, a grey-headed old man, who stated his age to be 61, was charged with heing drunk and disorderly in Church-street, on the previous evening.—P.S. James said he was on his way home when he passed the prisoner, who was walking very quickly after another man who appeared to be endeavouring to get out of his way. Prisoner was cursing loudly, and the sergeant returned. Discovering that the officer was following him, the prisoner crossed the street, and commenced to use most filthy language to a number of women. He was then taken into custody. On him were found about half a dozen beg- ging letters, all couched in the following terms :—Most respectfully inform you I, the unfortunate petitioner, have been several years at the Deaf and Dumb Institution in London, where I have been taught to make fancy baskets ; now out of employment, totally desti- tute. In case you disbelieve my statement, you can observe I have been born without tongue and theretore most respectfully solicit your kind support to assist me, which will be thankfully received by your applicant Samuel Smith.— The letters were written in a good hand, and in reply to Alderman Davies prisoner said he had written them himself. He wrote his name on a piece of paper and it was similar to the signature to the letters. He had come from London with the intention of going to Liverpool where he hid a brother. He had never been in prison.—Prisoner was discharged on paving the lockup fees. VAOBANCY.—WiIIiam Priestly, a boy who said he came from St. Helens, was charged with being found asleep in the Swan Hotel yard on the previous night, and having no visible means of subsistence. Prisoner promised to at once return to St. Helens and he was discharged. THERSDAL—Before Captain Litton and E. Milner, Esq. STEALING AND RECEIVING.—John Joseph Houghton, 11 years of age, was charged with stealing from the shop of Miss Tunstall., pawnbroker, Winwick-street, on Saturday, the 18th June, aeliver lever watch, value £2, and Eliza Gres- well was charged with receiving the same knowing it to be stolen.—Mr. Moore appeared for the defence.—From the statement of the Chief-Constable, it appeared that Houghton is the adopted child of the female priaoner and her hue- bard, William Greswell, a tanner, residing at Ashton-street, Town's End. On Saturday afternoon, the day after Walk- ing Day, about a quarter to five a young woman named Kate Phillips went to prosecutor's shop and presented a pawn ticket for a watch which had been pledged for 21s. About the same time the male prisoner presented himself for the purpose of redeeming an apron that had been pledged in the name of Ellen Bailey. The watch was brought and the name on the ticket called out. The lad called out " here " twice, and put out his hand. The prosecutrix received the money for the watch but Miss Swinton, the assistant, fetched it and not having seen who presented the ticket, on the boy holding out his hand handed the watch to him. After a while the girl who came for the watch asked for it but Miss Swinton said "Oh I gave the watch to a little boy who put out his hand and said here.'" On the counter, however, was the parcel, produced, containing the apron. The police were called in and their enquiries resulted lathe recovery of the watch at the female prisoner's house, and the arrest of the prisoners.—Evidence in support of the charge having been given, Mr. Moore submitted that there was no case against the female prisoner, who had lived in Warrington 30 or 40 years, and bad borne an-irreproachable character. if the watcb had got into her possession it had got there by mistake. The lad was sent to Miss Tunstall's shop with a pawn ticket and bad to bring the article named on it, and as he did not know what was on the ticket it was only likely he would bring the articles given to him.—The Bench decided that the boy was acting under the instruc- tions of the female prisoner, who was very much more to blame than he. The boy would be discharged with a caution, and the female prisoner dried 40s. and costs, total £3, Is.. or in default one month.—Prisoner pleaded for time to pay the money, but the Bench refused the application, saying that they had-treated her very leniently M giving her the option of a fine. _

RESISTING PARENTAL CFLASTISEMENT. A young man named John Mullen was charged, on warrant, with baying, on the 28th June, assaulted and beaten his mother, Mary Mullen.—Prosecutrix asked her son if be was going to work and "thrust her hand on him and hit him." He then turned on her, hit and kicked her, and knocked her down.—Pri- soner admitted having pushed bis mother, who struck him, and she fell down.—The Assistant-Clerk remarked that the soother had a right to chastise her son.—Prisoner was dis- charged on payment of CocAs 7s. ed. 25th nit., assaulted his wife, Mary Jane Poole.—Prosecutrix said the prisoner struck her on Saturday night, and also on Monday, and had threatened her life many times, until she was afraid and dare not go out of doors. She was locked out on Saturday night, and had to walk the streets all night. She had not been home since, as she was afraid of her life. In reply to the Bench, prosecutrix said she had been mar- ried to the prisoner nine years, but had no family. She was a dressmaker, and partly maintained herself, although her husband earned enough to keep both of them.—Prisoner said he had been drinking; and Captain Litton remarked that a short imprisonment would do the prisoner good.—Prosecu- trix, however, did not wish her husband to be imprisoned.— He was bound over, himself in £lO, and two sureties of IS each, to keep the peace for six months; and the Bench advised him to make his wife an allowance, and live apart from her.

LE EXAMINER SATURDAY, JULY 2, 1881 SUTTON CRICKET CLUB ATHLETIC I FESTIVAL. The eighth annual amateur athletic sports took place on the Sutton cricket ground, near the railway station, on Friday and Saturday. The days being fine there was a good attendance of both sexes who enjoyed the races. The grand stand was fairly patronised, and in front on a table the prizes, to the amount of nearly £lOO, were displayed. Amongst those present were Councillors Brook and Wilcock. The committee wisely varied the events as in former years, but this year a novelty in the mirth-exciting obstacle race was added and the events were more numerous. The excite- ment of the spectators ran very low, especially in some of the flat races, but this in a measure may be accounted for by the fact that many of the competitors who entered either did not turn up or refrained from engaging in the contests. The leg of mutton, worth 7s. 6d., which was offered for climbing the masy pole attracted no entries, but the more substantial prizes of a new hat, value 10s. 6d., induced one man to come forward who after several unsuccessful attempts to reach the top unlike Bruce's spider gave up the task in despair, and this is not to be wondered at when the amount of Tinker's soap used on the pole is taken into account. In the 100 yards flat race handicap (open) the first heat was run in ten seconds and three-fifths and the third in 11 seconds. In the third heat J. Slevin, of Wigan, who was the scratch man fell at the finish of the race, and complained that the winner, G. F. Barton, of Liverpool, had " crossed " him. Seven entered in the half-mile flat race handicap (open.) This was a good race, and the length of S. J. Hewitt's legs no doubt gained him the first prize. He came in easily. P. Walsh, of Warrington, who had 50 yards start came in second: and W. Marriott, of Liverpool, 40 yards, third. In the one mile bicycle race handicap (open) four ran in the first heat. In the first lap McKenzie who had 125 yards start ran away from H. A. Smith, of South- port, who started from the same point, and passed G. Messiter, of Warrington, who started 25 yards in advance and who ultimately retired. Smith tumbled and enabled C. Fone, of Farnworth (scratch), to get before him. At the finish McKenzie was first, C. Fone second, and Smith third; time, 4 min. 3 secs. and 2-sths. In the second heat T. Reid, Peasley Cross, and J. Makin, of Sutton, ran, and both being sure to run in the final took it moderately comfortable. Seven ran in the third heat. W. Barton, of Wigan, and A. Smith, of Manchester, collided and both fell causing a great dispute. Barton resumed the race, but Smith did not and appealed to the committee who decided to put him in the final heat. Near the finish of the race a sharp contest took place between W. Smith, junr., of Appleton, and R. Black- ledge, of Wigan, for the first place, but the latter who started 30 yards in advance of his rival came in first, W. Smith being second, and C. H. Hodgkinson, of Wigan, third. The competitors in the final heat-McKenzie, Fone, Smith (Southport), Makin (Sutton), Reid (Peasley Cross), Blackledge (Wigan), Smith (Appleton), and Hodgkinson (Wigan), being displeased at the action of the committee in placing A. Smith, of Manchester, in the final heat refused to ran on the ground that it was a breach of the rules of the Northern Counties Association; but immediately before the last event of the afternoon was announced the committee gave the malcontents "another chance," which they took advantage of. McKenzie kept the lead for a good part of the race, but was passed by Reid, the champion of the St. Helens 8.C., when two laps remained to be run. Reid came in easily; W. Smith, junr., of Appleton, made a spurt in the last 20 yards, passed McKenzie, and came second; McKenzie being third. The one mile walking race handicap (open), with the exception of the obstacle race, was the most exciting and amusing event of the afternoon. The competitors were J. Worrell, Liverpool, 30 yards •, W. Howard, Bromborough, 80; T. Kay, Manchester, 120; J. Lea, Widnes. 130; G. Ashton, Widnes, 140; W. Potter, Sutton, 150; S. Hazeldine, Earlestown, 160; J. Maddison, Sutton, 160; J. Wright, Widnes, 170; H. Haseldine (41 years of age), Earlestown, 180. Roars of laughter was caused by Potter's style of walking. He com- menced by taking prodigious strides, averaging about a yard and a half, and in this fashion he continued until the end of the race, thus giving him a most ungraceful and comical appearance. At times there appeared but a short space between his foremost foot and head. He bore the laughter of the spectators with stoical indifference. He passed all his rivals, but-was eventually overtaken by Wor- rell, of Liverpool, a very quick and graceful walker, who came in at the finish in front of Potter by several yards. W. Howard was awarded the third prize. One of the cempeti- tors took objection to Potter being allowed the second prize, as he considered Potter to run rather than walk on being followed closely by the winner. Mr. Wilcock, the judge, however, ruled in Potter's favour. The mile was finished in 7mins. and 44secs. In the first heat of the two mile bicycle race handicap (open), five competed :-C. Fone, 90 yards; C. H. Hodgkinson, Wigan, 120; T. Reid. Peasley Cross, 190; W. Smith, jun., Appleton, 190; and R. Black- ledge, Wigan, 260. After some distance had been run the two first named retired from the race. Reid came in first easily, Smith second, and Blackledge third. In the second heat a very exciting struggle appeared to be going on between W. Doming, jun., of Appleton, and F. Gandy, of Wigan. They passed each other several times. At the close of the race Doming was first, Gandy second, and H. A. Smith, of Southport, third. In the final heat Reid won easily, W. Smith, jun., Appleton, being second, and Gandy third. In the one mile flat race open handicap sixteen ran, but in the course of the race several retired. C. W. Blun- dell, of Tranmere, 60 yards, reached the goal first; E. Wright, Widnes 201 yards, followed close behind, and .T. Concannon, Widnes, 50, was third. The 600 yards obstacle scratch race was the most exciting event of the afternoon, and being a novelty in this district provoked much amuse- ment and curiosity. Competitors were compelled to creep through narrow barrels, get under a long pole raised about twelve inches from the ground, and drop from a horizontal pole at a distance of about twelve feet from the ground, which was to be reached by means of poles placed against it. Great hopes were entertained that Potter, the amusing walker, would win the race, because shortly before the race commenced he shot through a barrel apparently without any difficulty. In actual race, however, it was different, no doubt owing to the excitement and enervating effects of the run- ning. W. Marriott, of Liverpoor, reached the horizontal bar with great skill, scaling the pole to it with his back to the ground. The other competitors found this a difficult task to accomplish, and Marriott left his rivals a long way in the rear. He came in first, P. Walsh, of Warrington, second, and J. Traverse, St. Helens, third. The following is a com- plete return of the races:- 100 Yards Flat Race Handicap.-lst, S. Wilson,Warring- ten, 4 yards start; 2nd, B. Pierpoint, Newton, 4 yards; 3rd, J. Livesey,Wigan, scratch. Half-Mile Flat Race Handicap-let, E. Dunn, Liverpool ; 2nd, S. Boardman, Warrington; 3rd, S. J. Hewitt, Newton. Time, 2mins. and 3-ssecs. One Mile Bicycle Race Handicap.-lst, T. D. McKenzie St. Helens; 2nd, T. Finney, St. Helens; 3rd, J. Harwood, St. Helens. Time 4mins.2 1-5 secs. 300 Yards Handicap Hurdle Race (district).---lst, C. Bryan Liverpool; 2nd, T. Galvin, Leigh; 3rd, C. Cunliffe, St. Helens. Half-Mile Flat Race Handicap (open).-1, S. J. Hewitt, Newton, scratch; 2, P. Walsh. Warrington; 3, W. Mar- riott, Liverpool. Time, 2 mins. 3-5 secs. Won by three yards. 100 Yards Flat Race Handicap (district), for Youths under 18 years of age.-1, S. Wilson, Warrington; 2; B. Pierpoint, Newton; 3. J. Livesey, Wigan. Time, 11- 3-5 secs. 100 Yards Flat Race Handicap (district).-1, C. Cun- liffe, St. Helens 2, T. Galvin, Leigh; 3, J. Valentine, St. Helens. Time. 101 secs. An objection on the ground of jostling was raised against Cunliffe, but the judges ruled that his course was taken up, and that he merely pushed through. 260 Yards Boys' Race Handicap (open).-1, H. Green, Warrington; 2, W. Smith, Ashton; 3, A. Morris, Newton. Time, 32 3-5 BACS. 220 Yards Flat Race Handicap (district).-1, T. Pem- berton, Warrington; 2, D. A. Harding, Widnes; 3, T. Monks, St. Helens. Time, 25 3-5 secs. One Mile Walking Handicap Race (open).-1, J. Worrall, Liverpool; 2, W. Potter, Sutton; 3, W. Howard, Brombor- ouch. Time, 7 mins. 44 secs. 100 Yards Flat Race Handicap (open).-In the second heat F. H. Wilson (Warrington) and J. Stirzaker (Liverpool) ran a dead heat, and both competed in the final, which resulted as follows :-1, J. Rimmer, Southport ; 2, G. F. Barton, Liverpool; 3, F. H. Wilson, Warrington. Time, 10 3-5 sees. Putting the Shot (161b5).-1, J. Battle, St. Helens, 31ft. 7io. (4fl. 6in. given); A C. Cunliffe, St. Helens, 301 t. 3in. (7ft. Gin, given). Tug of War.-Six men of the Sutton Oddfellows (W. Whittaker, captain) against six men of the Rock Club, Thatto Heath (ft. Brownhill, captain). The Rock Club pulled their opponents over twice easily. 100 Yards Hurdle Race Handicap (open).-1, C. Cunliffe, St Helens; 2, T. Galvin, Leigh; 3, E. Berry, Liverpool. Time, 13 4-5 secs. One Mile Bicycle Handicap (open).-1, T. Reid, Peaseley Cross; 2, W. Smith. jun., Appleton; 3, T. McKenzie, St. Helens. Time, 3 mins. 57 secs. One Mile Flat Race Handicap (open) -1. C. W. Blundell, Tranmere; 2, E. Wright, Widnes; 3, J. Concannon, Widnes. Time, 4 mins. 41 secs. 220 Yards Flat Race Open Handicap.-1, J. G. Hughes, Liverpool : 2, T. Pemberton, Warrington ; 3, J. W. Clegg, Wigan. Time, 24 1-5 secs. Two Mile Bicycle Handicap.-1, T.'Reid, Peasley Cross; 2. W. Smith, jun.. Appleton; 3, F. Gandy, Wigan. Won by 20 yards. Time, 8 mins. 10 2-5 secs. One Mile Steeplechase Handicap.-Eight started, but only three croaSed the tape, as follows : -1, W. Houghton, Wid- nes; 2. W. Warriott, Liverpool; 3,3. Concannon, Widnes. Time, 5 mins. 37 2-5 secs. Quarter-Mile Flat Race Handicap (open), -1, H. H. Tilley, Widnes ; 2,3. Hewitt, Newton. For third place, S. Board- roan, Warrington, and E. Dunn, Liverpool, tied. 600 Yards Obstacle Race.-1, W. Marriott, Liverpool ;2, P. Walsh, Warrington ; 3, J. Travers, St. Helens. Mhs Brook presented the prizes at the close of the sports.
