TIIIIRSDAY.—Before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, Judge. Flamm° vortBIGET. Peter Gleave sued Joseph Birchall for 'Ts. for butter supplied.—Mr. P. Davies de- fended.—On the 31st January plaintiff supplied defendant with 941bs. of butter at 6d. per lb., and he had only received payment for SOlbs. He had made a mistake in the weight, which he found after he had delivered the butter. Mr. Davies put in a receipt, signed by plaintiff's wife, which stated the tare of the firkin of butter to be 941bs. and the nett SOlbs.—Plaintiff said he had no witnesses present who could prove that the weight of the butter was 941bs, and if his Honour would adjourn the case he would bring them forward.—His Honour said he could have the case adjourned, but plaintiff must pay the costs, and if it went on he would be obliged to give anon-suit.--Plaintiff said he was fighting the case for a working man in County Mayo, Ireland, and it had nothing to do with him. However, right was right, and be would have the case adjourned.—Mr. Daviest I have four witnesses—Plaintiff: I don't care if you have a hundred. Right's right. (Laughter.)—[A Voice; And wrong's no- body's.] A SINGULAR Casa.—Richard Hodson, farmer, Rixton, claimed from John Cawley £35, for having converted to his own use, on the 2nd June, two cows, the property of the plaintiff.—Mr. Cottingham (instructed by Mr. Addenbrooke) appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. P. Davies for the defend- ant.—Mr. Cottingham, in opening the case, said the defend- ant and his wife were not on the best of terms, and as the result of illusage she was obliged to leave her husband and seek her own maintenance. On the 20th June Mrs. Cawley went to plaintiff with two cows, and asked him to keep them for her at so much per week. He did so, but after- wards purchased them for £27, which money was paid to Mrs. Cawley.—Mr. Davies: I deny that she sold them at all .—Mr. Cottingham (proceeding) said sometime after ' plaintiff had possession of the MIS he was =prised by Mr. Cawley coming to him and demanding them, saying they were his property. Plaintiff refused to deliver them up, and defendant forcibly took them away:" Plaintiff afterwards recovered them from defendant. and again defendant took them away. That was the conversion of which they corn- plained.—His Honour: How do you say that a married woman could convey her title to the cows ?—Mr. Cotting- ham: That is for you to decide.—His Honour: It had I better be decided now, for thq whole action is based upon that.—Mr. Cottingham said Mrs. Cawley bought the cows at Chester fair with her own money, and a woman driven from her home by her husband would be entitled to pledge his credit for a livelihood. Therefore, if she purchased these I cows for the purpose of earning a livelihood,. he submittea that that to the innocent pur- chaser would make the title. His Honour said she might get anything for her subsistence, but the law was against him as he stated the facts.—Mr. Cottingham: Her husband. drives her from his house by ill- usage, and she is entitled to pledge his credit for necessaries, and also entitled to borrow money and spend it in neces- saries.—His Honour: I admit that, but it is a different thing to buying cows.—Mr. Cottingham: She purchased these cows to make money of them with which to supply herself with necessaries, which her husband was bound to find her. He quoted a case Dear v. Sutton in "Law Reports in Equity" to show that a person advancing money to a married woman deserted by her husband was entitled in equity, but not in law, to recover the money from her hus- band. He contended that the onus of proving his title to the property rested with the defendant. Plaintiff had acquired the property lawfully.—His Honour: That is the question. Is it acquired lawfully 7—Mr. Cottingham: In this sense, that it is not stolen property.—His Honour said that while the wife had power to pledge her husband's credit she had no right to appropriate her husband's money or-pro- perty.—Mr. Cottingham said that where the husband was under obligation to support his wife, the wife was entitled by the virtue of that obligation to possess herself of her hus- band's property if she could get it.—His Honour: In that I differ from you.—Mr. Cottingham: If not, she might starve. —His Honour: No, she need not starve. She can pledge his credit or go to the workhouse, and then the aothorities can take steps to compel him to keep her.—His Honour decided to hear the evidence before deciding the question of title.— The plaintiff said that on Friday 20th May last, defendant's wife brought two cows to his farm to be grazed, and it was agreed that she was to pay ss. per week for them. They calved whilst with witness, but defendant's wife did not sell any milk. The day after Mrs. Cawley brought the cows, plaintiff bought them for £27, and received a receipt from Mrs. Cawley. On the 2nd June defendant went to plaintiff's house and said be had two heifers of his, and asked if plaintiff was going to turn them out of the shippon. Plaintiff replied that they were .his, and defendant had nothing to do with them. Defendant then entered the shippon and drove the cows away. Next morning plaintiff went to defendant's and took them back, when defendant again fetched them away, and refused to return them. The cows were good healthy beasts and worth £3l, and the value of the milk which would have been got from them since defendant had had them would be about £1 per week. —Elizabeth Rimmer and Stephen Wareing, plaintiff's servants, said they remembered the cows being brought to plaintiff's house, and also the money being paid to Mrs. Cawley by the mistress.—Nancy Cawley, the wife of the defendant, said she had been living away from her husband three months. He abused her, and had turned her out three or four times previously. He had never made her any allowance, and said be would not do so. He had knocked her to the ground, pulled her hair, and " lugged " her ears. When with her husband she milked the cows and did other work, and she had frequently purchased cows for him.. About two months after she left her husband she purchased two cows at Chester fair, which she sold to Hodson for £27. She sold them because her husband had threatened to take them saying what was hers was his. She was living with Mr. Daniels, the overseer.—By Mr. Davies: She had once taken two beds away from home, when her husband had offered her IGs. 6d. per week to support her away from him. On another occasion she took £35, but it was hers. Her father had left her a house and some money. When she went to Chester fair to buy the cowt; she took some of the money which she had taken from her husband's house, and some which she had borrowed from Mrs. Daniels. She had never told a man named Grey that she had bought one of the beasts with money of which she had robbed her husband.— His Honour said that after the cross-examination of the last witness he considered the question of title not ma.de out. She purchased 'the cows at Chester fair with money taken from her husband's house, and he did not believe that she had borrowed any money from Mrs. Daniels. And even if she had the commingling of that with the other would not affect the matter in the least. There was nothing to show that the cows were purchased by her own earnings, and they were her husband's property. He must, therefore, non-suit the plaintiff.—in answer to Mr. Cottingham, His Honour said it would have the same effect as finding for the defen- dant. Costs would follow in the usual way. CLAIM UPON AN ARBITRATOR'S AWARD.—John Clayton sued Thomas Orrell Speakman to recover £57 10s.—Mr. Ledgard appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. W. H. Brook for the defendant.—Mr. Ledgard said that in 1875 defendant kept a public-house at Seacombe, in Cheshire, and employed the plaintiff for a considerable time. Plaintiff received no wages whatever and he was very summarily dismissed by the defendant. In order to obviate the unpleasantness of bringing an action an agreement was el-tired into to refer the matter to arbitration. Mr. Win. Clayton was appointed arbitrator and awarded the plaintiff £57 10s. and all costs. The only defence set up was that they were not indebted.— Mr. Brook admitted the agreement to arbitrate, and asked that as the action was based upon the award it should be produced.—This was eventually done, when it wasdiscoyered that it was not stamped.—The claim was therefore dis- missed with octets.

div.head: LABOUR MARKET.
div.p: THE LABOUR MARKET.

The labour market has entered on few important changes during the week. No great activity prevails in the iron trade, and in some districts there is considerable depression. At Birmingham the various hardware branches continue to show improvement, and at Sheffield most of the heavy trades are well employed. Iron shipbuilders, marine enginee-s, and steel makers remain generally busy. In North Wales the slate quarrymen are complaining of irregular work, but Welsh industries generally are fairly employed. In London miscellaneous trades are on the whole well engaged, but ad- vertisements for mechanics are not numerous. Navvies are in demand for works in Northumberland, Lincolnshire, and Sussex, and a fair number of new works are announeed. In Staffordshire the nail workers have struck or an advance in wages and are out in large numbers. The textile trades do not show any important change, but at Kidderminster the worsted spinning mills are running full time. At Notting- ham the lace trade is brisk, but at Leicester the elastic web branch shows little or no improvement. Dundee linen and sail-cloth remain slack. The boot and shoe trades at the leading centres are brisk. Ira the United States great activity in railway construction is still reported, and a de- mand for labour in New Mexico is announced. Building at New York is active, but several branches are unsettled on the wages question. A new railway is projected in Chili, and in South Africa a large expenditure on railway and other works may soon be expected.— Labour News.

It is consoling to find in these times of depression and anxiety that the harvest prospects are such as afford material for congratulation. Satisfactory accounts are being received from all parts of England respecting the crops, and if we travel farther afield reports of a similar encouraging character are met with in all directioas. Throughout Europe the harvest promises to be exceptionally good this This, of course, is owing chiefly to favourable :neteorological conditions, but it is in part due to the fact that the area sown with cereals is larger than the average for several years past.

div.head: ST. HELENS POLICE COURT.
div.p: ST. HELENS POLICE COURT.

FRlDAY.—Before the Mayor (Mr. Alderman Harrison) and Mr. H. S. Hall. A RUNAWAY COUPLE BROUGHT TO JUSTICE.—WiIIiam Burrows, Windle, was charged with running away and leaving his wife and six children chargeable to the Prescot Union; and Elizabeth Whitfield, of Windle, with a similar offence by leaving her three children chargeable to the Union.—Mr. S. H. Hartley, clerk to the Guardians, prose- cuted.—lt appeared that Burrows went away about a fort- night ago, and was apprehended at Birkenhead, and on being ckarged he said, "lain a fool; I have been led into it by that woman," meaning _Elizabeth Whitfield. The woman
was not to be found aEßirkenhead, although she had been there, and was apprehended at Southport. She had been receiving 4s. a week on account of her children, as her hus- . .

band had deserted her, and the relieving officer received a letter from one of her neighbours that she had gane away, and that the children would require looking after. The children were subsequently taken to the workhouse. Mr. Hartley said that 250 children were now in the workhouse . . . . .

having been deserted by their parents, and it was becoming very common. During the last five or six years the amount of money expende6l in out-door relief had morethan doubled; in 1875 it amounted to £5,000, and now it was about

£ll,OOO. There might be a legal objection to convicting the female prisoner, but "Glen" distinctly pointed out the liability of the mother. Irish families could not be removed to Ireland in the absence of the head of the family, but "Glen" said the wife was equally punishable, and therefore could not leave her children behind her, and a similar ren- dering of the law was recorded in Botte.—After a conference with the magistrates' clerk, the Mayor said they could not convict the woman for running away.—Mr. Hartley: Then I will ask that an information may be laid against her for neglect.—The Chairman: A married woman is not bound to maintain her children if her husband has left her, unless she has separate property.—Mr. Hartley asked that the case might be adjourned, because he scarcely thought that was the actual rendering of the law.—The case was adjourned.— Female prisoner: Oh, Mr. Harrison, don't adjourn it again; it has been adjourned before. As for keeping them, I cannot; the youngest is nearly eight years of age.—The Mayor: Can you find bail 7—Female prisoner: I have not any friends here, but I have all my enemies, and as for living with this man, I only saw him on Saturday. (A voice in court: "Oh ; " and expressions of astonishment from several per- sons, chiefly women, one imputing bad conduct on the part of the female prisoner.) I have witnesses to say that I left Southport at 20 minutes past three on Saturday afternoon. —The male prisoner was sent to prison for a month, with hard labour, and the other case was adjourned, bail being allowed.

PLAYING GAMES FOR MONEY.—Garßett Norton and Walter Stanley, boys, were fined 6d. and costs for playing at pitch and toss, in a public passage off Waterloo-street, at 20 minutes to 12 on Sunday morning.—Patrick Framey, a boy, was mulcted in a similar penalty for a similar offence, in a public court off Parr-street.—Henry and Thomas Lofthouse, William Bickerstaffe, and George Doyle, for playing at a game called "shooting off the mark," on tbe 20th inst., were each fined 2s. 6d. and costs. OBSTRUCTING THE FOOTPATH.—Emma Willets, a young woman in the fish business, was fined 10s. and costs or 14

days, for obstructing a public footpath by leaving a hand- cart on the footpath in Church-street; and Edward Forber was fined 2s. 6d. and costs for allowing a wheelbarrow on the footpath on Saturday evening. PROPANE LANGUAGE.—Ann Monaghan was fined ss. and costs for using profane language in the street, and Bridget Gormley was fined ss. and costs for using obscene language on Sunday morning. MONDAY.—Before Messrs. R. Pennington, jun., and T. Pilkington. CHASTISING HIS WlFE—Patrick Collins was charged with committing a breach of the peace by fighting with his wife in Greenbank, Eccleston, on Saturday night. Prisoner said that his wife was in a neighbour's house when she ought to have been attending to the child, which was in great danger from the fire. He remonstrated with her, and ultimately struck her. He was bound over to keep the peace for three months'. A NUISANCE.—Edward Scott and Henry McCormack, boys, were charged with exposing their persons on the 21st inst. From the evidence of the police it appeared the boys were running along the highway near Hare's Finch House, the only covering they had on being their shirts. A lady and gentleman complained that it was "shameful walking on the highway." They were each fined Is. and COSI& RUNNING AWAY WITH ANOTHER WOMAN'S HUSBAND.— Elizabeth Whitfield (35), who resided in Hope-street, was again charged with unlawfully running away from the township, and leaving her three children chargeable to the Present Union.—Prisoner pleaded not guilty.—Mr. S. H. Hartley, clerk to the guardians, said the case was proved on Friday before His Worship the Mayor and Mr. Hall, but a legal objection was taken at that time, a case being quoted in which it was held that a deserted wife was not liable for the maintenance of her own children, unless she had means of her own to maintain them with. The fact of the guar- dians having allowed the woman money for the children, the case was not analogous to the one quoted, as he had then means apart from her separate income for the support of the children. If she had not been in receipt of relief, she would not have been liable for the maintenance, but the guardians had allowed the woman 4s a week for the last 15 months. The woman went away on the very day she received her last money. It was a very had case, because , ' she was found cohabiting with another woman's husband, and she was apprehended at Southport.— Charles Morris Stuart, relieving officer, said he found the prisoner's children in an empty room. He made enquiries from the prisoner's son and landlady as to the whereabouts of prisoner, and he ascertained that the boy had carried a box to the railway station for his mother. He relieved the children, and on the following day gave them an order for their admittance to the workhouse. The children were in the house all night by themselves. There was a bundle of old rags in the corner apparently used for a bed.—Samuel F. Wensley said the ages of the children were eleven, nine, and seven.—Prisoner said the• bundle of rags constituted the bed she slept on.—Mrs. Borrows, wife of the prisoner's paramour: How many times have you slept with my hus- band, you brazen face ?—Prisoner : The bed that you found on my premises was the bed I laid on myself. Are you aware that I slept on it P—Mr. Stuart: No—Prisoner: Well, but I did. And you found a blanket didn't you ? No, I only found a bundle of old rans.—Alexander Scott Campbell, shiprigger, Abbott-street, Birkenhead, said he saw the woman on Saturday week going out of the yard of his I house. The prisoner Borrows, who was committed on Fri-1 I day, was with her. They lodged at his house that night. She represented that Burrows was her husband, and that she had nine children at St. Helens. He afterwards found the statement was false, as Burrows' wife came to the door on Saturday night and asked if her husband was there. She gave him a description of the man, but as he did not ceme in until nine o'clock she went away. On Sunday morning the prisoner and Burrows went to church, and on re- turning, and after having breakfast, they went to bed, where they stayed all day.—Prisoner: I never told you that I was his wife.—Yes you did.—Prisoner: You never saw me before Saturday.—Witness : No, nor I don't want to see you any more. (Laughter and clapping of hands, which drew forth a remonstrance from the magistrates' clerk).— For the prosecution Henry Whitfield, eleven years of age, was put into the box, and he burst into tears. The prisoner encouraged the child by saying "Don't cry, my son, speak for your mother." Witness spoke to carrying a bag and box, with the assistance of a girl named Wilson, to the rail- way station.—Magistrate (to prisoner) : Have you anything to say P—Prisoner : I have a great deal to say.—Magis- trate : Well, let us have it then—Prisoner: What is that gentleman's name (meaning Mr.'llartley) P—Magistrate : I don't know, I am sure. If you have anything to say, let us hear it—Prisoner: I asked for the gentleman's name so Writ I could allude to him. I left Southport a few hours after I got there, so that I could not have lived with him there. I cannot ' support my children; that boy will eat as much as sixpennyworth at a time. I sent these children to their grandmother, but she would not give them a crust from the table, although they are rolling in plenty. But it is because they are my children, and because I am a Catholic; and they have despised me for eleven years. My husband is alive, but has left me, and is making 308. and £2 a week, and has done for the last seven months, I know of myself. —Mr. Pennington: What have you got to say about run- ning away and leaving the children ?—Prisoner : Well, I got a situation, but I was not strong enough to manage the work.—Mr. Pennington: Is that all you have got to say—Prisoner: Yes; I think it is. The case has been remanded from Wednesday, and this is the third time I have been tried in this court for the same case.— After a long conversation with the magistrates' clerk, Mr. Pennington said they regretted they had to dismiss the case. —Mr. Hartley then said he would lay an information against the prisoner for neglecting to provide adequate food, clothing, and lodging, for het children. —Subsequeptly she was charged with this offence.—Mr. Hartley said that on the morning she ran away she was provided with means for the support of her children.—C. M. Stuart said there was no food in the honse when he visited the place, and the children were badly clothed. He ascertained that the pri- soner had gone away the day previous.—C. F. Wensley said he apprehended the prisoner at Southport.—The prisoner said Mr. Wensley was one of her enemies; and she pro- ceeded to say that it was the duty of the relieving officer to have asked her sole when he came to the house if she (pri- soner) had given him the money when she left by rail. She said "He is one of my enemies, but let' them do their very most there is a just God in Heaven, and my husband will be punished the same as he has punished me. When ray hus- band is here I shall not be here to hear him tried, and I hope your lordships will give him his punishment. I have worked for nine years for these children, and on the 14th Decem- ber, 1865, my husband was the murderer of my only son, now lying in Appleton churchyard ; and his sister sent me her compliments last night and hoped the devil would take —wTithhehßarednclahbsoeunr: —Prisoner: strh°:ric,ip'mo sSoeini tethhdsei di mfgaupoir,tieesro nri iTghea'tgliberty now.—The sentence appeared to give general satisfaction outsb4e the court. A group of women discussed the case with evident delight. A BOOKMAKER'S CLERK WITH A GOOD REPUTATION.— Jhn Brown a stranger, was charged with being drunk on the licensed premises of William Taylor. Duke-street, on o, Saturday and also with assaulting P.C. Peebles, whilst in , he execution of his duty.—Prisoner pleaded not guilty.— tPC. Peebles said the prisoner was drunk and selling some literatnre referring to the Newton races. He interfered, and the prisoner struck him several times. With the assistance of another man he took him to the police station —Prisoner said he only had "a gill "on Saturday from t) e Newton 'axes. I gave this gentleman (meaning sornevue iU the

public-house) a tip for the Thunder and Plate. I never re- ceived such treatment in the days of my life in a town in Lancashire. lam a bookmaker's clerk on the road, and I have a good reputation—never been in prison in my life before.—For being drunk he was fined ss. and costs, and 109. and costs for the assault, or 21 days' imprisonment. BRIDGET'S 111TH APPEARANCE AND USUAL REBUKE TO THE COURT.—Bridget Kildare was charged with being drunk and disorderly, on the 25th June, in Naylor-street, South.— Inspector Wood said the prisoner had been there 110 times before. (Sensation.) Prisoner: You have summat to laugh at. Better to laugh at yoursel than to laugh at a poor unfortunate soul. You should be more ill-off than to laugh at a poor woman.—She was sent to prison for a month with hard labour. THE " DUMMY " AND Hts DOINGS.—Henry Bramhall, a deaf and dumb young man, was charged with being drunk land disorderly en the 25th, from which date he had been locked up. A piece of paper bearing the charge was handed to him, upon which he wrote, "No, I was not drunk."— Sergeant Whittaker said the prisoner had been some time in the town, and was very troublesome, being nearly always drunk.—P. C. Wellwood said that on the day in question a large crowd of people were around him in Tontine-street. He "shoved" the prisoner on for some distance to get him ; away from the crowd, when he became very violent, and kicked at a man at the bottom of Bridge-street, and nearly broke his leg.—Mr. Pennington: Is he quiet when sober?— P. C. Wellwood: I very seldom see him sober; he is frequently drunk. I have seen him up at three o'clock in the morning with a lot of roughs on Greenbank. A VIOLENT FELLow.—John Fairclough, a young man, was charged with being drunk and disorderly at Sutton, on Saturday, and also a ith assaailting P. C. Carter whilst in the execution of his duty.—The police officer said he was in Marshall's Cross-road, and a man and two women com- plained that the prisoner, who was a short distance behind, had been insulting them. The prisoner soon came up, drunk. He said his sister lived near, and he took him to the place, where be stayed a short time. He came out and behaved "shameful," so that he was obliged to take him into custody. Prisoner kicked the officer causing him great pain, which he had felt ever since. He was also charged with assaulting a man named John Christian in Bridge-street, and with assaulting P. C. Wellwood whilst in the execution of his duty. He pleaded guilty to the former charge, and not guilty to the latter.—lt appeared from the evidence of P. C. Wellwcod that he was attempting to take Mary Ann Willets into custody, and whilst proceeding along Exchange-street, the prisoner, with others, obstructed him, and also assaulted him. The officer blew his whistle, and two constables came upon the scene. Christian, who was rendering assistance, was struck is the face by the prisoner causing blood to flow from his mouth and nose. Prisoner„ who had been convicted several times previously for various offences, amongst which were those of picking pockets and attempting to pick pockets, was tined £2 for each assault on the police, and 20s. for the assault on Christian and COM. HIS QUIVER Too Ft:lLL.—Patrick Bowe was summoned to show cause why be should not be ordered to contribute to- wards the maintenance of his son Martin Bowe, who is now in St. Ann's industrial school, Liverpool.—P.C. Peebles said the defendant was a chemical labourer, and he had ascertained that his wages for the last six weeks averaged £1 13s 41.—Defendant said he had seven children depen- dent upon him, the eldest of whom was 14 years of age and the youngest two mocths.—Mr. Pennington: You will have to pay 2s. a week—Defendant: I cannot afford to pay that. —Mr. Pennington: Well, if you get children you must keep them. AN EARLY BIRD CAUGHT.—Joseph Parr, of St. Helens, was charged with using a dog for the purpose of taking game, he not having a game license.—P.O. Ratcliffe was coming to St. Helens early in the morning of Sunday, and on passing along Owen's•lane at a quarter-past three he met the defendant and three other men. Two lurcher dogs were with them. He bade the defendant " Good morning," as he knew him very well, and added, "You have had a night of it, then." Defendant, who returned the salute, said they had done nothing wrong. The police officer said, " Oh, you are only going," to which defendant said, "It will be all right," and ultimately "good morning" passed between them, and the men and the police officer separated. Later _

on the police officer and P.C. Duerden, of Red Cat, watched the men hunt over land and a plantation in the occupation of Robert Birchall, and they succeeded in capturing the defendant.—He was fiaed 40s and costs.

THE LOST LICENSE.—Sarah Scott, wife of a clergyman, now abroad, was summoned for keeping a dog without a license.—Mr. Swift defended, and said that defendant's hus- band had taken away the license, and that she had written for it, but it had not arrived. She therefore took out a license after the policeman had called, and reported the case. It was also contended that Mrs. Scott was a "nonentity in the eye of the law," and ought not to have been summoned. —The case was dismissed.

ASSAULTING A WOMAN—Joseph Woodward, Whiston, was charged with assaulting Mary Ann Taylor, en Saturday.— Complainant said "she was protecting a lonely woman and taking her to the workhouse," when the prisoner and others tried to take the woman away from her, and abused both of them.—Prisoner, whom complainant said was not the " worsest " of the lot," was fined 20s and costs.
WEDNESDAY.—Before His Worship the Mayor (Mr. Alder-
man Harrison).

A DISTURBANCE AT THE RAILWAY STATION.—Peter Dolan, a young " touter " at the railway station, was charged with being drunk and disorderly at the railway station.—A railway official said that on Tuesday night shortly after eight o'clock prisoner entered the railway station and caused a great disturbance. He pulled off his hat, coat, and waistcoat, and challenged to fight one of the porters—Prisoner, who had been convicted twice pre- viously, was fined 7s. Gd. and costs or seven days. A BAD DEDINNINC3.—Annie Forhor, 15 years of aCce, we charged with having, on the previous afternoon, stolen a purse containing a shilling from a dwelling-house in Glover- street, Eccleston.—Mary Eccleston, a single woman, said she lodged in a house in Glover-street. About three o'clock on the previous afternoon prisoner came into the house and staved about half an hour. soon after prisoner had gone out she missed a purse which she had left on the table.— Prisoner was remanded until Friday.—Priaoner's mother was proceeding to make a statement, when Inspector Wood interposed a remark to the effect that the mother knew that the girl had been in the habit of bringing home things which could not have been, and were not Atained honestly.

div.head: IRON AND COAL TRADES.
div.p: IRON AND COAL TRADES.

LANCASHIRE, WEDNESDAY.-The Coal trade throughout Lancashire continues in a very depressed condition, and the output from the collieries is so much in excess of the re- quirements of the market that already in some of the large colliery districts, notwithstanding flee complete clearance effected during the late strike, extremely heavy stocks have already accumulated. A few of the large collieries, prin- cipally those in the Manchester district, are still being kept on full time, but at numbers of the pits three to four days a week now represent the full extent to which they are work- ing. The leading Manchester colliery firms are maintaining their June prices, and in other districts the month closes without any announced alteration of the nominal list rates. Generally, however, prices are weak, and for anything like quantities business is done very considerably under the nominal rates, stocks under load especially being pressed at extremely low figures. So far as round coals are concerned, the only inquiries of importance at present coming into the market are for gas-making purposes, and for good screened Lancashire gas coal the average price at the pit remains at about Cs. 6d. to 6s. 9d. per ton. The requirements for house fire coals are extremely limited, and they are being stacked heavily; the best sorts at the pit average about Ss. 6d. to 95., with inferior sorts down to about 6s. to 6s. 6d. per ton. Common round coals for iron-making and steam purposes continue a drug, and in these there is a good deal of push- ing at very low figures, 4s. 9d. to ss. 6d. per ton being about the average prices quoted at the pit mouth. For engine classes of fuel a fairly steady demand is maintained, and the better qualities of slack continue scarce. For good burgy at the pit mouth the average mice is about 4s. 3d. to 4s. 9d. per ton, and for good slack 3s. 9d. to 4s. 3d. The shipping trade generally continues dull, and for steam coals very low prices are being taken. Coke is in moderate de- mand, and prices at the ovens range from Ss. to 10s. for small, up to 12s. and 14s. per ton for large cokes. In the iron trade the improved tone noticed last week is fairly main- tained: but up to the present there has not been any very marked accession of actual new business, and buyers still show a disinclination to pay any material advance upon late rates. There is, however, a disposition to buy which has been conspicuously absent for the last three or four months, and sellers are able to command better prices than could have been obtained a rew weeks back. During the week Lancashire makers of pig iron have been doing a fair amount of business which is additionally satisfactory inas- much as the iron is going into the hands of consumers. Orders have also not only been more nutnereus, but con- sumers have shown more confidence by purchasing larger quantities than they have been taking of late, and sales could be made freely up to the end of the year, but local makers decline to go further than the next three or four months. No alteration has yet been made in the quoted prices, hut makers are very firm at late rates, and for delivery into the Manchester district the minimum quotations are 435. for forge and 445. for foundry, less 21 per cent. Sales of Lincolnshire iron have been made at the slight advance put on last week, orders for forge iron having been placed at 439. 10d., and for foundry at 445. 10d., less 21.- per cent., delivered equal to Manchester; but for other outside brands the prices asked prevent any considerable business being done here. For finished iron a fair demand is reported both on export and home account, chiefly in bars, hooPs, and sheets, for which delivered equal to Manchester the quota- tions are £5 15s. to £5 178. 6d. for bars, £6 ss. to £6 100. for hoops, and £7 12s. 6d. up to £7 15s. for ordinary sheets. A fair number of American orders for machinery are now coming into this district, and local firms are at present sending out general tools, such as radial drills, slotting planing, and drilling machines.

THE LAST OF THE CATERPILLARS AT CLITHEROE.--We , are glad to be in a position to state that the caterpillars, who have caused se much commotion in the district, have almost if not entirely disappeared. The other day we paid another visit to Wellsprings, in the immediate vicinity of which the reptiles were once SO numerous, and discovered that the in- vaders had no rapidly diminished in numbers that nothing except the "dead and the dying" were to be seen of them. A few, however, yet remain above the Wellprings Inn, but it will not be the fault of the crows or the visitors If these do not likewise make a speedy departure.

ODDFELLOWSHIP AT WHISTON.
HALF-YEARLY MEETING OF THE PRESCOT DISTRICT.

On Monday the half-yearly meeting of the delegates of the various lodges (ten in number). comprising the Prescot district of the Independent Order of Oddfellows, Manchester Unity, was held at the George and Dragon Inn, Whiston, Prov. G. M. Aaron Gore, of Maypole Lodge, Knowsley, presiding. After the transaction of some minor business, the district balance was submitted and read, from which it appeared that the receipts during the past half-year in the sick and funeral fund had been £123 165., which together with abalance of £347 lls. 7d. brought forward from the previous half-year made a total of £471 70. 7d. The ex- penditure amounted to £7O, leaving a balance of £40175. 7d., being an increase of £53 16s. on the half-year ending De- cember last. The management fund accounts showed that that at the beginning of the half-year there was a balance in hand af £l7 ss. 11d., and that there had been receiged since the sum of £3l 16s. 3d.; total, £49 2s. 2d. The expenses in connection with this fund had been £2O 10s. 5d., leaving a balance of £2B us. 9d., an increase on the pre- vious half-year of £ll ss. 10d. There had been no expen- diture in connection with either the Widow and Orphans' Institution or the Widow and Orphans' Institution Manage- ment Fund, the amount standing to the credit of the former being £207 14s. 7d., and ot the latter £1 2s. 10d. The balance sheet was unanimously approved of. Secretary Thomas Bowstead, of the Victoria Lodge, Prescot, district auditor, submitted his annual report, from which it appeared that the total amount of lodge funds in December, 1880, was £8,329 115. 3P.; total amount of district funds, £364 17s. 6d.; value of lodges' property, £7O; value of district property, £5O; amount of District Widow and Orphans' Funds, £202 Is. 7d.•' total worth of funds and property, £9,016 16s. ; total worth of funds and property in 1879, £8,614 16s. 7d; gain during the year, £4Ol 19s. 91d. There had been paid to sick members during the year the sum of £763 48. The total amount gained in the lodge funds, alone, was £442 ss. Bid. The number of members on the books in December, 1879, was 1,213; admitted during 1880, 61; total, 1,274. There had died during the year, 17; left through non-payment, 48; left by clearance, 1; expelled, 1; total, 67; leaving the total number of members in the dis- trict at 1,207, or a decrease of 6on the year. There were 10 honorary members in the district. The average worth per member was £7 9s. 5d.; and the average age 33 years. The report was passed, and secretary Bowstead was re-appointed auditor of the lodges' accounts for the year ending June 1882. It was resolved that the amalgamation of the Orphans' Protection and Countess of Sef ten Lodges in the Briton's Pride Lodge, be confirmed, and that all funds in possession of, and money due to, the first two mentioned lodges, after all just debt had been discharged, be paid over to the Britons' Pride Lodge. The following men:theca were nominated to attend the next A.M.C., to be held at Cardiff, in 1882 - P.P.GM. Henry Makin, P.P.G.M. Richard Gore, P.P.O.M. James Stott, P.P.G.M. John Bixter, P.P.G.M. William Brea- nand, secretary James Holt, and P.G. Robert Wright. Prov. D.G.M. James Bixter, Victoria Lodge, was nominated for the Prov. G.M., and the following were nominated for the Prov. D.G.M. :-P.G. Wright, and P.G. James Stott, of the Farmers' Rest Lodge. Tarbock ; P.G. William Pascall, and P.G. Thomas Houghton, Earl of Derby Lodge, Prescot ; secretary, James Holt, Earl of Sefton Lodge, Kirkby; P.G. Edwin Rimmer, Lord Stanley Lodge, Roby; P.G. William Smeatham; Prince Alfred Lodge, Hainhill ; and secretary Thomas Bowstead, Victoria Lodge, Prescot. The election will take place on the 26th December, at the Stanley Arms Hotel, Roby, where the next half yearly meeting will b held. A vote .:)f thanks was passed to the district officers for their services during the past half year, and a similar compliment having been paid the chairman, the meeting closed.

We had about a dozen bright Arab girls dancing and skipping around us as we stood near to Pompey's Pill sr. One carried a little child, which remained fast asleep on her shoulder, leaning against her head, while she danced and jumped about like an automaton. WHAT CAN VEGETARIANISM DO FOR THE WORM- INGMAN "—This was the title of a lecture delivered on the Warrington Fair Ground. on Monday evening, by Mr Peter Foxcroft, of Manchester, under the auspices of the Warrington Vegetarian Society. The lecturer remarked that be had been a vegetarian for 34 wears and therefore spoke from experience. Vegetarianism be defined as total abstinence from fish, flesh, and fowl and observed that S mairayr people said they could not live without flesh meat. statements were made in the early days of teetotalism,ibmutit had been proved that people could live without using in- toxicating liquors, and it had also been proved that people could live without flesh meat of any description. LYM/f CONGRECIATIONLL CIIIIRCR.—On Sunday last the 19th anniversary services of this church were held, the sermon in the morning being preached hy the Rev. James Bedell (the esteemed pastor), and in the evening by the Rev. Caleb Scott, president of the Lancashire Independent College. Collections were made at each of the services in aid of the funds, and a sum of £2l realised. During the past year the school and church have been cleaned and repaired, and £92 has been received and expended on the work. A further sum of £34 is still needed to pay for the inside furnishing of the schools, for the outside repairs and painting, and for the chippings laid on the walks. RzsioNATION OF 11111 RECTOR OF LIMM.—The Rev. Thomas R. Branfoot, M.A., has resigned the rectory of Lymrn, which he has held since 1833. Mr. Branfoot is ;1 graduate of Trinity College, Oxford, where be took his Arti degrees in 1834 and 1842 respectively. He was ordained deacon in 1836 and priest in 1837 by the Bishop of Jamaica. For several years he filled the positions of chaplain and , secretary to the Bishop of Jamaica and registrar of the diocese, and was, in addition, ecclesiastical cotnmissioner for Port Royal. Mr. Branfoot has been successively curate of Harrietsham, Kensington, Cripplegate, Ilford, and Kensing- ton for the second time, during which, in 1863, he was pre- ferred to the Rectory of Lymm. lhe living is in the gift of Mr. Egerton Leigh, and is worth about £4OO, with glebe and house.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 2, 1881.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 2, 1881.
RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.

Tuesnay.—Before Mr. W. Wynnt) Foulkes, Judge. A HALTON Tarr BELPLZADER CANA In this Case Mr. Thomas Massey Green, of Hale, and Mr. John Frodsham, solicitor's clerk, Frodsham, were the blairaants, and Mr. Thomas Horabin trustee in the estate of Messrs. Pickering and Woodfin, Chester, was the execution creditor.—Mr. Shand, barrister (instructed by Mr. Hitchen), appeared for the claimants, and Mr. Mason, of Chester, for the execution creditor.—Mrs. Watkin, the wife of the debtor, a Mr. Wat- kin commission agent and butcher, of Halton, was called, and said she was the daughter of Mrs. Mary Vaughan, who died on the 6th November last. Her parents formerly lived at Birkenhead. After the death of her father in 1882 (he having previously left "the city of the future,") her mother removed to Preston Brook, and ultimately to Halton. Wit- ness married Mr. Watkin in 1889, whilst living with her mother at Halton; and resided with her until her death in November. Her mother provided a large amount of furni. tare for them; and they did dot need to purchase any. They lived in the house until the sth March, this year; and up to the time of her death her mother paid the rent, and partly supported witness and her children from a private in- come of which she was possessed. She asked permission of Mr. Frodsham, one of the trustees, to remove the furniture to the house in which they now lived at Summer-hill, and this was granted.—la cross-examination, witness said that at the time of her marriage to Mr. Within, he had no furniture and "brought nothing with him." At the time when her husband filed his petition, no claim was made upon the furniture by the trustees. In fact, her husband had no furniture, as it was her mother's, and, there- fore:they could not claim it. She had received no money from her husband with which to pay the rent, and she had discharged that out of money of her own. He found her about £1 per week, after his expenses were paid. It was not true that anyone ever " put her up to" placing the house in the name of the trustees. Mr. Smith, of the Chester Chronicle office, was the landlord.—Re-examined : Her mother was blind, and she was of great assistance to her through living with her. The trustees never consented to , her putting the house in witness's own name.—Mr. Henry Watkin, husband of last witness, said he had no furniture at the time he went to live with his wife.—Cross-examined : Then you have been content to live on this old lady since your marriage? Yes.--And contract your debts right and left? Sometimes I have had losses.-1 dare say you have with your large business, and being a commission agent for almost everything. What was the amount you failed for in 1876? About £6oo.—What did your creditors get? About 4s. 6d. in the £. In answer to further questions, witness admitted that sometimes he was not able to even find his wife 201. per week. Sometimes he paid her £5, after which he might have a loss of £2O or £3O. They had six children. All he bought at a sale which took place at the Raven pubilic-house was a trap and some other little matters, which he gold again.—Mr. John Mack, valuer, Runcorn, gave evidence as to taking an inventory of the goods for probate purposes, in December last.—Mr. John Frodsham, one of the claimants, and an executor under Mrs. Vaughan's will,aaid that when Mr. Watkin filed his petition no claim was made on the furniture by the trustee. Wit- ness refused to allow the furniture to be removed to the house at Summer -Hill unless the place was taken in the name of the trustees.—In cross-examination, witness said the executors had paid £9, the cost of probate, out of their own pockets.—Mr. George Tony, bailiff of the court, next gave evidence as to testing the accuracy of the inventory. —Mr. Mason mibmitted that what the wife had done in this ease was really the action of the husband. No doubt the little rase of the wife going to the landlord of the premises and getting them put in the name of the trustrees, had been gone through. He considered that the goods had been left to the trustees, upon trust, to sell. Mr. Watkins had so condacted his affairs as to lead his creditors to believe that he was a man of -substance. After some further remarks from Mr. Mason as to the alleged unfairness of the debtor in dealing with his creditors, His Honour said that upon the evidence he could do no other than give judgment for the claimants. The costs of the execution must be taken out of the, money in court. In that way they would have to be pa id by the claimants, but they would be allowed costs as against the execution creditor. JURY CASE: SINGULAR ACTION AGAINST A RUNCORN Cr] urrLEMAN.—Mr. Thomas Livesey, grocer and tea dealer, an d Margaret, his wife, sued Mr. William Griffith, ship- owner, formerly tea dealer, to recover the sum of £2l 10s., being the balance of an account alleged to be owing by him. Mr. W. H. Linaker appeared for the plaintiffs and Mr. Sh and, barrister (instructed by Mr. S. Lloyd Jones, of Liver- po el), for the defence.—Mr. Linaker, in opening the case, said the action was to recover the cost of maintenance of defendant's daughter Fanny. Plaintiff's wife was defen- ds.nt's sister-in-law. In 1872 the defendant's first wife died, and Mr. Griffiths requested Mrs. Livesey, who was then Mrs. Helms, to take his daughter home with her to the Isle of man, and he would make her an allowance. From that time to the beginning of 1875 defendant's daughter lived with her at the Isle of Man, and defendant each year sent over a cheque for £lO, being the amount which Mrs. Helms ha .d agreed to take as the price of the lodging and board. At. the latter end of 1878 plaintiff and her husband removed to Rock Ferry, and they requested defendant to take his daughter for a few weeks during the time occupied in . changing their residence, and he agreed to do so. At that ' time £7 105 was due to Mrs. Helms for the three-quarters of . a year which the child had been with her. Defendant, who had got married again, then arranged to keep Fanny at home, but no settlement was come to as to the debt. One tSunday in th.) early part of the year 1875 defendant went (aver to Rock Ferry with his little girl, and begged of Mrs. Helm to take charge of her, as there had been some differences at home, and he should much prcfer her being away. She consented, and defendant wis,bed to make an arrangement as to what the allowance short ld be, but as it was Sunday, the lady said she did not wish to enter i nto a bargain that day. Defendant consented to thi.'s proposal, and gave Mrs. Helms a sovereign, after agreeing to fina 1 his daughter some clothing. At the end of six months the girl was again taken away, and for this six months board rind maintenance, Mrs. Helms made a claim of £l5, tire total amount sued for, after deducting the sovereign I laid, being £2l 15s. The question was simply one of conb met, as to whether defendant did really agree to pay the st im named for the maintenance.—Mrs. Livesey (formerly H elms) was then called, and said that her sister left three ch ildren, when she died, one being a girl and the other two bre vs. She gave evidence in support of the opening statement.-1 n cross-examination, witness said that when defendant's dr tughter left her, she did not ask for the balance owing to her, , as she was afraid to do so, fearing that he, being of a pea diar temperament, would not allow her to see her sister's c hildren if she offended him in any way. —Mr. Shand: For two years you were afraid, bet on Hie 19th May this I tear, you plucked up courage to proceed with the matter? I did, because I had nothing to fear from him then. (Proceed lug): She and her sister were great friends. There was no arrangement that Mr. Helms was to invest the £3O for the benefit of the child. She gave up the bank book in which tin 3 amounts were put down to the defendant after Fanny was taken away, the first time she saw him.— At this part of tire case defendant went very near to the jury, and the jut lge, addressing him, said: Let the gentle- man stand away t mm the jury and not make signs to them. If von do that agt tin I shall order you out of court.—Wit- ness (proceeding): The arrangement was that she was to bring the child up : as her adopted daughter, as she had no children then, but had two now. It was a fact that Mr. Griffiths had show n her and her hustand considerable kindness, but not b a the way of business. He had a half share with the defendant in the fiat Edward Whitley, and she was in partnership with Mr. Griffith in two other flats named the Ruby and the Gleaner. There had been a dispute between her husbnnd and defendant as to some freight be- longing to the fiat Ed ward Whitley. Her husband withheld his share of the freigt it until the defendant had made good the two ropes which he had used, having no right, she alleged, to them. Th ere was certainly an idea in her mind before the dispute as tt )the freight taking place, as to charg- ing for the maintenam le, but she was afraid to do so.—The court then adjourned for luncheon, and on re-assembling, Mr. Shand addressed the jury for the defence. He said his client altogether denied ever having refute the payment of £1 spoken of by the last witness. It appeared that two I months after the death, of Mr. Helms, the female plaintiff took unto herself anot her spouse—Mr. Livesey, and the business of Mr. Griffith, in Camden Buildings, Runcorn, was bought for MOO, by ?4 re. Livesey. Nothing, however, not even a syllable, was said about any payment for the main- tenance of the child. ' The key to the action arising might be found in the fact thal` in either April or May a disagree- ment arose with regard to the freight of the flat Edward Whitley, in consequenc 3 of which Mr. Livesey was obliged to pay over a certain amount for freight in dispute with the defendant. It seemed that after this Mr. Livesey determined to "have it out." On th e 19th May this year, the firstletter on the matter was written as follows:—" Sir, I think it is quite time you and I had a settlement for the maintenance of your daughter Fanny. I herewith enclose your account for the same. Yourstruly, MARGARET LIVEsEY." Let the jury look at that letter, which was written as if the lady had made repeated applications for the money. Mrs. Livesey "took the high line" at once. The postcript ran, " Please remit balance by return, to save further trouble." The de- fendant was in no way liable to pay this money to the plaintiff. The child went, as any child might, as a niece to its aunt's, to stay, at the request of a sister who was be- loved and dead. However, in consequence of disputes on the freight question, Mrs. Livesey brought the action, and might be supposed to have said to herself, "I have no other means of worrying Mr. Griffith, and I will bring this suit because his daughter stayed with me as a I friend during the times referred to."—Mr. William Griffith, the defendant, was called and said his first wife died in. 1872. His sister-in-law, Mrs. Helms, was at his house some few days before his wife died; and Mrs. Griffith asked him if he would agree to let her have thecustodyof her daughter Fanny after her death. He replied "No' I cannot part with the child, because she will be a comfort to me here- after." His wife, however, asked him the same question at night, and. he consented to agree to her request. On saving so his wife said, "Now I shall die in peace." Mrs. Helms was "at him daily" to take his daughter away, and an arrangement was altered into by which he agreed to pay '£lo per annum to Mrs. Helms for the benefit of the child, the money to be placed in the bank until Fanny came of age. Mrs. Helms agreed to clothe and feed his daughter, and not one word was said about any payment. When he took his daughter back Mrs. Livesey did not ask him for a penny. When the bank book was given back to him not a word was said about it being taken to Liverpool for the pur- pose of being balanced. It was after the dispute about the freight of the fiat that he received the letter enclosing the

account for maintenance. He had been as kind as be possi- i bly could to her husband, because he was a good friend of I his. He used to visit him, "and he was such a good man." (A laugh.)—Mrs. Sarah Rowles, wife of Mr. Richd. Rowles, licensed victualler, having given evidence in support of de- fendant's case, Mr. Linaker addressed a few words to the jury, and remarked that even if the plaintiffs never thought of bringing the action until the difference as to the freight arose, or never even contemplated making the claim, there was nothing in these matters to prevent their bringing it before the court then.—ln summing up, the Judge said the question which the jury had to answer, was simply whether there was a contract in the case or not, but this was not an easy one to which to return a reply, owing to the conflicting evidence which had been given. They mast consider whether the reason alleged by Mrs. Livesey for not bringing the action sooner was a reasonable one. If they thought that it was not so, that was a strong reason why they should hesitate to accept her view of the transaction. Then was it a claim which had been suggested to the minds of the plaintiffs, in consequence of the disputes which had arisen about the freight. Mr. Shand had argued that the letters of Mrs. Helms proved she had adopted Fanny, and had no notion of receiving pay for her maintenance. She spoke of Fanny as "my little daughter."—The jury then retired, amid after about ten minutes deliberation returned into court, on which Mr. Thomas Handley. the foreman, said their verdict was in favour of the plaintiffs, and for ' £lo.—Mr. Shand: I do not know, your honour, whether you will give me leave to move for a new trial, on the ground that (be verdict is against the weight of evidence.— ' The Judge : I could not do that; I think there was evidence on both sides, and that it was specially a ease for a jury.— Mr. Shand: I do not know whether you would think that on tLe whole evidence in this case, the costs ought to follow the event P—The Judge: Oh, yes.—This terminated the business of the court.

(Laughter.)—There were no volunteers, and no action was taken.

The following-latet7;;;-Tead.:---;7iii.-i'isher, Runcorn, —Dear, sir,—With reference to your interview relating to the reduction of rent of the premises in High-street, Run- corn, held by the poor law guardians, I am desired to inform you that the executors of the late Charles Hazlehurst have agreed to reduce the rent from £25 to £22. Trusting this may be satisfactory, I am, yours truly, ROBERT FOULKES." —A motion was made that the house be occupied at the re- duced rent, but it was ultimately resolved, on the advice of the clerk, who said a suitable house could be had for much less rent, to give up the house at the quarter end, when better terms coull probably be obtained.

div.p: ANNUAL VISIT TO COUNTY LUNATIC ASYLUM.,
A committee, consisting of the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Norman, Handley, Challoner, and the Clerk, were appointed to make the annual visit to the County Asylum at Chester.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The Rev. Canon Barclay presided at the fortnightly meet- ing held on Tuesday at Dutton Workhouse. There were also present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. J. Ashton, Chas. Rigby, John Mclntyre, Thos. Andrews, John Chat- loner, James Darbyshire, ROLL Ashton, Wm. Whitlow, John Darbyshire, John Weir, W. Jackson, Henry Neild, W. V. Fox, Chas. Reynolds, Henry Linaker (clerk) and Hy. Ban- croft (Engineer).

WIDNES POLICE COURT. WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. Holbrook Gaskell (chairman, George Pilkington, arid Holbrook Gaskell, jun. ' DRUNK IN CHARGE OF A HORSE AND CART.—MattiU Mannion was fined 10s. and costs for having been drunk in charge or a horse and cart, at Farnworth, or in default of payment be imprisoned 14 days.—Edward Loftus, a man who iaterfered with Mannion at the time, and was also drunk, was fined a similar amount and costs or 14 days' imprisonment. DEFAMATORY LANGUAGE.—Maria Osborn was summoned for using defamatory language to Charlotte Weir, on the 28th alt.—Complainant, who is a married woman, stated that she had a quarrel with the defendant, who, during the coaversation, charged her with gross immorality.—Wit- nesses were called in support of this statement—The Chair- man said the defendant, even though she had been provoked, had no right to use such an improper, gross, and horrible imputation against the complainant, and she would be bound over in two sureties of £5 to keep the peace for three months. A BRICK THROWER DESERVEDLY PUNISHED.—SiMOII Kilroy, a youth about 12 years of age, was summoned for seriously injuring a married woman named Ann Heyes, by 'titre wing a stone at her face.—Complainant said that about half-past ten o'clock on Monday night the defendant and , 1 a number of other lads were throwing stones and 1 causing a great row at the back of her house, in an empty dwelling. She called to her own lad, asking him to come in for the purpose of going to bed, and also re- I marked that a policeman ought to be sent for. No sooner I bad she said this than the boy picked up a pice of brick and threw it at her. It struck her on the left cheek and caused her a very serious wound, which was now plaistered up, and a black eye. She went to Dr. Pattison, who said she had received a serious wound which would affect her for life.—The Chairman said the case was a very bad one, and the assault most unprovoked. The lad, who had evidently been very badly brought up, might have blinded the woman; and his parents would be fined 20s. and the costs. In default of payment he would be sent to gaol 14 days.—The mother of the boy, who is a rather combative female, ex- pressed her strong dissent at the decision of the Bench as she was walking out of the court —The Chairman ordered her to be called back, and told her that it was quite evident she was letting the lad grow up in a very neglected manner. She ought to be thoroughly ashamed of herself.—She denied the truth of this imputation, and became rather excited, on which the Inspector of Police ordered her to be put out of the court. A WARNING TO WIFE BEATERS.—Thomas Welsh was charged with assaulting his wife Elizabeth, a respectable looking woman. Complainant stated that on the 29th ult., the family removed to another house, and as everything was in a disorderly state at night, she put one of the children into her bed. When her husband retired to rest, and found the girl in his bed, he told her that if she did not take her out be would throw complainant upon the floor. She told him she thought he might manage to make a a shift" for the night, but he would not, jumped on the floor, pulled the clothes off her, and dragged her out of bed, struck her on the back. and said that if she did not keepquiet he would throw her down stairs. The son asked defendant not to hit his mother, on which be gave him a blow on the face.—Defen- dant said he was prepared to admit the truth of everything his wife had stated. He had had "A drop of beer" that night, and did not know what he was doing.—Complainant in reply to the Bench, said her husband had frequently M- used her, and she dared not have lived with him as long as she had done if it had not been that the lodgers had frequently interfered to prevent him proceeding beyond a certain point. He had frequently threatened to take her life. —The Chairman said the assault was a very violent and brutal one. Fellows like the defendant appeared to think they were at liberty to treat their wives as if they were dogs, but the magistrates were determined to teach them that they could not do so. Defendant would be sent to gaol one month, with hard labour, and they hoped the punishment would prove a lesson to him. P.. for Mid-Cheshire, in which he stated he had pre- 1 sented the petition of the Board in favour of closing public houses on Snndays.—The CHAIRMAN: He doesn't say he supports the prayer of the petition (Laughter.)—Mr. Darby- shire : May I ask who signed the petition 7—The CHAIRMA I N: I did, as chairman of the Board.—Mr. ASHTON (smilingly): I The resolution said chairman of the Board, Mr. Derbyshire. POOR LAW CONFERENCE. The CLERK read a letter which he had received from Mr. John Holgate, secretary to the North-Western Poor Law Conference District, stating that as the time was approach-

THE FRODSHAM SEWERAGE SCHEME. The CLERIC submitted a number of tenders which he had received for the work of carrying out: the proposed sewer- age scheme for Frodsham and Frodsham and Frodsham Lord- ship. There were ten tenders varying in amount from £2,879 to £5,269. The tender of Mr. FRANK DAWSON of Bury, for £2,879 was accepted, subject to him being able to give satisfactory references and sureties for the due perfcrm- ance of the work.

THE STATE OF STOCKTON HEATH SEWERS. Mr. JOHN DARBYSHIRE said he should like to ask Mr. Bancroft as to the progress of the work at Stockton Heath. He had been over the roads with Mr. Bancroft, and the con- tractors were also asked to do so but they evidently did not think it necessary, and did not put in an appearance. In his (Mr. Derbyshire's) opinion the work was not progressing satisfactorily. If he remembered rightly it was stated in the specifications that the cutting of the sewers should be open. This had been deviated from, and he should like Mr. Ban- croft's public explanation, why the deviation had been allowed. He considered that a great portion of the road where the sewer had gone was quite unsuitable to allow what some people call tunnelling. The whole of it ought to have been open cutting.—Mr. BANatorr said he had written to the contractors that he was going over the ground with Mr. Darbyshire the surveyor of the roads, but none of them pit in an appearance. He went over the roads with Mr. Darby- shire and found that the contractors had not fully carried out his orders. He again wrote to the contractors specifying the different points to which he wished them to give their immediate attention, and a week ago he went over the ground again. Nothing whatever had been done, and on inquiry he found that Mr. John Turner, who had been residing at Wilderspool, had lately taken a contract at Wrexham, and gone away. He then wrote to Mr. Turner, senior, who replied that he had some urgent work at Warrington and Wrexham, and was very sorry that the work had been delayed, but that every- thing complained of should be properly attended to. Mr. Bancroft then told him that if it was not done he should put the contract into force, and obtain a man to do the work, and deduct the cost from his retention money. With regard to the deviation from the specification, under the contract he had the power to do so. His reason for doing so was that he was obliged by the rules of the Local Government Board to have his public mains in straight lines, and some of the roads twisted a good deal, and he had to cress them diagon- ally. In one part of the read, near the Red Lion Inn, if he had had open cutting he should have had to stop the traffic. There was also such a thin layer of metal on the roads that he wished to disturb them as little as possible.—The Chair- man: Is the tunnelling as satisfactory as if it had been open cutting?—Mr. BANCROFT said it had stood now for nine months. He had examined the work about once a week, and he had given distinct orders that it was to be well filled in and rammed, and the clerk of the works told him on the last occasion that that had been done.—The CHAIR- MAW: Was the ground of such a nature that you con- sidered it safe to tunnel 7—Mr. BANatorr answered in the affirmative, and said that where there was anything like deep cutting, the work was always done in the way in which he had had it done. He had done it at Northwich and other places.—The CHAIRMAN: It must be done with your approval.—Mr. Bancroft: Oh, yes; certainly.—Mr. JOHN DARBYSHIRE asked whether Mr. Bancroft was aware that there had been two or three subsidencies of the road. He gave several instances where carts had fallen to a depth of two or three feet, and remarked that it was very likely there I would be further subsidencies in the future.—Mr. BANCROFT said that whether open cutting or not, they could not help those subsidencies taking place from time to time.— Mr. JAs. DARBYSHIRE said the roads were in a bad state all winter, and not fit to pass.—A MEMBER: Far from it.— Mr. CHALLONER thought they could manage without all this drilling.—Mr. BANCROFT said if there was anything wrong, he should be glad for anyone to draw his attention to it.—The subject then dropped. div.head: MEETING OF RUNCORN EATEPAYERS.
div.p: MEETING OF RUNCORN EATEPAYERS.

On Thursday evening, a ratepayer's meeting, called by the overseers, Messrs William Handley, and Wm. Whittaker, was held at the overseers' offices, Alcock-street, Runcorn, for the purpose of appointing three persons, being rate- payers of the township, to be members of the Burial Board in the place of Messrs Thomas Norman, James Handley, and George Marshall, who went out of office by rotation that day, but were eligible for re-election. Amongst those present were Messrs. Wm. Sutton' Wm. Hindley, James Curzon, John Crank, Wm. Pritchard, Samuel Burrow, Henry Cole- burn, J. R. Williamson, Thomas Riley, Joseph Ormson, Thomas Stringfellow, James Moores, Albeit Derbyshire, W. Rushton, Daniel Bisbrown, William Brown, William Dyer, Dr. McDougall, Wm. Littler and others.—The Chair- man said thst before the business of the meeting ,was really commenced he would state that Mr. Salkeld had very kindly placed the Public Hall at their disposal. He might state that would be the last meeting they would hold at the over- seers' office, as the Local Government Board had approved of the case entered into for renting Bethesda school room. The assembly decided to remain where they were.—The Chairman observed that it might be as well to state that the order of their proceedings would be settled by precedent. Upon a name being submitted to them, and approved of, the proposition would become final. Any ratepayer could move an amendment, and demand a poll, but unless this were done the matter wou'd be at an end.—Mr. W. Rushton proposed, and Mr. D. Bistr3wn seconded, that Mr. James Handley be re-elected for the ensuing three years. The motion was carried unanimously.-11 was moved by Mr. T. Riley, and seconded by Mr. Stringfellow, that Mr. George Moss be elected a member of the Burial Board.—The motion was carried nem dis.—On the proposition of Mr. Brazendale, seconded by Mr. Wm. Brown, Mr. Thomas Norman was re- elected a member of the Board.—The Chairman said that completed the business of the meeting.—On the motion of Dr. McDougall, a hearty vote of tlaanks was passed to Mr. Handley for presiding; and a cheer given to Mr. Salkeld for his offer of the Public Hall.—At the conclusion of the pro- ceedings, Mr. Curzon, a well-known orator at ratepayers' meetings, took the opportunity of delivering a graphic harangue to those assembled on the town's business, and the alleged gross mismanagement of the Commissioners in town's matters. He drew a most touching picture of the condition of the scavengers who had been so unceremo- niously discharged. He alleged that the real key to the dis- charge of the poor fellows might be found in the fact that since the Workmen's Liability Act had passed, there was a fear that some of the old men would be run over, and the Board of Commissioners would be proceeded against for heavy compensation. He indignantly maintained that there was no fear of this, as the old men were quite as " fause "as any commissioner, and knew too well how to keep out of the road of the carts to be in any danger of being killed. The speaker was received with enthusiastic applause, and after a little good natured chaff, the assernby dispersed.

A CLERGYMAN ATTACKED ON THE CHESHIRE LINES. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Friday, be- fore Captain Reynolds, Alderman Davies, and Mr. John White, Nicholas Cashennelli, described as an ice cream manufacturer, and residing at 26, Green-street, Manchester, was charged with being drunk in a railway carriage, on the Cheshire Lines Railway. He was also charged with vio- lently assaulting and unlawfully wounding the Rev. J. G. Holt, in a carriage on the line between Liverpool and War- rington. Mr. Slater (Messrs. Robert Davies & Co.) ap- peared for the prisoner. The prosecutor; said he was a clerk in holy orders at Cartnell, Lancashire, but was now coming into this district. On the previous evening he was coining from the Central Station, Liverpool, to Manchester, by the 9-30 express. He entered a third class carriage, and shortly afterwards the prisoner entered with a large parcel wrapped up in green cloth, which he placed on the seat opposite the prosecutor. Before the train started prisoner acted in a very disorderly manner, shouting to a person on the platform. Prosecutor did not like the looks of the man, and he told a porter he wished to change his carriage, but the porter said he could not do that then as the train was on the move. The train had just set in motion. Prisoner sat down in the diagonal corner to the prosecutor, and for a quarter of an hour after the starting of the train he remained quiet. He was drunk, but appeared capable of controlling his movements, and could carry the parcel. Prosecutor reclined in a recumbent position in his corner, as if to sleep, but did not do so. "At the expiration of the quarter of an hour, prisoner went over to his parcel, jostling against prosecutor as he went. He took hold of the parcel, which proved to be a barrel organ, and began to play a tune, standing with his back to presecutor, and causing him much inconvenience. He said, in a very mild way, "Come, my good fellow, I wish you would rest or let me rest." Priso- ner made no reply, but turned round and gave him three violent blows in quick succession—two behind the left ear and one on the eye. Prosecutor was just rising from his recumbent position when the prisoner attacked him. When he recovered himself after the blows be was at the other end of the carriage. He did not think prisoner had any in- strument. Captain Reynolds : But still there is a clear cut. Prosecutor thought that would be done by his spectacles, which he usually wore, and which were now missing, having probably been broken to pieces. The blows caused prosecutor to feel very faint, and a great deal of blood flowed from the cut on the eye down his face, hands, and coat. Prisoner was seated in the corner where the cord was, and he had no opportunity of getting to the commu- nicator. Captain Reynolds: Then you did think of using the communicator? Prosecutor said the first thing he thought of was to pull the communicator, but he could not get to it. Prosecutor (continuing) said prisoner then sat down in the corner which he had left, and he never said anything, or if he did prosecutor was in too great pain to take any notice. He also stopped turning the organ. Pro- secutor could not say exactly what took place afterwards, but prisoner did not assault him again. In five minutes after the assault the train-arrived at Warrington, and he called the guard and gave the prisoner in charge. Prose- cutor was taken out of tl e carriage and remained on the platform until the policeman took him to the Warrington Infirmary where his wounds were dressed. In answer to Mr. Slater, prosecutor said he did not give prisoner a push when he went between him and the organ to turn it. Captain Reynolds said it was a most serious case, and it would be unsafe for people to travel on railways if these things were allowed to go on. People were travelling every day and were liable to the treatment to which the clergyman had been subjected. Dr. Richmond, resident surgeon at the Infirmary, said the prosecutor was brought to the Infirmary late on the previous night suffering from a contused wound over the right eye about an inch long, a contused eye, and a small contusion over the left ear. The wound over the eye was not a clear cut, avid was one which might have been caused by a violent blow from a man's fist. He stitched the wound up. Mr. Slater said the case was undoubtedly one of a very serious nature. It was a case in a hundred, and might not occur again for the next fifty years. It was not a deliberate attack such as the Brighton case where a man was knocked on the head frem behind. Captain Reynolds said it was an unprovoked assault, and might occur often if an example was not made of the people who committed these acts. Mr. Slater said the man was so drunk that he did not know what he was doing. Alderman Davies observed that the prisoner was able to take care of himself and his organ. Mr. Hunt said it was very probable bail would be asked for the prisoner, and it was usual to remand the prisoner, to ascertain his character and antecedents. Nothing whatever was known of the prisoner.—Prisoner was remanded until Monday for the enquiries to be made. Mr. Slator said he understood then that it was certain that the prisoner would be committed to the sessions. Captain Reynolds remarked that if the case had been dealt with that day, no doubt prisoner would have been committed to the assizes, but another bench of magistrates would try the case on Monday. Mr. Slater: Don't you think it within your power to bring it into a common assault to-day. Captain Reynolds said he thought it was a very serious offence for a man to enter a railway carriage and be sub- jected to an aggravated assault. Though it might be due to drink, it would be little consolation to him if he could not defend himself.

PRESCOT UNION.—APPOINTIKENT of ASSISTANT OVER- SEERS for the Bold and Whiston Districts.—The Guar- dians of this Union will, at their meeting to be held on the 14th day of July next, proceed to the appointment of an Assistant Overseer for the Bold District, which comprises the townships of Bold, Crouton, and Ditton, at a salary of £4B per annum. They will also appoint an Assistant Overseer for the township of Whitton at a salary of £3O per annum. Bond will be required through a guarantee society for each district in the sum 01 £2OO. The persons appointed will be required to reside in their respective districts, to enter upon their duties (which are set forth in the General Consolidated and other Orders of the Local Government Board) forthwith. . The appointments will be made subject to the approval of the Local Government Board.
